docs.title: System Design, Deeply.
docs.text:
A complete, bilingual learning path for system design — built chapter-by-chapter around Alex Xu's System Design Interview – An Insider's Guide, then pushed further with deeper explanations, original diagrams, Java code, worked numbers, interactive widgets, and interview drills.

Every page exists in English and Hinglish — flip between them with the 🌐 switch in the header.

docs.title: What system design actually is
docs.text:
Writing code solves a problem for one request. System design solves it for millions of requests, all at once, while machines fail, networks slow down, and data keeps growing.

So a system design question is really four questions stacked on top of each other:

  1. What must the system do? (functional requirements — "users can shorten a URL")
  2. How well must it do it? (non-functional — latency, availability, consistency, cost)
  3. How big is it? (scale — users, requests per second, bytes stored)
  4. What breaks first, and what do we do about it? (bottlenecks, failures, trade-offs)

Every chapter on this site answers those four questions for one system or one component.

flowchart LR
    A[Vague problem<br/>'Design YouTube'] --> B[Clarify scope<br/>features + scale]
    B --> C[Estimate<br/>QPS, storage, bandwidth]
    C --> D[High-level design<br/>boxes + arrows]
    D --> E[Deep dive<br/>the 2-3 hard parts]
    E --> F[Trade-offs,<br/>failures, wrap-up]

docs.title: How to use this site
docs.text:
The 3-pass method

  1. Pass 1 — understand. Read the chapter top to bottom. Draw every diagram yourself on paper before looking at it closely. Play with the interactive widgets where they exist.
  2. Pass 2 — reproduce. Close the page. Set a 35-minute timer and design the system from scratch on a whiteboard or paper, talking out loud. Then compare with the chapter.
  3. Pass 3 — defend. Open the Interviewer follow-ups section and answer each question out loud before expanding the answer.

English or Hinglish? Both versions carry the same depth. Use whichever helps you think. A useful trick: read in Hinglish to build intuition, then re-read the English version so you can say it fluently in an interview.

docs.title: Suggested 4-week plan
docs.text:
Week Chapters Goal 1 01 Scale · 02 Estimation · 03 Framework Vocabulary + the method. You should be able to draw the "millions of users" architecture from memory and estimate QPS/storage in under 3 minutes. 2 04 Rate Limiter · 05 Consistent Hashing · 06 KV Store · 07 Unique IDs The building blocks. These show up inside every later design — don't rush them. 3 08 URL Shortener · 09 Crawler · 10 Notifications · 11 News Feed First four case studies. Do each one timed (pass 2) at least once. 4 12 Chat · 13 Autocomplete · 14 YouTube · 15 Google Drive · 16 Cheat Sheet Last four case studies + revision. End with two full mock interviews.

If you have only one week: do 01, 02, 03 fully, skim 05 and 06, then do 08, 11, 12 and 14 timed.

docs.title: The vocabulary you need on day one
docs.text:
You'll meet these words constantly. Each gets a proper explanation later, but here's the one-liner. The Glossary has 100+ more.

Term One-liner Latency How long one request takes (ms). Throughput / QPS How many requests the system handles per second. Availability Fraction of time the system is up and answering (99.9% = ~8.8 h downtime/year). Scalability Ability to handle more load by adding resources. Horizontal vs vertical scaling More machines vs a bigger machine. Replication Keeping copies of the same data on several machines. Sharding / partitioning Splitting data so each machine holds only a part. Cache A fast, small, temporary store that holds hot data to avoid slow work. Load balancer Spreads incoming requests across many servers. Message queue A buffer that lets producers and consumers work at different speeds. Consistency Whether every reader sees the latest write. Idempotency Doing the same operation twice has the same effect as doing it once.

docs.text: Code samples are in Java (the most common interview language). They're written to be readable and correct, not production-hardened — think of them as executable explanations.

This site is a companion to Alex Xu, System Design Interview – An Insider's Guide (2nd ed.). The chapter order follows the book. All prose, diagrams, code and examples here are original; nothing is copied from the book. Please buy it — it's worth it.

Begin Chapter 1

docs.title: 04 · Design a Rate Limiter
docs.text:
⏱ 50 min read 🔥 Very common standalone question + used inside every other design Book: Chapter 4

TL;DR

  • A rate limiter caps how many requests a client (user, IP, API key, device) can make in a time window; excess requests get HTTP 429 Too Many Requests.
  • Put it on the server side, usually as middleware / in the API gateway — never trust the client.
  • Five algorithms: token bucket (bursts OK, most popular), leaky bucket (smooth fixed outflow), fixed window (simple, but 2× burst at window edges), sliding log (exact, memory-hungry), sliding window counter (approximate, cheap — the usual best choice).
  • Store counters in Redis (in-memory, INCR + EXPIRE), and make check-and-update atomic with a Lua script to avoid race conditions.
  • Rules live in config files (cached by the limiter); tell clients their quota with X-RateLimit-* / Retry-After headers; fail open if the limiter itself breaks.

docs.title: The intuition: the metro turnstile
docs.text:
At a busy metro station, turnstiles let people through one at a time. When a train empties out, the staff close some gates so the platform doesn't overflow — people wait or take another route. Nobody inside the station is harmed by the crowd outside.

A rate limiter is that turnstile for your API. Examples of rules:

  • A user can post at most 2 times per second.
  • At most 5 sign-ups per hour from one IP address.
  • A device can claim a reward at most 5 times per week.
  • An OTP can be requested at most 3 times per 10 minutes per phone number.

docs.title: Why bother?
docs.text:
1. Stop resource starvation / DoS — accidental (a buggy client in a retry loop) or deliberate. Almost every public API (GitHub, Twitter/X, Google APIs, Stripe) enforces limits.
  2. Control cost — fewer servers; and crucially, protect calls to paid third-party APIs (credit checks, SMS, payments, LLM calls) that bill per request.
  3. Prevent overload — filter out bots and misbehaving users so legitimate traffic stays fast.
  4. Fairness — one heavy tenant shouldn't degrade everyone else in a multi-tenant system.

docs.title: Step 1 · Scope the problem
docs.text:
Clarifying conversation

You: Are we protecting our own HTTP APIs, or limiting calls we make to someone else? — Interviewer: Our own public APIs. You: What identifies a client — API key, user, IP? — I: All of those; different endpoints use different keys. You: Roughly how much traffic? — I: Peak of a few hundred thousand requests per second. You: One server or a fleet behind a load balancer? — I: A large fleet, in two regions. You: Strict limits, or is small overshoot OK? — I: Small overshoot is fine for most endpoints; login must be strict. You: Should clients learn their remaining quota? — I: Yes, return it in responses.

Requirements

Functional Non-functional Limit requests per configurable key (user, IP, API key, endpoint) Low latency — must not noticeably slow requests (< 1–2 ms added) Support many rules at once (per endpoint, per tier) Accurate — don't let a lot of excess through; don't block legit users Tell throttled clients clearly (429 + headers) Memory-efficient — millions of keys Distributed — shared across all API servers / processes Fault-tolerant — if the limiter's cache dies, the API keeps working

docs.title: Step 2 · Where does the rate limiter live?
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph A["Option 1 · client side"]
      c1[Client with limiter] --> s1[API servers]
    end
    subgraph B["Option 2 · inside each API server"]
      c2[Client] --> s2["API servers<br/>(limiter in code)"]
    end
    subgraph C["Option 3 · middleware / API gateway"]
      c3[Client] --> g["Rate limiter<br/>middleware / gateway"] --> s3[API servers]
    end
  • Client side — unreliable: anyone can modify or forge client requests, and you often don't control the client. (It's still polite for SDKs to self-throttle, but never rely on it.)
  • In the API server — full control, but every service re-implements it, and limits are per-process unless state is shared.
  • Middleware / API gateway — the common answer. Gateways (Kong, Envoy, NGINX, AWS API Gateway, Apigee) already do auth, TLS termination, IP allow-lists — rate limiting fits naturally.

Example: limit = 2 req/s. A client sends 3 requests in one second → the middleware forwards the first two and answers the third itself with 429 Too Many Requests.

How to decide — it's a judgement call, so say what would tip you either way:

  • Already running a gateway for auth/TLS? Then that's the natural home — one hop, one config.
  • Need an unusual algorithm or per-request cost weighting? Building it yourself (a library or sidecar) gives full control; off-the-shelf gateways support a fixed menu.
  • Hot-path cost — the check runs on every request, so it must be cheap in your runtime (a Redis round trip ≈ 0.5–1 ms in-DC).
  • Team size — a managed gateway is often the right call for a small team; building and operating your own is real work.

docs.title: The five algorithms
docs.text: Use the simulator to feel the most popular one before reading the theory:

docs.title: 1 · Token bucket
docs.text:
A bucket holds up to capacity tokens. A refiller adds tokens at a fixed refill rate; once the bucket is full, extra tokens overflow and are lost. Each request takes one token; if the bucket is empty, the request is rejected.

flowchart LR
    R["Refiller<br/>+r tokens/sec"] --> B[("Bucket<br/>capacity = C")]
    Q[Request] --> D{token available?}
    B --- D
    D -->|yes: take 1| OK[Forward to API]
    D -->|no| X[Drop → 429]

Worked trace — capacity 5, refill 1 token every 2 seconds (added at :02, :04, :06 …), bucket starts full at 10:00:00:

Time Event Tokens before Decision Tokens after 10:00:00 4 requests (page load) 5 ✅✅✅✅ 1 10:00:01 2 requests 1 ✅ ❌ 0 10:00:02 +1 refill, 1 request 0 → 1 ✅ 0 10:00:03 1 request 0 ❌ 429 0 10:00:12 +5 refills (capped at 5) 0 → 5 — 5 10:00:12 5 requests 5 ✅✅✅✅✅ 0

The burst at 10:00:00 sails through (that's the point of capacity), but the sustained rate can never exceed 1 request every 2 seconds.

You don't actually need a background "refiller". Store tokens and lastRefillTime, and refill lazily on each request based on elapsed time:

public final class TokenBucket {
    private final long capacity;
    private final double refillPerNano;     // tokens added per nanosecond
    private double tokens;
    private long lastRefill;

    public TokenBucket(long capacity, double tokensPerSecond) {
        this.capacity = capacity;
        this.refillPerNano = tokensPerSecond / 1_000_000_000.0;
        this.tokens = capacity;             // start full: allows an initial burst
        this.lastRefill = System.nanoTime();
    }

    public synchronized boolean tryAcquire() {
        long now = System.nanoTime();
        tokens = Math.min(capacity, tokens + (now - lastRefill) * refillPerNano);
        lastRefill = now;
        if (tokens >= 1) { tokens -= 1; return true; }
        return false;
    }
}

Parameters: bucket size (max burst) and refill rate (sustained rate).

How many buckets? One per (key, rule):

  • Per-endpoint rules: "1 post/sec, 150 friend-adds/day, 5 likes/sec" → 3 buckets per user.
  • Per-IP throttling → one bucket per IP.
  • A global cap ("10,000 req/s total") → one shared global bucket.
✅ Pros ❌ Cons Simple, memory-efficient (2 numbers per key) Two parameters that can be tricky to tune Allows short bursts (up to capacity) while enforcing an average rate Bursts may be unwanted when the downstream needs smooth load

Used by: AWS API Gateway, Stripe (among many others).

docs.title: 2 · Leaky bucket
docs.text:
Like a bucket with a hole: requests enter a FIFO queue of fixed size; a worker drains it at a fixed outflow rate. If the queue is full, new requests are dropped.

flowchart LR
    Q[Incoming requests] --> F{queue full?}
    F -->|no| QU[["FIFO queue (size N)"]]
    F -->|yes| X[Drop → 429]
    QU -->|"fixed rate: r req/sec"| P[Processor / API]

Parameters: bucket (queue) size and outflow rate.

✅ Pros ❌ Cons Memory-bounded (queue size) A burst fills the queue with old requests; newer ones get dropped even if they're more important Perfectly smooth output — great when downstream needs a stable rate (e.g. a payment provider that allows exactly 100 TPS) Adds queueing latency; two parameters to tune

Used by: Shopify's API (leaky-bucket style). Also the classic traffic-shaping algorithm in networking.

Token vs leaky bucket in one line

Token bucket limits the average rate and permits bursts. Leaky bucket enforces a constant output rate and absorbs bursts in a queue.

docs.title: 3 · Fixed window counter
docs.text:
Split time into fixed windows (e.g. each calendar second or minute). Keep a counter per window; each request increments it; once it hits the limit, reject until the next window starts.

// Redis-style: key = "rl:{user}:{epochMinute}"
long window = System.currentTimeMillis() / 60_000;
String key = "rl:" + userId + ":" + window;
long count = redis.incr(key);
if (count == 1) redis.expire(key, 60);   // first hit in this window sets the TTL
boolean allowed = count <= LIMIT;

The edge problem. Limit = 100 per minute, windows start on round minutes. A script fires 100 requests between 9:14:50 and 9:14:59, then 100 more between 9:15:00 and 9:15:09. Each window sees exactly 100 — all allowed. But in the 20 seconds around the boundary, 200 requests got through: double the per-minute limit.

9:14:00 9:15:00 9:16:00 window 1: 100 req ✓ window 2: 100 req ✓ 20 s around the boundary → 200 requests (2× the per-minute limit)

Bursts on both sides of a window boundary let twice the limit through. ✅ Pros ❌ Cons Very memory-efficient (1 counter per key) Up to 2× the limit at window edges Easy to understand and implement Synchronised resets: everyone's quota resets at the same instant → thundering herd Quota resetting on round time units fits some products ("1,000 calls per day")

docs.title: 4 · Sliding window log
docs.text:
Fixes the edge problem exactly. Keep a log of request timestamps per key (e.g. a Redis sorted set, score = timestamp). On each request:

  1. Remove timestamps older than now − window.
  2. Add the new request's timestamp.
  3. If the log size ≤ limit → allow; else reject.

Trace — limit 3 requests per 10 seconds (log stores every request, accepted or not):

Arrives Log after cleanup + insert Size Decision 12:00:01 [:01] 1 ✅ 12:00:03 [:01, :03] 2 ✅ 12:00:04 [:01, :03, :04] 3 ✅ 12:00:07 [:01, :03, :04, :07] 4 ❌ (timestamp still stored) 12:00:12 window is (12:00:02, 12:00:12] → drop :01 → [:03, :04, :07, :12] 4 ❌ 12:00:15 drop :03, :04 → [:07, :12, :15] 3 ✅ 
public boolean allow(String key, long nowMs) {
    Deque<Long> log = logs.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ArrayDeque<>());
    synchronized (log) {
        while (!log.isEmpty() && log.peekFirst() <= nowMs - WINDOW_MS) log.pollFirst();
        log.addLast(nowMs);                 // book's variant: rejected requests are logged too
        return log.size() <= LIMIT;
    }
}

A design choice hidden in step 2

The variant above logs rejected requests too — so a client that keeps hammering stays blocked (it's punished for retrying). Many implementations only log accepted requests, which lets a client back in as soon as old requests expire. Mention which one you're choosing.

✅ Pros ❌ Cons Exact — no rolling window ever exceeds the limit Memory-hungry: one entry per request (100 req/min limit × 1M users = 100M timestamps) Cleanup work on every request

docs.title: 5 · Sliding window counter (the hybrid)
docs.text:
Keep just two fixed-window counters — current and previous — and estimate the rolling count by assuming the previous window's requests were spread evenly:

estimated = current_count + previous_count × (overlap of rolling window with previous window)

Example: limit 10/min. The previous minute had 8 requests; the current minute has 4 so far. A new request arrives 40% into the current minute → the rolling window still overlaps the last 60% of the previous minute.

estimated = 4 + 8 × 0.6 = 8.8 → 8.8 < 10 → allow (current becomes 5). Two more requests at the same moment would push the estimate to 10.8 → the second one is rejected. (Whether you compare the raw estimate or round it up/down is a policy choice — rounding down is slightly more permissive.)

previous minute: 8 requests current minute: 4 so far rolling 1-minute window 60% of previous 40% into current now

estimate = 4 + 8 × 0.6 = 8.8 requests in the last minute. 
public synchronized boolean allow(String key, long nowMs) {
    long window = nowMs / WINDOW_MS;
    double elapsedFraction = (nowMs % WINDOW_MS) / (double) WINDOW_MS;
    long curr = counters.getOrDefault(key + ":" + window, 0L);
    long prev = counters.getOrDefault(key + ":" + (window - 1), 0L);
    double estimated = curr + prev * (1.0 - elapsedFraction);
    if (estimated >= LIMIT) return false;
    counters.merge(key + ":" + window, 1L, Long::sum);  // (old windows expire via TTL in Redis)
    return true;
}
✅ Pros ❌ Cons Smooths edge spikes (uses the previous window's average) Approximate — assumes the previous window was uniform Memory-efficient — 2 counters per key Not suitable when the limit must be strict to the request

How bad is the approximation in practice? Cloudflare measured it on 400 million requests: only 0.003% were wrongly allowed or rate-limited. That's why it's often the best default.

docs.title: Algorithm comparison
docs.text: Algorithm Memory / key Accuracy Bursts Best when Token bucket O(1) — tokens + timestamp Good ✅ allows up to capacity General APIs; bursts are fine Leaky bucket O(queue size) Good ❌ smoothed into queue Downstream needs constant rate Fixed window O(1) — 1 counter ❌ 2× at edges ⚠ edge bursts Simple quotas ("1,000/day") Sliding log O(limit) timestamps ✅ exact ❌ Low limits needing exactness (OTP, login attempts) Sliding window counter O(1) — 2 counters ≈ (99.997%) Smoothed High-volume APIs — the usual best pick

docs.title: High-level architecture
docs.text:
All algorithms need the same primitive: a fast shared counter per key with expiry. A database is too slow (disk). An in-memory store like Redis is ideal: it's fast and supports time-based expiry.

  • INCR key — atomically increment a counter (creates it at 1 if missing).
  • EXPIRE key seconds — auto-delete the key after a timeout.
flowchart LR
    C[Client] --> M{{Rate limiter<br/>middleware}}
    M <-->|"fetch / increment counter"| R[(Redis)]
    M -->|under limit| API[API servers]
    M -->|over limit| X["429 Too Many Requests"]
  1. The client sends a request to the rate-limiter middleware.
  2. The middleware fetches the counter for the right bucket from Redis and checks the limit.
  3. Over the limit → reject (429). Under → forward to the API servers and increment the counter.

docs.title: Rules: where they live and what they look like
docs.text:
Rules are usually written in config files (YAML) and stored on disk / in a config service. Here's an illustrative format, similar in spirit to the descriptor-based config used by Envoy's open-source rate-limit service:

domain: public_api
descriptors:
  - key: plan
    value: free
    rate_limit: { unit: minute, requests_per_unit: 60 }     # free tier: 60 calls/min per API key
  - key: plan
    value: pro
    rate_limit: { unit: minute, requests_per_unit: 1000 }   # paid tier
---
domain: otp
descriptors:
  - key: phone_number
    rate_limit: { unit: hour, requests_per_unit: 5 }        # at most 5 OTP sends per phone per hour

Workers periodically pull rules from disk/config service and keep them in a local cache inside the rate limiter, so rule lookup costs nothing on the hot path.

docs.title: Telling clients they're throttled
docs.text:
Return HTTP 429 Too Many Requests with headers so well-behaved clients can back off:

Header Meaning X-RateLimit-Limit How many calls the client may make per window X-RateLimit-Remaining How many are left in the current window X-RateLimit-Retry-After (or standard Retry-After) Seconds to wait before retrying

(There's an IETF draft standardising these as RateLimit-Limit, RateLimit-Remaining, RateLimit-Reset.)

Throttled requests can be dropped, or enqueued for later processing (e.g. orders throttled during a spike shouldn't just vanish).

docs.title: The detailed design
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph CFG[Rules]
      D[(Rules on disk /<br/>config service)] --> WK[Workers] --> RC[(Rules cache)]
    end
    C[Client] --> RL{{Rate limiter middleware}}
    RC --> RL
    RL <--> RD[("Redis<br/>counters + timestamps")]
    RL -->|allowed| API[API servers]
    RL -->|"rejected: 429 + headers"| C
    RL -.->|"option: enqueue throttled"| MQ[[Message queue]]

docs.title: Problem 1 — race conditions
docs.text:
Two API servers handle requests from the same user at the same instant. Limit = 4, counter = 3.

Server A: GET counter → 3          Server B: GET counter → 3
Server A: 3 < 4 → allow, SET 4     Server B: 3 < 4 → allow, SET 4
Result: 5 requests allowed, counter says 4.  ❌

The read-check-write isn't atomic. Fixes:

  • Locks — correct but slow; a distributed lock on every request kills latency.
  • Atomic operations — INCR then check (INCR returns the new value atomically).
  • Lua scripts in Redis — Redis runs a script atomically, so the whole read-modify-write happens as one step.
  • Redis sorted sets (for the sliding log) inside a MULTI/Lua block.

A token-bucket check as one atomic Lua script:

-- KEYS[1] = bucket key ; ARGV = capacity, refill_per_sec, now_ms, cost
local cap    = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local rate   = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local now    = tonumber(ARGV[3])
local cost   = tonumber(ARGV[4])
local b      = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens = tonumber(b[1]) or cap
local ts     = tonumber(b[2]) or now
tokens = math.min(cap, tokens + (now - ts) / 1000 * rate)   -- lazy refill
local allowed = 0
if tokens >= cost then tokens = tokens - cost; allowed = 1 end
redis.call('HMSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', now)
redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], math.ceil(cap / rate * 1000) * 2)
return { allowed, math.floor(tokens) }

Called from Java with Jedis/Lettuce via EVALSHA (the script is loaded once and referenced by its SHA).

docs.title: Problem 2 — synchronisation across many limiters
docs.text:
You'll run many rate-limiter instances. With stateless web tiers, consecutive requests from one client can hit different limiter instances. If each kept counters in local memory, the client would get N× its limit.

  • Sticky sessions (always route a client to the same limiter) — works but isn't scalable or flexible. Avoid.
  • Centralised data store (Redis) — all instances share the same counters. ✅ The standard answer.

docs.title: Problem 3 — performance
docs.text:
• Multi-data-center / edge: latency to a far-away Redis is high for distant users. Put rate limiters at edge locations close to users (Cloudflare runs limiting across hundreds of edge servers) and route traffic to the nearest.
  • Eventual consistency between DCs: sync counters asynchronously across regions; a tiny over-allowance during sync is an acceptable trade for low latency.
  • Local pre-check: keep a small local token bucket per instance that absorbs most decisions and periodically reconciles with Redis — fewer network round-trips at the cost of slight inaccuracy.

docs.title: Problem 4 — monitoring
docs.text:
Collect metrics to check that the limiter is effective:

  • Is the algorithm right? If you see bursty flash-sale traffic being dropped heavily, token bucket (which tolerates bursts) may suit better than a strict window.
  • Are the rules right? If many legitimate requests get 429s, the rules are too strict — relax them.
  • Track: allowed vs throttled per rule, p99 added latency, Redis errors, top throttled keys (abuse detection).

docs.title: Failure mode: fail open or fail closed?
docs.text: If Redis is unreachable, should requests be allowed (fail open) or blocked (fail closed)? For most APIs: fail open — availability matters more than perfect limiting, and the requirement said a limiter failure must not take down the system. For security-critical limits (login attempts, OTP sends) consider fail closed or a conservative local fallback limiter.

docs.title: Step 4 · Wrap up — extra topics
docs.text:
• Hard vs soft limits. Hard: never exceed the threshold. Soft: may exceed briefly (useful for bursty but benign traffic).
  • Limiting at other layers. We built a Layer-7 (HTTP) limiter. You can also limit at Layer 3 by IP with iptables/firewalls — cheap, but coarse (can't see users or endpoints). OSI layers: physical, data link, network (3), transport (4), session, presentation, application (7).
  • Client best practices to avoid being limited:
    • Cache responses to avoid repeat calls.
    • Understand the limits and don't send bursts in a short time.
    • Catch 429s/errors and recover gracefully.
    • Retry with exponential backoff + jitter, respecting Retry-After.
  • Tiered limits — free vs paid plans with different buckets; per-tenant fairness in SaaS.

docs.title: Interviewer follow-ups
docs.text:
Token bucket or sliding window counter for a public REST API? Justify.

For a general public API I'd pick token bucket if I want to allow short legitimate bursts (page loads fire many calls) with O(1) memory, or sliding window counter if I want a smoother "N per minute" semantic without edge spikes. Both are O(1) per key and easy to implement atomically in Redis. I'd avoid fixed window (edge bursts) and sliding log (memory) unless the limit is tiny and must be exact (login attempts).

Your Redis cluster handling counters goes down. What happens?

The limiter should fail open: catch the error/timeout quickly (tight client timeout ~5–10 ms), allow the request, emit a metric and alert. Optionally fall back to a per-instance in-memory limiter with conservative limits so abusive clients are still somewhat constrained. Run Redis with replicas + automatic failover (Sentinel/Cluster) to make this rare.

How do you rate-limit across 3 regions with 1 global quota per user?

Options: (1) route each user to a home region that owns their counter (simple, accurate); (2) each region keeps a local counter and asynchronously syncs — allow a small over-limit during sync lag; (3) split the quota between regions (e.g. by recent traffic share) and rebalance periodically. Strict global accuracy would need a cross-region round trip per request — too slow — so we accept approximate enforcement.

How much memory do counters need for 10M users and 3 rules each?

Sliding window counter: 2 counters per (user, rule). Key ~40 bytes + value 8 bytes + Redis overhead ~50 bytes ≈ 100 B per counter → 10M × 3 × 2 × 100 B = 6 GB — fits easily on a small Redis cluster. A sliding log with limit 100 would need up to 100 entries per key → ~100× more (hundreds of GB).

Where should the user ID come from if the limiter runs before auth?

Either run limiting after authentication in the gateway (so it can read the verified user/API key), or use layered limits: a coarse per-IP limit before auth (protects the auth service itself from credential stuffing), then per-user / per-key limits after auth.

Should rejected requests count against the client?

It's a policy choice. Counting them (as in the sliding-log variant) punishes clients that ignore 429s and keep hammering. Not counting them is friendlier for clients that retry correctly. For abuse-sensitive endpoints, count them; for normal APIs, usually don't — and publish Retry-After so good clients wait.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
Avoid these

  • Putting the limiter only on the client.
  • Using a relational database for counters (disk latency on every request).
  • Get-then-set without atomicity → race conditions let extra requests through.
  • Per-instance in-memory counters behind a load balancer → each client gets N× the limit.
  • Forgetting to say what happens when the limiter itself fails.
  • Returning 500/403 instead of 429 + retry information.

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
Practice 1 — Trace the token bucket

Capacity 3, refill 1 token/second, starts full at t=0. Requests arrive at t = 0, 0, 0, 0, 0.5, 1.2, 1.3, 3.0. Which are allowed?

Solution. t=0: tokens 3 → allow (2), allow (1), allow (0), reject (0). t=0.5: tokens 0.5 → reject. t=1.2: tokens 1.2 → allow (0.2). t=1.3: tokens 0.3 → reject. t=3.0: tokens 0.3 + 1.7 = 2.0 → allow (1.0). Allowed: 5 of 8.

Practice 2 — Sliding window counter

Limit 100/min. Previous minute: 84 requests. Current minute: 36 requests so far. A request arrives 25% into the current minute. Allow or reject?

Solution. Overlap with previous = 75%. Estimate = 36 + 84 × 0.75 = 36 + 63 = 99 < 100 → allow (count becomes 37). The next request at the same moment would estimate 100 → reject.

Practice 3 — Design an OTP limiter

Requirements: max 3 OTP requests per phone per 10 minutes, max 10 per phone per day, and max 100 per IP per hour. Which algorithm(s) and data structures?

Solution. Low limits that must be exact → sliding window log in Redis sorted sets for the 10-minute rule (ZREMRANGEBYSCORE, ZADD, ZCARD in one Lua script). Daily rule → fixed window counter keyed by phone:yyyy-mm-dd (calendar-day semantics are fine). IP rule → sliding window counter. Check all three atomically; reject if any fails; fail closed if Redis is down (SMS costs money and is an abuse target).

Practice 4 — Leaky bucket sizing

A downstream payment gateway allows exactly 50 TPS. Your checkout traffic peaks at 200 TPS for ~20 seconds during flash sales. Design the limiter.

Solution. A leaky bucket draining at 50/s in front of the gateway. A 20 s spike at 200/s brings 4,000 requests of which 1,000 drain during the spike → queue needs ~3,000 slots to avoid drops, and the last request waits ~60 s. That's too long for a synchronous checkout → accept the order, enqueue the payment, return "processing", and notify on completion; or add a waiting-room in front of the sale.

docs.title: Revision checklist
docs.text:
• I can explain why rate limiting is needed (DoS, cost, overload, fairness).
  • I can compare client-side, in-server and gateway placement.
  • I can explain all five algorithms with a trace, pros/cons, and when to use each.
  • I can show the fixed-window edge problem with numbers and compute a sliding-window-counter estimate.
  • I can draw the architecture with Redis, rules cache and 429 responses with headers.
  • I can explain the race condition and fix it with atomic ops / Lua.
  • I know how to sync limiters across instances and data centers, and fail-open vs fail-closed.

Next: 05 · Consistent Hashing

docs.title: 05 · Design Consistent Hashing
docs.text:
⏱ 35 min read 🔥 Shows up inside caches, KV stores, sharding, load balancers Book: Chapter 5

TL;DR

  • server = hash(key) % N spreads keys evenly — until N changes. Then almost every key maps to a different server → cache-miss storm / massive data movement.
  • Consistent hashing places servers and keys on a ring (the hash space bent into a circle). A key belongs to the first server clockwise from it.
  • Adding or removing a server only moves the keys in one arc of the ring — on average k/n keys (k keys, n servers), not ~all of them.
  • Plain rings give uneven arcs. Fix: virtual nodes — each server appears at 100–200 points on the ring, so load evens out (std-dev drops to ~5–10%).
  • Implement with a sorted map (TreeMap.ceilingEntry) → O(log V) lookup. Used by Dynamo, Cassandra, Riak, Discord, Akamai, Envoy/Maglev-style LBs.

docs.title: The intuition: assigning students to exam halls
docs.text:
A college assigns students to exam halls by roll_number % number_of_halls. Works fine — until one hall's AC breaks on exam morning. Now it's % 3 instead of % 4, and almost every student is sent to a different hall, not just the ones from the broken hall. Chaos at every door.

A smarter rule: arrange halls around a circular corridor; each student walks clockwise from their "seat number" position and enters the first open hall. If one hall closes, only its students walk a bit further to the next hall. Everyone else is unaffected. That's consistent hashing.

docs.title: The rehashing problem
docs.text:
With N cache servers, the obvious way to pick a server is:

serverIndex = hash(key) % N

Let's use 4 servers and 8 keys. (Pretend hash() returns these small numbers so the maths is easy.)

Key hash hash % 4 Server (N = 4) user:alpha 10 2 S2 user:bravo 21 1 S1 user:charlie 32 0 S0 user:delta 43 3 S3 user:echo 54 2 S2 user:foxtrot 65 1 S1 user:golf 76 0 S0 user:hotel 87 3 S3

Each server holds exactly 2 keys — beautiful. Now S1 crashes. The pool is [S0, S2, S3], so we use % 3:

Key hash % 3 New server Moved? user:alpha 1 S2 — stays user:bravo 0 S0 ✔ (had to — S1 died) user:charlie 2 S3 ✔ moved for no reason user:delta 1 S2 ✔ moved for no reason user:echo 0 S0 ✔ moved for no reason user:foxtrot 2 S3 ✔ (had to — S1 died) user:golf 1 S2 ✔ moved for no reason user:hotel 0 S0 ✔ moved for no reason

7 of 8 keys moved, although only 2 lived on the dead server. For a cache, that means a sudden storm of cache misses that hammers the database. For a sharded database, it means moving most of the data. In general, going from N to N±1 servers relocates about N/(N+1) of all keys — nearly everything.

docs.title: Consistent hashing
docs.text: Consistent hashing is a hashing scheme where, when the number of slots changes, only about k/n keys need to move on average (k = keys, n = slots), instead of nearly all of them.

docs.title: Step 1 · The hash space becomes a ring
docs.text: Pick a hash function with a big output range — e.g. SHA-1 outputs 0 … 2¹⁶⁰ − 1 (in practice systems use fast non-cryptographic hashes like MurmurHash or xxHash with a 32/64-bit range). Bend that range into a circle, so the largest value is followed by 0. That's the hash ring.

docs.title: Step 2 · Place servers on the ring
docs.text: Hash each server's name or IP with the same hash function, and put it at that point on the ring.

docs.title: Step 3 · Place keys on the ring
docs.text: Hash each key onto the same ring. Note: there's no % N any more.

docs.title: Step 4 · Lookup — walk clockwise
docs.text:
A key is stored on the first server you meet walking clockwise from the key's position.

S0 S1 S2 S3 k0 k1 k2 k3 walk clockwise → first server owns the key

Each key (orange) is owned by the first server (teal) clockwise from it: k0→S0, k1→S1, k2→S2, k3→S3.

docs.title: Adding a server
docs.text:
Add S4 on the ring between k0 and S0. Walking clockwise from k0, the first server is now S4, so only k0 moves (from S0 to S4). k1, k2 and k3 don't move at all.

Which keys move? Exactly those in the arc between S4 and the previous server going anticlockwise (S3). Those keys used to belong to S0; now S4 takes them.

docs.title: Removing a server
docs.text:
Remove S1. Only the keys in the arc between S0 (anticlockwise neighbour) and S1 — here k1 — move, and they move to the next server clockwise (S2). Everyone else stays put.

flowchart TB
    subgraph B1["Before"]
      direction LR
      a1["S0 arc"] --- b1["S1 arc · holds k1"] --- c1["S2 arc"]
    end
    subgraph A1["After S1 is removed"]
      direction LR
      a2["S0 arc"] --- c2["S2 arc · now also holds k1"]
    end
    B1 -->|"only S1's arc changes owner"| A1

Try it yourself — add and remove servers, and compare how many keys move versus hash % N:

What to notice in the widget

With 1 virtual node per server, the load bars are wildly uneven and "max/avg" is often 2× or worse. Slide virtual nodes up to 50+ and watch the spread collapse towards 1.1×. Then add a server: consistent hashing moves roughly 1/(N+1) of the keys; hash % N moves most of them.

docs.title: Two problems with the basic ring
docs.text:
1. Uneven partitions. Servers land at random points, so the arcs between them have random sizes. One server may own 40% of the ring while another owns 5%. And when a server is removed, its whole arc goes to one neighbour, which suddenly carries double load.
  2. Non-uniform key distribution. Even with equal arcs, real keys can cluster (hot ranges), piling onto one server.

docs.title: Virtual nodes (vnodes)
docs.text:
Instead of placing each physical server once, place it many times — e.g. S0#0, S0#1, … S0#199 — each a virtual node that maps back to the physical server S0.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Ring["Ring positions (clockwise)"]
      direction LR
      a["S0 · v3"] --> b["S2 · v7"] --> c["S1 · v0"] --> d["S0 · v9"] --> e["S2 · v1"] --> f["S1 · v5"] --> g["S0 · v4"] --> h["S1 · v2"] --> i["S2 · v4"]
    end

Why it works:

  • Each server now owns many small arcs scattered around the ring, so its total share averages out. With ~100 vnodes per server, the standard deviation of load is roughly 10% of the mean; with ~200, about 5%.
  • When a server leaves, its many small arcs are absorbed by many different neighbours — the load spreads instead of dumping on one server.
  • Heterogeneous hardware: give a big server 300 vnodes and a small one 100 → it gets ~3× the keys.

The cost: more ring entries to store (metadata) and slightly more work when membership changes. With a sorted structure that's trivial — 100 servers × 200 vnodes = 20,000 entries.

docs.title: Implementation in Java
docs.text:
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.security.MessageDigest;
import java.util.*;

public final class ConsistentHashRing<N> {
    private final NavigableMap<Long, N> ring = new TreeMap<>();
    private final int virtualNodes;

    public ConsistentHashRing(int virtualNodes) { this.virtualNodes = virtualNodes; }

    public synchronized void addNode(N node) {
        for (int i = 0; i < virtualNodes; i++) ring.put(hash(node + "#" + i), node);
    }

    public synchronized void removeNode(N node) {
        for (int i = 0; i < virtualNodes; i++) ring.remove(hash(node + "#" + i));
    }

    /** First node clockwise from the key's position (wraps around at the end). */
    public synchronized N nodeFor(String key) {
        if (ring.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalStateException("no nodes");
        Map.Entry<Long, N> e = ring.ceilingEntry(hash(key));
        return (e != null ? e : ring.firstEntry()).getValue();
    }

    /** N distinct physical nodes clockwise — the replica "preference list" (Chapter 6). */
    public synchronized List<N> nodesFor(String key, int replicas) {
        LinkedHashSet<N> out = new LinkedHashSet<>();
        for (N n : ring.tailMap(hash(key), true).values()) { out.add(n); if (out.size() == replicas) return new ArrayList<>(out); }
        for (N n : ring.values())                           { out.add(n); if (out.size() == replicas) break; }
        return new ArrayList<>(out);
    }

    private static long hash(String s) {
        try {
            byte[] d = MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5").digest(s.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
            long h = 0;
            for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) h = (h << 8) | (d[i] & 0xff);   // first 64 bits
            return h;
        } catch (Exception e) { throw new RuntimeException(e); }
    }
}
  • Lookup is ceilingEntry on a red-black tree → O(log V) where V = total virtual nodes.
  • MD5 is used here only because it's in the JDK; production systems use MurmurHash3 / xxHash (much faster, non-cryptographic).
  • Every client (or the router) must see the same ring. Membership is usually spread with gossip or kept in a coordination service like ZooKeeper/etcd (Chapter 6).

docs.title: Going deeper: alternatives you can mention
docs.text: Technique Idea Why/when Rendezvous (HRW) hashing For each key, compute score = hash(key, server) for every server; pick the highest No ring or vnodes; perfectly even; O(N) per lookup — fine for tens of servers Jump consistent hash (Google) A tiny arithmetic function maps key → bucket 0..N−1 with minimal movement O(ln N), no memory — but buckets can only be added/removed at the end (great for numbered shards, bad for arbitrary node failures) Maglev hashing (Google LB) Builds a fixed-size lookup table with near-perfect balance Very fast lookups for load balancers; small disruption on changes Consistent hashing with bounded loads Cap each server at (1+ε) × average; overflow goes to the next server Prevents hotspots — used in some proxies/caches (e.g. HAProxy option, Vimeo)

docs.title: Where it's used in the real world
docs.text:
• Partitioning in Dynamo-style databases — Amazon Dynamo, Apache Cassandra, Riak (Chapter 6 builds on this).
  • Discord — routing chat traffic for a guild/channel to the right server.
  • Akamai — the original 1997 paper was about distributing web caches across CDN servers.
  • Load balancers / proxies — Envoy's ring-hash and Maglev load-balancing policies, NGINX hash … consistent.
  • Distributed caches — Memcached client libraries (ketama), Redis client-side sharding.

docs.title: Interviewer follow-ups
docs.text:
Exactly which keys move when a server is added?

Only keys whose position lies in the arc between the new server and the previous server anticlockwise. They move from the new server's clockwise successor onto the new server. With vnodes, that's many small arcs — one per new vnode — each taking keys from a different successor, so the load is drawn evenly from the existing servers.

How many virtual nodes should I use?

Enough to bring load imbalance within your tolerance — typically 100–256 per server. More vnodes = better balance but more metadata and more ring entries to update on membership changes. Cassandra historically defaulted to 256 tokens per node, later recommending fewer (e.g. 16) combined with a smarter token-allocation algorithm.

Consistent hashing gives an even spread of keys — does that guarantee even load?

No. It balances key count, not traffic. A single hot key (a celebrity profile, a viral video) still lands on one server. Mitigations: cache hot keys in front, replicate hot keys to several servers and spread reads, split the key (key#1..#n), or use bounded-load consistent hashing.

How do clients know the current ring?

Either (1) a router/proxy tier owns the ring and clients talk to it; or (2) every node holds the ring and membership changes propagate via gossip; or (3) a coordination service (ZooKeeper/etcd) stores membership and clients watch it. Brief disagreement during changes is tolerated — a node receiving a key it doesn't own forwards it.

Why not just use hash % N and re-shard offline?

For a cache, re-sharding means a miss storm that can take down the database. For a database, it means moving ~100% of the data, during which you need double-reads or downtime. Consistent hashing makes membership changes cheap and incremental, which matters when nodes fail routinely at scale.

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
Practice 1 — Movement fraction

You have 9 cache servers with consistent hashing (many vnodes) and 90 million keys. You add a 10th server. Roughly how many keys move? What if you were using hash % N?

Solution. Consistent hashing: the new server takes ~1/10 of the ring → ~9M keys move. hash % N: a key stays only if h % 9 == h % 10, which happens for ~1/10 of keys → ~81M keys move (90%).

Practice 2 — Weighted servers

You have three servers with 64 GB, 64 GB and 128 GB RAM. How do you make the 128 GB server hold twice the keys?

Solution. Give it twice as many virtual nodes (e.g. 200, 200, 400). Its share of the ring ≈ 400/800 = 50%, the others 25% each.

Practice 3 — Trace a lookup

Ring positions (0–99): S_A at 15, S_B at 40, S_C at 72. Keys hash to 5, 16, 40, 41, 80, 99. Who owns each? Then S_B is removed — who owns them now?

Solution. Clockwise to the first server ≥ key (wrapping): 5→S_A, 16→S_B, 40→S_B (equal counts as owner), 41→S_C, 80→S_A (wraps), 99→S_A. After removing S_B: 16→S_C, 40→S_C; all others unchanged. Only S_B's 2 keys moved.

docs.title: Revision checklist
docs.text:
• I can show with numbers why hash % N relocates most keys when N changes.
  • I can explain the ring, clockwise lookup, and exactly which keys move on add/remove.
  • I can explain the two problems of the basic ring and how virtual nodes fix them (incl. weighting).
  • I can implement the ring with a TreeMap and get N replicas from it.
  • I know that even key spread ≠ even traffic, and how to handle hot keys.
  • I can name real systems using it and at least two alternatives (rendezvous, jump hash).

Next: 06 · Key-Value Store

docs.title: 06 · Design a Key-Value Store
docs.text:
⏱ 60 min read 🔥 The densest chapter — distributed-systems core Book: Chapter 6

TL;DR

  • A key-value store is a giant Map<key, value> with put(key, value) and get(key). One machine is easy; the challenge is spreading it over hundreds of machines that fail.
  • CAP: during a network partition you must choose consistency (CP — refuse some requests) or availability (AP — answer, maybe stale). Dynamo/Cassandra choose AP + eventual consistency.
  • Partition with consistent hashing (+ vnodes), replicate each key to the next N distinct servers on the ring, and tune consistency with quorums: W + R > N ⇒ reads see the latest write.
  • Detect conflicts with vector clocks; detect failures with gossip; survive temporary failures with sloppy quorum + hinted handoff; repair permanent divergence with Merkle trees.
  • Storage engine: commit log → memtable → SSTables (LSM tree). Reads check memtable, then a Bloom filter per SSTable to skip files that can't contain the key.

docs.title: The intuition: a library with many branches
docs.text:
Imagine a city library system storing millions of books across 50 branches.

  • Which branch holds which book? A rule based on the book's ID → partitioning.
  • What if a branch floods? Keep copies of each book in 3 nearby branches → replication.
  • Two branches update the same book's catalog card differently while their phone line is down? You need a way to notice the conflict and merge → versioning / vector clocks.
  • How do branches know another branch is closed? They chat with a few neighbours every few minutes and pass the news along → gossip.
  • A branch is closed for a day — where do new returns go? A neighbour holds them temporarily and hands them back later → hinted handoff.
  • After a long outage, how do two branches find which cards differ without comparing all million? Compare summaries of shelves, then only the shelves that differ → Merkle trees.

docs.title: Step 1 · Scope
docs.text:
A KV store (also called a key-value database) stores unique keys mapped to values. Keys can be plain text ("user:42:profile") or hashed; values are opaque blobs — strings, lists, JSON — the store doesn't care. Well-known examples: Amazon DynamoDB, Redis, Memcached, Apache Cassandra, etcd, RocksDB (embedded).

API:

void put(String key, byte[] value);
byte[] get(String key);

Requirements we'll design for (every design is a set of trade-offs — these are ours):

Requirement Target (our assumptions) Value size Typically ≤ 1 KB, hard cap 64 KB (big blobs belong in object storage) Total data Hundreds of TB, growing — far beyond one machine Availability Reads and writes keep working while individual nodes or a rack are down Durability An acknowledged write is never lost Elasticity Add or remove nodes without downtime; data rebalances itself Consistency Per-request tunable — eventual by default, stronger when the caller asks Latency p99 under ~10 ms inside a region

docs.title: Single-server key-value store
docs.text:
Easy: an in-memory hash table. Two tricks extend it:

  • Compress values.
  • Keep only hot data in memory, the rest on disk.

But a single server runs out of memory and disk eventually, and it's a single point of failure. We need a distributed key-value store (a distributed hash table).

docs.title: CAP theorem
docs.text:
A distributed system can't simultaneously guarantee all three of:

  • Consistency (C) — a read from any node returns the most recent write — all clients agree on the current value.
  • Availability (A) — every request gets a (non-error) response, even if some nodes are down.
  • Partition tolerance (P) — the system keeps working despite network partitions (lost/delayed messages between nodes).
flowchart TB
    subgraph CAP
      C((Consistency)) --- A((Availability))
      A --- P((Partition<br/>tolerance))
      P --- C
    end
    CP["CP: e.g. HBase, MongoDB (default), etcd/ZooKeeper"] -.-> C
    AP["AP: e.g. Cassandra, DynamoDB-style, CouchDB"] -.-> A
    CA["CA: only without partitions —<br/>not a real option for distributed systems"] -.-> P

The key insight: in a distributed system, network partitions will happen (switches fail, cables get cut, GC pauses look like partitions). So "P" isn't optional. The real choice is what to do during a partition:

docs.title: A worked scenario
docs.text:
Three replicas n1, n2, n3 hold the key stock:item-77 = 10. The network splits: n3 can no longer talk to n1/n2.

  • A client writes stock:item-77 = 9 to n1. n1 replicates to n2 — but can't reach n3.
  • Another client reads from n3.
Choice What happens Good for CP n3 (and possibly the minority side) refuses reads/writes it can't confirm are up to date → returns an error/timeout until the partition heals Bank balances, inventory with strict no-oversell, leader election AP n3 answers with 10 (stale). Writes are accepted on both sides; conflicts are reconciled after the partition heals Shopping carts, social feeds, likes, session data

PACELC — the more complete version

CAP only talks about partitions. PACELC adds: Else (no partition), you still trade Latency vs Consistency — e.g. waiting for all replicas is consistent but slow. Dynamo/Cassandra: PA/EL. Spanner: PC/EC.

Our store: AP with tunable consistency.

docs.title: System components
docs.text:
We'll build up the design from these pieces, most of them borrowed from Amazon's Dynamo paper and Cassandra/BigTable:

  1. Data partitioning
  2. Data replication
  3. Consistency (quorums)
  4. Inconsistency resolution (versioning, vector clocks)
  5. Handling failures (gossip, sloppy quorum, hinted handoff, Merkle trees, DC outages)
  6. System architecture
  7. Write path
  8. Read path

docs.title: 1 · Data partitioning
docs.text:
Big data can't fit on one server, so we split it. Two goals: spread data evenly and minimise movement when nodes join/leave. That's exactly consistent hashing (Chapter 5):

  • Servers (as virtual nodes) sit on a hash ring; a key belongs to the first server clockwise.
  • Automatic scaling: adding/removing servers moves only neighbouring arcs.
  • Heterogeneity: bigger servers get more virtual nodes.

docs.title: 2 · Data replication
docs.text:
For durability and availability, each key is stored on N servers (N is configurable, commonly 3). Walk clockwise from the key's position and pick the first N distinct physical servers — this is the key's preference list.

flowchart LR
    K(("key0")) --> S1["s1 (coordinator)"] --> S2[s2] --> S3[s3]
    S1 -.- n1["replica 1"]
    S2 -.- n2["replica 2"]
    S3 -.- n3["replica 3"]
  • With virtual nodes, the next N positions might belong to the same physical server → skip duplicates so you get N distinct machines.
  • Servers in one data center can fail together (power, network) → spread replicas across racks / availability zones / data centers.

docs.title: 3 · Consistency with quorums
docs.text:
Replicas must be kept in sync. Define:

  • N = number of replicas
  • W = write quorum: a write succeeds after W replicas acknowledge it
  • R = read quorum: a read succeeds after R replicas respond

A coordinator (any node that receives the request — a proxy between client and replicas) forwards the request to all N replicas and waits for W (or R) responses.

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant Co as Coordinator
    participant A as Replica A
    participant B as Replica B
    participant D as Replica C
    C->>Co: put(k, v)
    par fan out to N=3
      Co->>A: write
      Co->>B: write
      Co->>D: write
    end
    A-->>Co: ack
    B-->>Co: ack
    Note over Co: W=2 acks received → success
    Co-->>C: OK
    D-->>Co: ack (late, still applied)

Why W + R > N gives strong consistency: the set of W nodes that took the write and the set of R nodes you read from must overlap in at least one node — so at least one reply carries the latest version.

Config (N = 3) Behaviour Use when W=1, R=3 Writes fast, reads must hit everyone Write-heavy, reads rare W=3, R=1 Reads fast, writes wait for all Read-heavy, writes rare W=2, R=2 W+R=4 > 3 → strong consistency (overlap guaranteed), balanced latency The classic default W=1, R=1 W+R=2 ≤ 3 → fastest, eventual consistency only Caches, metrics, likes

Latency is determined by the slowest of the W (or R) replicas you wait for, so smaller quorums are faster.

docs.title: Consistency models
docs.text:
Model Promise Strong A read always returns the most recently written value. Never stale. Weak A read may not see the latest write — no guarantees on when. Eventual A special case of weak: if writes stop, all replicas converge to the same value eventually.

Strong consistency usually requires a replica to refuse new reads/writes until all replicas agree on the current write — bad for availability. Dynamo and Cassandra choose eventual consistency: concurrent writes can land on different replicas, so the system must detect and reconcile conflicts. That's what versioning does.

docs.title: 4 · Inconsistency resolution: versioning and vector clocks
docs.text:
Versioning treats every modification as a new immutable version of the value. The problem is telling apart "B replaced A" (just keep B) from "A and B were written concurrently" (a conflict to merge).

A vector clock is a list of [server, counter] pairs attached to each version: D([S1, v1], [S2, v2], …). When server Si writes a version:

  • If [Si, vi] exists in the clock, increment vi.
  • Otherwise, add [Si, 1].

Comparing two versions X and Y:

  • X is an ancestor of Y (no conflict — Y wins) if every counter in X ≤ the matching counter in Y.
  • X and Y are siblings (conflict) if each has some counter greater than the other's.

Worked example — a shopping cart under a partition:

flowchart TB
    D1["D1 · cart = [milk]<br/>clock: (A,1)"] -->|"written via node A"| D2["D2 · cart = [milk, bread]<br/>clock: (A,2)"]
    D2 -->|"phone writes via B (partition!)"| D3["D3 · [milk, bread, eggs]<br/>clock: (A,2),(B,1)"]
    D2 -->|"laptop writes via C"| D4["D4 · [milk, bread, tea]<br/>clock: (A,2),(C,1)"]
    D3 --> D5["D5 · merged by client · [milk, bread, eggs, tea]<br/>clock: (A,3),(B,1),(C,1)"]
    D4 --> D5
  1. Node A writes [milk] → D1 (A,1); then [milk, bread] → D2 (A,2). D1 is an ancestor of D2 — D1 can be discarded.
  2. A partition happens. The user's phone adds eggs via node B → D3 (A,2),(B,1). The laptop adds tea via node C → D4 (A,2),(C,1).
  3. A later read gets both D3 and D4. Compare: D3 has B:1 > 0, D4 has C:1 > 0 → neither is an ancestor → conflict.
  4. The client reconciles (for a cart: union of items) and writes back via A → D5 (A,3),(B,1),(C,1), which descends from both.
enum Order { BEFORE, AFTER, EQUAL, CONCURRENT }

static Order compare(Map<String,Integer> x, Map<String,Integer> y) {
    boolean xBigger = false, yBigger = false;
    Set<String> nodes = new HashSet<>(x.keySet()); nodes.addAll(y.keySet());
    for (String n : nodes) {
        int a = x.getOrDefault(n, 0), b = y.getOrDefault(n, 0);
        if (a > b) xBigger = true;
        if (b > a) yBigger = true;
    }
    if (xBigger && yBigger) return Order.CONCURRENT;   // siblings → conflict
    if (xBigger) return Order.AFTER;                   // x descends from y
    if (yBigger) return Order.BEFORE;                  // y descends from x
    return Order.EQUAL;
}

Downsides of vector clocks:

  • Complexity pushed to clients — they must implement merge logic per data type.
  • Clocks grow with every server that coordinated a write. Fix: cap the length (e.g. 10 entries) and drop the oldest; this can occasionally fail to detect ancestry (rare, accepted in Dynamo's experience).

Alternatives you can mention

Last-write-wins (LWW) with timestamps (Cassandra's default): simple, but silently loses one of two concurrent writes and depends on clock sync. CRDTs (conflict-free replicated data types — counters, sets, maps that merge automatically) avoid client-side merge code; used by Riak, Redis Enterprise, collaborative editors.

docs.title: 5 · Handling failures
docs.text: At scale, failures aren't exceptional — they're constant. We need to detect them and resolve them.

docs.title: Failure detection: gossip
docs.text:
You can't declare a server dead because one other server says so. Asking every node to ping every other node (all-to-all multicasting) is correct but O(n²) messages — too much with hundreds of nodes.

Gossip protocol (decentralised failure detection):

  1. Each node keeps a membership list: member ID → heartbeat counter + local time it last increased.
  2. Each node increments its own heartbeat periodically.
  3. Periodically, each node sends its list to a few random nodes, who merge it (keeping the higher counters) and pass it on.
  4. If a member's heartbeat hasn't increased for a threshold period, it's considered offline.
Node s0's view Heartbeat Last increased (s0's clock) s0 1820 10:41:07 s1 1793 10:41:05 s2 1650 10:39:22 ← stale for 100 s → suspect s2 is down s3 1802 10:41:06

s0 then gossips "s2 looks down" to others; once several independently agree, s2 is marked down.

docs.title: Temporary failures: sloppy quorum + hinted handoff
docs.text:
A strict quorum blocks reads/writes when too few of the key's designated N replicas are up — bad for availability.

Sloppy quorum: instead of insisting on the designated replicas, pick the first W (or R) healthy servers on the ring, skipping the dead ones.

Hinted handoff: if server s2 is down, its writes go to the next healthy server, say s4, with a hint ("this belongs to s2"). When s2 comes back (gossip tells us), s4 hands the data back and deletes its copy.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Co as Coordinator
    participant S1 as s1
    participant S2 as s2 (down)
    participant S4 as s4 (stand-in)
    Co->>S1: write k
    Co-xS2: write k (timeout)
    Co->>S4: write k + hint "owner = s2"
    Note over S2: ...comes back online
    S4->>S2: hand off k
    S4->>S4: delete hinted copy

docs.title: Permanent failures: anti-entropy with Merkle trees
docs.text:
If a replica is gone for a long time (or hinted data was lost), replicas diverge. We need to sync them, but comparing every key across terabytes is too expensive. A Merkle tree (hash tree) lets two replicas find the differences while transferring very little.

Building it (say keys hash into a range split into 8 buckets):

  1. Split the key space into buckets.
  2. Hash each key's value; then compute one hash per bucket from its keys' hashes.
  3. Build a binary tree upward: each parent = hash(left child + right child). The root summarises everything.
flowchart TB
    R["root: H(ab|cd)"] --> AB["H(a|b)"] & CD["H(c|d)"]
    AB --> A["a = H(b1|b2)"] & B["b = H(b3|b4)"]
    CD --> C["c = H(b5|b6)"] & D["d = H(b7|b8)"]
    A --> b1[bucket 1] & b2[bucket 2]
    B --> b3[bucket 3] & b4[bucket 4]
    C --> b5[bucket 5] & b6["bucket 6 ⚠"]
    D --> b7[bucket 7] & b8[bucket 8]

Comparing two replicas: compare roots. Equal → in sync, done. Different → compare the two children, recurse only into the subtree whose hashes differ. Here only the path root → CD → c → bucket 6 differs, so only bucket 6's keys are exchanged.

Work is proportional to the differences, not the data size. Example: 1 billion keys in 1 million buckets → ~1,000 keys per bucket; if one key differs, you walk ~20 levels and ship ~1,000 keys instead of 1 billion.

docs.title: Data center outage
docs.text: Power cuts, network failures and natural disasters take out whole DCs. Replicate across multiple data centers so users can still read/write from another one.

docs.title: 6 · System architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Cl[Client] -->|"get / put"| Co["Coordinator node<br/>(any node)"]
    Co --> n1[node] & n2[node] & n3[node]
    subgraph Ring["Hash ring — every node identical"]
      n1 --- n2 --- n3 --- n4[node] --- n5[node] --- n6[node] --- n1
    end

There is no master. Any node can receive a client's get/put; for that request it acts as the coordinator, works out the key's preference list from the ring, and talks to those replicas. Because every node runs identical software — request handling, gossip membership, replication, hinted-handoff storage, anti-entropy and the local LSM storage engine — you scale by adding identical boxes, and losing any one box loses nothing unique. (Some clients skip the extra hop by being "ring-aware" and sending the request straight to a replica.)

docs.title: 7 · Write path (LSM-tree, as in Cassandra)
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    W["put(k, v)"] --> L["1 · append to<br/>commit log (disk)"]
    L --> M["2 · write to<br/>memtable (memory, sorted)"]
    M -->|"3 · memtable full → flush"| S["SSTable (immutable,<br/>sorted, on disk)"]
    S -.->|background| CP["compaction:<br/>merge SSTables, drop<br/>overwritten/deleted keys"]
  1. The write is appended to a commit log (sequential disk write — fast, and lets us recover the memtable after a crash).
  2. It's inserted into the memtable, an in-memory sorted structure.
  3. When the memtable reaches a threshold, it's flushed to disk as an SSTable (Sorted String Table): an immutable, sorted file of key-value pairs.
  4. Compaction merges SSTables in the background, discarding overwritten values and tombstones (deletion markers).

Why this design? Writes are sequential (no random disk seeks — recall Chapter 2's latency table), so write throughput is huge.

docs.title: 8 · Read path
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    R["get(k)"] --> M{in memtable?}
    M -->|yes| RET[return value]
    M -->|no| BF{"Bloom filters:<br/>which SSTables<br/>might have k?"}
    BF --> SS["read only those SSTables<br/>(newest first)"] --> RET
  1. Check the memtable — if found, return it.
  2. Otherwise, consult each SSTable's Bloom filter to find which SSTables might contain the key.
  3. Read those SSTables (newest first) and return the value.

Bloom filter in one paragraph: a bit array plus k hash functions. To add a key, set the k bits it hashes to. To query, check those k bits: if any is 0, the key is definitely not there; if all are 1, it's probably there. No false negatives, tunable false positives (~1% with ~10 bits per key). It lets the read path skip almost every SSTable that can't contain the key.

final class BloomFilter {
    private final BitSet bits; private final int m, k;
    BloomFilter(int m, int k) { this.bits = new BitSet(m); this.m = m; this.k = k; }
    private int idx(String key, int i) {                 // double hashing: h1 + i*h2
        int h1 = key.hashCode(), h2 = (h1 >>> 16) | 1;
        return Math.floorMod(h1 + i * h2, m);
    }
    void add(String key)              { for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) bits.set(idx(key, i)); }
    boolean mightContain(String key)  { for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) if (!bits.get(idx(key, i))) return false; return true; }
}

docs.title: Putting it together: the request's journey
docs.text:
The fastest way to revise this chapter is to follow one write and one read through every mechanism:

Moment What happens Mechanism What it costs Client calls put(k, v) Any node becomes coordinator; it hashes k onto the ring Consistent hashing + vnodes Ring metadata on every node Coordinator picks replicas First N distinct physical nodes clockwise, across racks/DCs Preference list Cross-DC bandwidth One replica is down Next healthy node stores the write with a hint Sloppy quorum + hinted handoff Quorum overlap no longer guaranteed W acks arrive Client gets OK; stragglers still apply it Quorum (N, W, R) Latency = slowest of the W On each replica Append to commit log, insert into memtable, later flush to SSTable LSM storage engine Compaction I/O in the background Later, get(k) Coordinator asks replicas, waits for R; sees two versions Vector clocks Clients must merge siblings Versions differed Coordinator writes the newest back to stale replicas Read repair Extra writes on reads On a replica, looking up k Memtable first, then only SSTables whose Bloom filter says "maybe" Bloom filters ~10 bits of RAM per key All the while Nodes exchange heartbeats with random peers Gossip Detection takes seconds, not milliseconds Periodically Replicas compare hash trees and sync only differing ranges Merkle-tree anti-entropy Tree rebuilds when ranges change

docs.title: Interviewer follow-ups
docs.text:
With N=3, W=2, R=2, can a read still return stale data?

In the steady state, no — the read set and write set overlap. But edge cases exist: with a sloppy quorum, the W acks may come from stand-in nodes outside the designated replicas, so the overlap guarantee breaks; concurrent writes can produce siblings; and a write that failed (fewer than W acks) may still have landed on some replicas. That's why Dynamo-style systems call this "tunable" consistency, not linearizability.

What's read repair?

When a coordinator does a quorum read and sees replicas returning different versions, it returns the newest (or siblings) to the client and writes the latest version back to the stale replicas. It fixes divergence on hot keys cheaply; Merkle-tree anti-entropy handles cold keys that are rarely read.

Why not just use timestamps (last-write-wins) instead of vector clocks?

LWW is simpler and widely used (Cassandra). But clocks on different machines drift, and LWW silently drops one of two concurrent writes — fine for "last known location", wrong for a shopping cart where both additions matter. Vector clocks detect concurrency so you can merge; CRDTs merge automatically for suitable data types.

How would you delete a key in this system?

You can't just remove it — a replica that missed the delete would "resurrect" the key during anti-entropy. Instead write a tombstone (a deletion marker with a version). Tombstones propagate like normal writes and are purged during compaction only after a grace period long enough for all replicas to have seen them (Cassandra: gc_grace_seconds).

When would you choose a CP store instead?

When correctness under partition beats availability: leader election and locks (etcd/ZooKeeper), financial ledgers, inventory where overselling is unacceptable, unique-username registration. These use consensus (Raft/Paxos) and reject requests on the minority side of a partition.

How does a node joining the cluster get its data?

It's assigned vnodes (tokens) on the ring; for each new arc, it streams the relevant key ranges from the current owners (the next replicas clockwise). Until streaming finishes, reads can still be served by the old owners; gossip spreads the new membership so coordinators start routing to it.

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
Practice 1 — Pick N, W, R

(a) A session store: 10:1 reads to writes, stale-by-a-second is fine, must stay up. (b) A configuration store where a read must reflect the last write. N=3 in both. Choose W and R.

Solution. (a) W=1, R=1 (or W=2,R=1) — fast and highly available; eventual consistency is acceptable. (b) W=2, R=2 (W+R > N), or W=3, R=1 if writes are rare and reads must be fastest. If a partition must never yield stale reads, use a CP system (etcd) instead.

Practice 2 — Compare vector clocks

For each pair, say ancestor/descendant or conflict: (i) (A,2),(B,1) vs (A,3),(B,1) · (ii) (A,1),(C,2) vs (A,2),(B,1) · (iii) (A,1) vs (A,1),(B,4)

Solution. (i) first is an ancestor of the second (2≤3, 1≤1). (ii) conflict — first has C:2 > 0, second has A:2 > 1 and B:1 > 0. (iii) first is an ancestor (missing B counts as 0 ≤ 4).

Practice 3 — Bloom filter sizing

A node has 200 million keys across its SSTables. You want ~1% false positives. Roughly how much memory do the Bloom filters need?

Solution. ~9.6 bits/key for 1% (optimal k ≈ 7) → 200M × 9.6 bits ≈ 1.92 × 10⁹ bits ≈ 240 MB. Cheap compared to avoiding disk reads for absent keys.

Practice 4 — Merkle tree savings

Two replicas each hold 500M keys in 2²⁰ (~1M) buckets. 300 keys differ, all in different buckets. How many buckets' worth of keys are transferred?

Solution. Only the 300 differing buckets (~500 keys each) → ~150K keys transferred, instead of 500M — about 0.03% of the data. The tree walk compares ~300 × 20 node hashes.

docs.title: Revision checklist
docs.text:
• I can state CAP correctly ("during a partition, choose C or A") and give CP/AP examples, plus PACELC.
  • I can explain partitioning + replication with a preference list of N distinct servers.
  • I can explain N/W/R, why W + R > N gives overlap, and pick values for a use case.
  • I can define strong / weak / eventual consistency.
  • I can run a vector-clock example and decide ancestor vs conflict; I know LWW and CRDTs as alternatives.
  • I can explain gossip, sloppy quorum, hinted handoff, Merkle trees and tombstones.
  • I can draw the LSM write path and read path and explain how a Bloom filter works.

Next: 07 · Unique ID Generator

docs.title: 07 · Design a Unique ID Generator in Distributed Systems
docs.text:
⏱ 35 min read 🔥 Needed by URL shortener, chat, feeds, payments… Book: Chapter 7

TL;DR

  • A single database's AUTO_INCREMENT can't keep up across many machines and is a single point of failure.
  • Options: multi-master with step (simple, not time-sortable, hard to scale), UUID (no coordination, but 128-bit and random), ticket server / range allocation (central counter, numeric, but a coordination point), Snowflake (64-bit = timestamp + datacenter + machine + sequence).
  • Snowflake fits the classic requirements: 64-bit, numeric, roughly time-ordered, ~4 million IDs/sec per machine, no coordination per ID.
  • Its weak spot is the clock: if a machine's clock goes backwards, it could repeat IDs — detect it and wait/fail. Its other limit: only ~69 years of timestamps from a custom epoch.
  • Modern alternatives: UUIDv7 / ULID — time-ordered 128-bit IDs that keep UUID's no-coordination property and index nicely.

docs.title: The intuition: token numbers at a hospital
docs.text:
A hospital with one reception desk hands out token numbers 1, 2, 3… — easy, but the queue for the token itself becomes the bottleneck, and if that desk closes, nobody gets a token.

Open 5 desks? You need a rule so no two desks hand out the same number. Desk 1 gives 1, 6, 11…; desk 2 gives 2, 7, 12… That works until you open a 6th desk. Or each token could be "time + desk number + a counter" — e.g. 10:42:07 · desk 3 · #12. Unique without any desk talking to another, and you can still roughly sort patients by arrival. That last idea is Snowflake.

docs.title: Step 1 · Scope
docs.text:
Clarifying conversation

You: What must the IDs satisfy beyond uniqueness? — Interviewer: Numeric only, and fit in a 64-bit integer. You: Do they need to be sortable? — I: Yes — if A was created clearly before B, A's ID should be smaller. Strict per-millisecond order isn't required. You: Throughput? — I: At least 10,000 IDs per second overall, with room to grow. You: Can IDs be guessable? — I: That's fine for this system (they're internal row IDs). You: Many data centers? — I: Yes, several.

Requirements: unique · numeric · 64-bit · ordered by creation time (approximately) · ≥10K IDs/s · no single point of failure · low latency (generated locally, no network hop ideally).

Why not just use the DB's auto-increment? In a distributed system there are many databases (shards), each with its own counter → duplicates. And a single global counter DB is a bottleneck and a SPOF.

docs.title: Option 1 · Multi-master replication with a step
docs.text:
Use AUTO_INCREMENT on each of k database servers, but increase by k instead of 1:

k = 3 servers
DB1: 1, 4, 7, 10, …     (start 1, step 3)
DB2: 2, 5, 8, 11, …     (start 2, step 3)
DB3: 3, 6, 9, 12, …     (start 3, step 3)
✅ ❌ Uses plain DB features; numeric; scales a bit with more DBs IDs are not time-ordered across servers (DB3's #9 may be created after DB1's #10) Adding/removing a server changes k → renumbering mess Doesn't scale well across multiple data centers

docs.title: Option 2 · UUID
docs.text:
A UUID is a 128-bit number generated locally (e.g. 09c93e62-50b4-468d-bf8a-c07e1040bfb2). The common version 4 is random: 122 random bits. Collisions are astronomically unlikely — you'd need to generate about 10⁹ UUIDs per second for ~86 years to reach a 50% chance of a single duplicate.

String id = java.util.UUID.randomUUID().toString();   // no coordination at all
✅ ❌ Trivial; every server generates independently — no coordination, no SPOF 128 bits, not 64 Scales perfectly — add servers freely Not time-ordered (v4 is random) Can be non-numeric (hex string with dashes) Random keys scatter writes across a B-tree index → page splits, poor cache locality

docs.title: Option 3 · Ticket server
docs.text:
A single, dedicated database whose only job is to hand out numbers (Flickr popularised this):

-- a table with one row; REPLACE bumps the auto-increment and returns a fresh ID
REPLACE INTO tickets64 (stub) VALUES ('a');
SELECT LAST_INSERT_ID();

Every service calls the ticket server for an ID.

✅ ❌ Numeric, simple, works well at small-to-medium scale Single point of failure — if it's down, nobody can create anything Every ID costs a network round trip Running two ticket servers (odd/even) brings back sync problems

Range allocation (hi/lo) — the practical upgrade: instead of one ID per call, the ticket server hands out a block (e.g. 10,000 IDs). Each app server burns through its block locally and asks for the next block when it's nearly empty. Network calls drop by 10,000×, and a ticket-server outage only hurts once blocks run out. Downside: IDs are only roughly ordered, and a crashed server "wastes" the rest of its block (gaps are fine).

docs.title: Option 4 · Twitter Snowflake
docs.text:
Divide a 64-bit ID into sections, each meaning something:

Section Bits Meaning Sign 1 Always 0 (keeps the number positive in signed 64-bit types) Timestamp 41 Milliseconds since a custom epoch Datacenter ID 5 2⁵ = 32 data centers Machine ID 5 2⁵ = 32 machines per data center Sequence 12 Counter within the same millisecond on the same machine; 2¹² = 4,096 values; resets to 0 every ms 
flowchart LR
    s["0<br/>sign · 1"] --- t["timestamp since epoch<br/>41 bits"] --- d["datacenter<br/>5 bits"] --- m["machine<br/>5 bits"] --- q["sequence<br/>12 bits"]

Datacenter and machine IDs are assigned at startup (from config or a coordination service like ZooKeeper) and don't change while the process runs. Timestamp and sequence are generated as the program runs.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text:
Approach Size Sortable by time Coordination per ID SPOF Scales across DCs Multi-master step 64 ❌ No No Poorly UUIDv4 128 ❌ No No ✅ Ticket server 64 ✅ (globally) Yes (network call) Yes ❌ Range allocation 64 ~ (per block) Rarely Partly OK Snowflake 64 ✅ (≈ by ms) No No ✅ UUIDv7 / ULID 128 ✅ (by ms) No No ✅

Snowflake meets all our requirements → let's go deep.

docs.title: The timestamp
docs.text:
41 bits of milliseconds. Shift the bits back to get the time:

id → binary → take bits 63..22 (41 bits) → decimal → add the epoch → Unix ms → date

How long does it last? 2⁴¹ − 1 ms ≈ 2.2 × 10¹² ms ≈ 69.7 years.

That's why you use a custom epoch close to your launch date rather than 1970. Twitter's epoch is 1288834974657 (Nov 04 2010, 01:42:54 UTC) → their IDs run out around 2080. Starting from 1970 you'd have already burned 40+ of those 69 years.

Because the timestamp sits in the high bits, IDs sort by time — and since IDs grow over time, new rows append at the end of B-tree indexes (good locality, unlike random UUIDs).

docs.title: The sequence number
docs.text: 12 bits → 4,096 IDs per millisecond per machine → ~4 million IDs/sec per machine. If a machine somehow needs more than 4,096 in one millisecond, it waits until the next millisecond.

docs.title: Capacity check
docs.text: 32 DCs × 32 machines × 4,096 IDs/ms ≈ 4.2 billion IDs per millisecond cluster-wide. Our requirement was 10K/s. Massive headroom.

docs.title: Java implementation
docs.text:
public final class Snowflake {
    private static final long EPOCH = 1_288_834_974_657L;         // custom epoch (ms)
    private static final int  DC_BITS = 5, MACHINE_BITS = 5, SEQ_BITS = 12;
    private static final long MAX_SEQ = (1L << SEQ_BITS) - 1;      // 4095
    private static final int  MACHINE_SHIFT = SEQ_BITS;            // 12
    private static final int  DC_SHIFT = SEQ_BITS + MACHINE_BITS;  // 17
    private static final int  TS_SHIFT = DC_SHIFT + DC_BITS;       // 22

    private final long datacenterId, machineId;
    private long lastTs = -1L, sequence = 0L;

    public Snowflake(long datacenterId, long machineId) {
        if (datacenterId < 0 || datacenterId > 31 || machineId < 0 || machineId > 31)
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("ids must be 0..31");
        this.datacenterId = datacenterId; this.machineId = machineId;
    }

    public synchronized long nextId() {
        long ts = System.currentTimeMillis();
        if (ts < lastTs) {                                    // clock moved backwards!
            long drift = lastTs - ts;
            if (drift > 5) throw new IllegalStateException("clock moved back " + drift + " ms");
            ts = waitUntil(lastTs);                           // small drift: just wait it out
        }
        if (ts == lastTs) {
            sequence = (sequence + 1) & MAX_SEQ;
            if (sequence == 0) ts = waitUntil(lastTs + 1);    // 4,096 used up this ms
        } else {
            sequence = 0;
        }
        lastTs = ts;
        return ((ts - EPOCH) << TS_SHIFT) | (datacenterId << DC_SHIFT)
             | (machineId << MACHINE_SHIFT) | sequence;
    }

    private static long waitUntil(long target) {
        long now = System.currentTimeMillis();
        while (now < target) { Thread.onSpinWait(); now = System.currentTimeMillis(); }
        return now;
    }
}

docs.title: Clock synchronisation
docs.text:
Snowflake assumes each machine's clock is sane. In reality:

  • Clocks drift; NTP corrects them, and a correction can move a clock backwards. If ts < lastTs, naïvely we'd reuse old timestamps and could repeat an ID. The code above waits for small drift and refuses (alerts) for large drift.
  • Leap seconds and VM pauses cause similar surprises. Many companies "smear" leap seconds across a day to avoid jumps.
  • Across machines, IDs are only roughly ordered — two machines' clocks differ by a few ms, so an ID from machine A can be smaller than one generated slightly earlier on machine B. That's usually fine ("k-sorted").

docs.title: Tuning the bit sections
docs.text:
The 41/5/5/12 split isn't sacred:

  • Low traffic but long lifetime → fewer sequence bits, more timestamp bits.
  • Many machines, one DC → merge datacenter + machine into a 10-bit worker ID (1,024 workers).
  • Need more than 4,096/ms on a machine → more sequence bits.

docs.title: Assigning machine IDs safely
