docs.text: Two processes with the same (datacenter, machine) would generate duplicates. Assign worker IDs via ZooKeeper/etcd ephemeral nodes, a database lease table, or Kubernetes StatefulSet ordinals — never by hand-editing config.

docs.title: High availability
docs.text: The generator is a library inside each service (no network hop) — or a tiny stateless service behind a load balancer. Either way there's no shared state to lose.

docs.title: Privacy / guessability
docs.text: Snowflake IDs leak creation time and roughly how many IDs a machine produced. For public-facing IDs where that matters (e.g. invoice numbers, user IDs in URLs), add an opaque layer: encrypt/permute the ID or expose a separate random public ID.

docs.title: Going deeper: UUIDv7, ULID, KSUID
docs.text:
Newer formats keep UUID's "no coordination, 128 bits" model but put a timestamp first, so they sort by time:

Format Layout Notes UUIDv7 (RFC 9562, 2024) 48-bit Unix ms timestamp + version bits + 74 random bits Standard UUID type, time-ordered → index-friendly in Postgres/MySQL. A great default today when 128 bits is OK. ULID 48-bit ms timestamp + 80 random bits, encoded as 26-char Crockford base-32 Lexicographically sortable strings; URL-safe KSUID (Segment) 32-bit seconds timestamp + 128 random bits → 160 bits, base-62 string Sortable to the second

When the requirement says 64-bit numeric, Snowflake (or a variant like Sonyflake, Instagram's Postgres-based shard IDs, or Discord's Snowflake) is still the answer.

docs.title: Interviewer follow-ups
docs.text:
Your NTP daemon moves a server's clock back by 2 seconds. What happens?

For up to 2 seconds that machine would produce timestamps it has already used. If the sequence also restarts, it could emit duplicate IDs. Mitigations: detect now < lastTs; for small drift, spin until the clock catches up; for large drift, refuse to generate (fail the request / take the node out of rotation) and alert. Also configure NTP to slew (adjust gradually) rather than step the clock.

How do you guarantee two machines never share a machine ID?

Don't rely on static config. On startup, acquire a worker ID from a coordination service — e.g. create an ephemeral sequential node in ZooKeeper, or claim a row with a lease in a DB and renew it periodically. If the lease is lost, stop generating IDs. In Kubernetes, StatefulSet pod ordinals are another stable source.

Are Snowflake IDs strictly increasing?

Per machine, yes (monotonic within a process). Globally, only approximately — ordered by millisecond, then by datacenter/machine bits, and different machines' clocks differ slightly. If you need a strict global order you need a single sequencer (or a consensus log), which reintroduces a bottleneck.

Why not just use UUIDv4 as a primary key?

It works, but it's 16 bytes (vs 8) — bigger indexes in every table that references it — and random inserts cause B-tree page splits and poor cache locality, hurting write throughput at scale. UUIDv7 fixes the ordering problem if 128 bits is acceptable.

You need 50,000 IDs per millisecond on one machine. What do you change?

4,096/ms isn't enough. Steal bits: e.g. 8 bits of machine space (if you have few machines per DC) → 16-bit sequence = 65,536/ms. Or run several generator instances with distinct worker IDs on the same host.

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
Practice 1 — Decode by hand

A Snowflake-style ID (Twitter layout) has the binary sections: timestamp = 1,000,000,000 ms after the epoch, datacenter = 3, machine = 17, sequence = 5. Write the formula for the 64-bit ID.

Solution. id = (1_000_000_000 << 22) | (3 << 17) | (17 << 12) | 5 = 4,194,304,000,000,000 + 393,216 + 69,632 + 5 = 4,194,304,000,462,853. (Verify with the widget by setting the timestamp to epoch + 1,000,000,000.)

Practice 2 — Lifetime

You redesign the layout as 1 sign + 39 timestamp bits (units of 10 ms) + 16 worker bits + 8 sequence bits (this is roughly Sonyflake). How long does it last, and what's the max rate per worker?

Solution. 2³⁹ × 10 ms ≈ 5.5 × 10¹² ms ≈ 174 years. Rate: 2⁸ = 256 IDs per 10 ms = 25,600 IDs/s per worker, with up to 65,536 workers.

Practice 3 — Choose an approach

For each, pick an ID scheme: (a) order IDs in a single-region monolith with Postgres; (b) chat message IDs for a global chat app; © public share links that shouldn't reveal volume.

Solution. (a) A Postgres BIGSERIAL/sequence is fine — one primary, no distribution needed. (b) Snowflake — 64-bit, time-ordered, generated locally on each chat server (Chapter 12 uses this). © Random IDs (UUIDv4 or a random base-62 string) or an encrypted Snowflake — avoid exposing creation time and counts.

docs.title: Revision checklist
docs.text:
• I can explain why DB auto-increment fails in a distributed system.
  • I can compare multi-master step, UUID, ticket server, range allocation and Snowflake on size, ordering, coordination, SPOF.
  • I can draw Snowflake's 1/41/5/5/12 layout and explain each section.
  • I can compute the 69-year lifetime and 4,096 IDs/ms/machine limit, and why a custom epoch matters.
  • I can implement Snowflake in Java including the clock-going-backwards case.
  • I know UUIDv7/ULID and when to prefer them.

Next: 08 · URL Shortener

docs.title: 08 · Design a URL Shortener
docs.text:
⏱ 40 min read 🔥 The most common "first" design question Book: Chapter 8

TL;DR

  • Two APIs: shorten (POST long URL → short code) and redirect (GET /{code} → 301/302 with Location).
  • Reads dwarf writes (tens of thousands of redirects/sec vs hundreds of creates/sec) → the redirect path must be cache-first.
  • 7 base-62 characters give 3.5 trillion codes — plenty for hundreds of billions of links.
  • Code generation: hash + collision check (simple, needs a DB/Bloom-filter check), unique ID → base-62 (no collisions, but sequential codes are guessable), or a pre-generated key service (fast, no collisions, an extra component).
  • 301 (permanent) lets browsers cache → less load, no per-click analytics. 302 (temporary) → every click hits you → analytics. Pick based on the product.

docs.title: The intuition: the cloakroom token
docs.text:
At a wedding cloakroom you hand over a bulky coat and get a small brass token "K-47". Later, you show K-47 and get the coat back. The token is short, unique, and meaningless by itself — it only works because the cloakroom keeps a register: K-47 → Riya's red coat.

A URL shortener is exactly that register: aZ3kQ9x → https://example.in/very/long/path?with=params.

docs.title: Step 1 · Scope
docs.text:
Clarifying conversation

You: Who creates links — anyone anonymously, or signed-in users? — Interviewer: Mostly signed-in marketers, but anonymous creation is allowed. You: Roughly how many links are created, and how often is each opened? — I: About 40 million new links a day; a link gets around 50 clicks over its life. You: Do marketers need click counts? — I: Yes, eventually — but the redirect itself must stay fast. You: Any constraint on what the short part looks like? — I: Keep it short and URL-safe: digits and letters only. You: Do links live forever? — I: Default is long-lived (we'll say 15 years); users can set an earlier expiry. You: Vanity names like /diwali-sale? — I: Nice-to-have.

Functional: shorten a URL; redirect a short URL to the original. (Stretch: custom alias, expiry, analytics.) Non-functional: very high availability and low latency on redirects; codes must not collide; scalable; codes shouldn't be trivially enumerable (nice to have).

docs.title: Estimates (from Chapter 2, worked example 4)
docs.text: Quantity Value New links 40 M/day → ~460 writes/sec Redirects (50:1) ~23K/sec avg, ~45K/sec peak Records in 15 years ~219 B Storage ~250 B × 219 B ≈ 55 TB (plus replicas) Code length 62⁷ ≈ 3.5 T ≥ 219 B → 7 chars Hot-link cache (20% of 1 month of links ≈ 240 M × 250 B) ~60 GB → a small Redis cluster

docs.title: API
docs.text:
POST /api/v1/links
     { "longUrl": "https://...", "alias": "diwali-sale" (optional), "expiresAt": "2027-01-01" (optional) }
  → 201 { "shortUrl": "https://sho.rt/aZ3kQ9x", "code": "aZ3kQ9x" }

GET /{code}
  → 301 or 302,  Location: https://...        (404 if unknown, 410 if expired)

docs.title: How a redirect works
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant S as sho.rt (redirect service)
    participant T as store.example.in
    B->>S: GET /aZ3kQ9x
    S-->>B: 301 Moved Permanently<br/>Location: https://store.example.in/catalog/kurta?...
    B->>T: GET /catalog/kurta?...
    T-->>B: 200 OK (the page)

docs.title: 301 vs 302 — a real product decision
docs.text:
301 Moved Permanently 302 Found (temporary; also 307) Browser behaviour Caches the mapping; later clicks go straight to the target Asks the shortener every time Load on us Lower Higher Click analytics ❌ we miss repeat clicks ✅ every click is seen Can we change the target later? Hard (browsers cached it) Yes Typical choice Pure redirect service, cost-sensitive Marketing links, analytics products (bit.ly-style)

(307/308 are the method-preserving versions of 302/301 — relevant only if a POST could hit the short URL.)

docs.title: The simplest version: a hash table
docs.text: Conceptually it's a map code → longUrl. Two functions: shorten(longUrl) → code and resolve(code) → longUrl. The interesting part is how to generate the code.

docs.title: Data model
docs.text:
A relational table is fine to start; at 219 B rows you'll shard it (or use a KV store like DynamoDB/Cassandra, since every access is by primary key).

CREATE TABLE links (
  code        VARCHAR(10) PRIMARY KEY,   -- 'aZ3kQ9x'
  long_url    TEXT        NOT NULL,
  owner_id    BIGINT,
  created_at  TIMESTAMP   NOT NULL,
  expires_at  TIMESTAMP   NULL
);
-- optional: dedupe identical long URLs per owner
CREATE INDEX idx_links_owner_url ON links (owner_id, long_url_hash);

docs.title: Approach A · Hash the long URL, then resolve collisions
docs.text:
Hash the long URL with a standard function and take the first 7 characters:

Hashing https://store.example.in/catalog/kurta?colour=indigo&size=m gives:

Hash Output size Output (hex) CRC32 32 bits → 8 hex chars 7e4f6003 MD5 128 bits → 32 hex chars ef6fccd4556105478a8f292ad9f21cf2 SHA-1 160 bits → 40 hex chars 6ab80c8af890410c521436aac154d5f54ace4960

Even the shortest is longer than 7, so we truncate — which increases collisions. Resolve them by appending a salt (a predefined string or counter) and re-hashing until the code is free:

flowchart LR
    I[longUrl] --> H["hash(longUrl + salt)<br/>take first 7 chars"] --> E{code exists<br/>in DB?}
    E -->|no| S[save code → longUrl]
    E -->|yes, collision| A["salt = salt + 1"] --> H
  • Each attempt costs a DB lookup → expensive. Speed it up with a Bloom filter of existing codes in memory: "definitely not used" answers skip the DB.
  • Nice property: the same long URL tends to produce the same code (natural dedupe), unless salted.

docs.title: Approach B · Unique ID → base-62
docs.text:
Generate a unique numeric ID (Chapter 7 — Snowflake, or a range-allocated counter), then convert it to base 62 using the alphabet 0-9 a-z A-Z.

Worked example: ID = 3,141,592,653,589

3141592653589 % 62 = 27  → 'r'     (quotient 50670849251)
50670849251   % 62 = 7   → '7'     (quotient 817271762)
817271762     % 62 = 38  → 'C'     (quotient 13181802)
13181802      % 62 = 44  → 'I'     (quotient 212609)
212609        % 62 = 11  → 'b'     (quotient 3429)
3429          % 62 = 19  → 'j'     (quotient 55)
55            % 62 = 55  → 'T'     (quotient 0)
read the remainders bottom → top:  "TjbIC7r"

Check (or try any number) with the converter:

private static final char[] ALPHABET =
    "0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ".toCharArray();

static String toBase62(long n) {
    if (n == 0) return "0";
    StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
    while (n > 0) { sb.append(ALPHABET[(int) (n % 62)]); n /= 62; }
    return sb.reverse().toString();
}

static long fromBase62(String s) {
    long n = 0;
    for (char c : s.toCharArray()) n = n * 62 + new String(ALPHABET).indexOf(c);
    return n;
}
  • No collisions by construction — unique ID in, unique code out. No DB existence check.
  • Code length grows with the ID: a 64-bit Snowflake ID is up to 11 base-62 characters. To stay at 7, use a counter-based ID (range allocation) that starts small, or keep a dedicated 42-bit ID space.
  • ⚠️ Guessable: sequential IDs → sequential codes. Anyone can enumerate …aVuA, …aVuB and scrape every link. Fix: pass the ID through a reversible permutation (e.g. a small Feistel cipher or multiply by a large odd constant modulo 62⁷) before encoding — still unique, no longer sequential.

docs.title: Approach C · Pre-generated key service (KGS)
docs.text:
Generate random 7-character codes offline, store them in a keys_unused table, and have a small Key Generation Service hand them out. App servers fetch batches (say 1,000) into memory so each create costs no remote call. Used keys move to keys_used (or are just deleted from unused).

  • ✅ Fast, no collisions, random-looking codes.
  • ❌ Another stateful service to run and make highly available; two servers must never get the same batch (atomic "claim batch" in the DB); keys held by a crashed server are lost (fine — 3.5 T exist).

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text:
A · Hash + check B · ID → base-62 C · Key service Code length Fixed (7) Grows with ID Fixed (7) Collisions Possible → retry None None Extra lookups DB/Bloom check per create None Batch fetch occasionally Needs ID generator / KGS No Yes (ID generator) Yes (KGS) Guessable No Yes unless permuted No Same URL → same code Naturally (unsalted) No (needs lookup) No (needs lookup)

A good interview answer: Approach B with a permuted counter, mentioning A and C as alternatives.

docs.title: The shortening flow (Approach B)
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    C[Client] -->|"POST /api/v1/links"| LB{{Load balancer}} --> API[API servers]
    API --> V{"valid URL?<br/>safe?<br/>rate limit OK?"}
    V -->|no| E[400 / 429]
    V -->|yes| D{"dedupe: already shortened<br/>by this owner?"}
    D -->|yes| R1[return existing code]
    D -->|no| ID[ID generator] --> ENC["permute + base-62"] --> W[(links DB)] --> R2[return new short URL]
  1. Validate the URL (format, length limit e.g. 2 KB), check it against a malware/phishing list, rate-limit the caller (Chapter 4).
  2. Optionally check if this owner already shortened this URL (lookup by long_url_hash) and return the existing code.
  3. Get a new unique ID, permute, encode to base-62.
  4. Insert the row; return the short URL.

docs.title: The redirect flow — make it fast
docs.text:
Redirects are ~50× the writes and must be fast and always up.

flowchart LR
    U[User click] --> CDN{{"CDN / edge<br/>(optional, for viral links)"}} --> LB{{LB}} --> RS[Redirect service]
    RS -->|"1. GET code"| CA[(Redis cache)]
    CA -->|hit| RS
    RS -->|"2. miss"| DB[(links DB<br/>sharded, replicas)]
    DB --> RS
    RS -->|"3. fill cache"| CA
    RS -->|"301/302"| U
    RS -.->|"click event (async)"| K[[Kafka]] -.-> AN[(Analytics store)]
  • Cache-aside with LRU: hot links stay in Redis. Our hot set (~60 GB) fits a small cluster.
  • Links are immutable → caching is easy (no invalidation except on expiry/deletion).
  • Read replicas serve cache misses; shard the table by code (hash-based) to spread data.
  • For viral links, even the edge/CDN can cache a 301 response for a short TTL.
  • Unknown code → 404. Expired → 410 Gone (and delete lazily).

docs.title: Extras worth mentioning
docs.text:
• Custom aliases: check availability (the alias is just a code); reserve a namespace so aliases can't collide with generated codes (e.g. generated codes are exactly 7 chars, aliases must be ≥ 8 or contain -).
  • Expiry: store expires_at; check on read (lazy), plus a periodic batch job to purge expired rows; codes can optionally be recycled after a long quarantine.
  • Analytics: don't write to the DB on the redirect path. Emit a click event (code, time, country from IP, referrer, device) to Kafka; aggregate into a columnar store (ClickHouse/BigQuery) for dashboards.
  • Abuse: shorteners are loved by phishers. Scan target URLs (Google Safe Browsing-style), rate-limit creation per user/IP, let users report links, and show an interstitial warning for flagged domains.
  • Availability: the redirect service is stateless; DB replicated across zones; cache replicated. Even if the DB is down, cached hot links still redirect.

docs.title: Interviewer follow-ups
docs.text:
Two users shorten the same long URL — same code or different?

Product decision. Same code saves space and gives shared analytics, but leaks that someone else shortened the URL and mixes their stats. Most products give per-user codes and dedupe only within an owner (lookup by owner_id + hash(long_url)). Anonymous links can be deduped globally.

How do you avoid people enumerating all short links?

Don't expose sequential IDs: use random codes (KGS / hash) or permute the counter before base-62 encoding. Also rate-limit GET per IP to slow scanners, and make sure private links (e.g. password-reset or document links) never rely on obscurity alone.

What happens at 10× the traffic?

Redirect QPS → ~450K at peak. Scale the stateless redirect tier horizontally, grow the Redis cluster (hot set still tiny), push more traffic to the CDN with short TTLs, and keep the DB mostly out of the hot path. Writes (~4.6K/s) are still easy for a sharded store.

How would you store 55 TB?

Shard by code across a KV store (DynamoDB/Cassandra) or sharded MySQL/Postgres with ~1–2 TB per shard → ~30–60 shards, each replicated 3×. Every access is a point lookup by primary key, so this partitions perfectly.

Why not generate a random 7-char code and just try to insert it?

That's Approach A without the hash. It works: with 3.5 T possible codes and, say, 200 B used, the chance a random code is taken is ~6% — so a retry happens sometimes, rarely twice. Use a unique constraint on insert and retry on conflict. It gets worse as the space fills, which is why you'd plan to move to 8 chars eventually.

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
Practice 1 — Code length for a different scale

A company-internal shortener creates 50K links/day and keeps them forever (assume 30 years). How many characters do you need with base-62? With base-36 (lower-case + digits only)?

Solution. 50K × 365 × 30 ≈ 548 M codes. Base-62: 62⁵ ≈ 916 M ✓ → 5 chars. Base-36: 36⁵ ≈ 60 M ✗, 36⁶ ≈ 2.2 B ✓ → 6 chars.

Practice 2 — Encode

Convert ID 11157 to base-62 with alphabet 0-9a-zA-Z.

Solution. 11157 % 62 = 59 → 'X', q = 179; 179 % 62 = 55 → 'T', q = 2; 2 → '2'. Read bottom→top: "2TX". Check: 2 × 62² + 55 × 62 + 59 = 7688 + 3410 + 59 = 11157 ✓.

Practice 3 — Cache sizing

20% of last month's links get 80% of clicks. Each cache entry is ~300 bytes with overhead. How much cache?

Solution. 40 M × 30 = 1.2 B links/month × 20% = 240 M entries × 300 B ≈ 72 GB → e.g. 3 × 32 GB Redis nodes (+ replicas).

docs.title: Revision checklist
docs.text:
• I can write the two APIs and explain 301 vs 302 as a product trade-off.
  • I can derive QPS, storage, code length and cache size from assumptions.
  • I can explain hash + collision resolution, ID → base-62, and a key-generation service, with pros/cons.
  • I can base-62 encode a number by hand and know why sequential codes are a problem.
  • I can draw the shortening and redirect flows, cache-first.
  • I can discuss custom aliases, expiry, analytics and abuse prevention.

Next: 09 · Web Crawler

docs.title: 09 · Design a Web Crawler
docs.text:
⏱ 45 min read 🔥 Tests queueing, dedup and politeness thinking Book: Chapter 9

TL;DR

  • A crawler repeatedly: take a URL → download → parse → dedupe content → extract links → filter → dedupe URLs → enqueue. It's BFS over the web graph.
  • The heart is the URL frontier: front queues decide priority (which pages matter more), back queues enforce politeness (one host per queue, a delay between requests to the same host).
  • Respect robots.txt (cached), cache DNS (it's slow), distribute crawlers geographically, use short timeouts.
  • Dedupe content with fingerprints/hashes (and SimHash for near-duplicates) and URLs with a Bloom filter / hash set.
  • Defend against spider traps (infinite URL spaces), redundant/low-value content, and keep pages fresh by recrawling in proportion to how often they change.

docs.title: The intuition: a newspaper's stringers
docs.text:
Imagine a newspaper that wants to read every local notice board in the country. It sends stringers out with a list of starting addresses. At each board they photograph the notices, note any new addresses mentioned, and add them to the office's to-visit list. Rules:

  • Don't send ten stringers to the same small office at once — they'll throw you out (politeness).
  • Visit the important boards (city centre) more often than a remote village (priority, freshness).
  • Don't photograph a notice you've already got (content dedup), and don't revisit an address already on the list (URL dedup).
  • Some buildings have a sign "no photography in the back room" (robots.txt).
  • Watch out for a building with a staircase that never ends (spider trap).

docs.title: Step 1 · Scope
docs.text:
What is a crawler for? It changes the design:

Purpose Example Emphasis Search engine indexing Googlebot, Bingbot Scale, freshness, priority Web archiving Internet Archive, national libraries Completeness, long-term storage Web mining / data collection Market research, training datasets Targeted domains, extraction Web monitoring Brand/copyright/price monitoring Specific sites, recrawl frequency

Clarifying conversation

You: What's the crawl for? — Interviewer: A search engine index. You: How many pages, how often? — I: About 2 billion pages a month. You: Content types? — I: HTML only for now. You: Include newly added/edited pages? — I: Yes, freshness matters. You: Do we store the pages? For how long? — I: Store raw HTML for 3 years. You: Duplicate pages? — I: Skip duplicate content.

Characteristics a good crawler needs:

  • Scalability — billions of pages → massively parallel.
  • Robustness — the web is full of broken HTML, unresponsive servers, crashes, malicious links. Don't fall over.
  • Politeness — never hammer a site with too many requests in a short time.
  • Extensibility — adding a new content type (images, PDFs) should be a plug-in, not a redesign.

docs.title: Estimates
docs.text: Quantity Value Pages/month 2 B Average download rate 2 B / (30 × 86,400) ≈ 770 pages/s Peak (×2) ~1,500 pages/s Average page size ~300 KB Storage/month 2 B × 300 KB = 600 TB Storage for 3 years 600 TB × 36 ≈ 21.6 PB (compress! HTML compresses 5–10×) Download bandwidth 1,500 × 300 KB ≈ 450 MB/s ≈ 3.6 Gbps at peak

docs.title: Step 2 · High-level design
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    SEED[Seed URLs] --> FR[[URL Frontier]]
    FR --> DL[HTML Downloader]
    DNS[(DNS resolver<br/>+ cache)] --- DL
    ROB[(robots.txt cache)] --- DL
    DL --> PAR[Content parser]
    PAR --> CS{Content seen?}
    CS -->|duplicate| X1[discard]
    CS -->|new| ST[(Content storage)]
    CS -->|new| LE[Link extractor]
    LE --> UF[URL filter]
    UF --> US{URL seen?}
    US -->|seen| X2[discard]
    US -->|new| UST[(URL storage)]
    US -->|new| FR
Component Job Seed URLs Starting points. Pick to cover the web well — e.g. by locality (popular sites per country) or topic (news, shopping, sports, education…). URL Frontier The to-download list (FIFO at its simplest — but much smarter in practice, see below). HTML Downloader Fetches pages over HTTP. DNS Resolver Turns hostnames into IPs (cached). Content Parser Parses and validates HTML; malformed pages are dropped. Run as a separate component so slow parsing doesn't block downloads. Content Seen? Detects pages whose content we already have — a large share of the web is duplicate (mirrors, syndication, printer-friendly copies). Compare hashes, not full text. Content Storage Most content on disk (blob storage, compressed); popular content cached in memory. Link Extractor Pulls links out of the HTML and converts relative links to absolute (/about → https://site.in/about). URL Filter Drops unwanted URLs: certain file types/extensions, error-prone links, blacklisted sites. URL Seen? Skips URLs already visited or already queued (avoids loops and repeat work). Bloom filter or hash table. URL Storage Record of visited URLs.

docs.title: The crawl loop, step by step
docs.text:
1. Add seed URLs to the frontier.
  2. The downloader takes URLs from the frontier, resolves DNS, downloads the page.
  3. The parser parses it and checks it's valid.
  4. "Content seen?" — if this exact content exists, drop it.
  5. Otherwise store it and send it to the link extractor.
  6. Extracted links go through the URL filter.
  7. "URL seen?" — new URLs go to URL storage and the frontier; known ones are dropped.
  8. Repeat.

docs.title: BFS, not DFS
docs.text:
The web is a directed graph: pages are nodes, links are edges. DFS dives arbitrarily deep into one site and can get lost. BFS (a FIFO queue) is the usual base. But plain BFS has two problems:

  1. Impoliteness. Most links on a page point to the same host. A FIFO queue full of wiki.example.org/... URLs means our parallel workers all hit that one host at once — effectively a DoS.
  2. No priority. A random forum post and a major news homepage get equal treatment. We want important and frequently-changing pages first.

The URL frontier fixes both.

docs.title: The URL frontier
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    IN[New URLs] --> PZ[Prioritizer] 
    PZ --> F1[["Front queue f1<br/>(highest priority)"]]
    PZ --> F2[["f2"]]
    PZ --> Fn[["fn (lowest)"]]
    F1 & F2 & Fn --> QS["Front queue selector<br/>(random, biased to high priority)"]
    QS --> BR["Back queue router<br/>(uses host → queue table)"]
    MT[("Mapping table<br/>host → back queue")] --- BR
    BR --> B1[["Back queue b1<br/>only news.example.in"]]
    BR --> B2[["b2<br/>only shop.example.com"]]
    BR --> Bn[["bn<br/>only some-blog.in"]]
    B1 --> W1[Worker 1]
    B2 --> W2[Worker 2]
    Bn --> Wn[Worker n]

Front queues → priority. A prioritizer scores each URL — by PageRank/link popularity, site traffic, update frequency, depth from the root — and puts it into one of n front queues (f1 = highest). A queue selector picks from front queues randomly but biased toward higher priority, so important pages go first while low-priority ones still make progress.

Back queues → politeness. Each back queue holds URLs from only one host. A mapping table records host → back queue. Each back queue is drained by one worker thread, which downloads one page at a time and waits a delay between requests (e.g. a few seconds, or whatever Crawl-delay in robots.txt says). So no host ever sees more than one concurrent request from us.

Mapping table news.example.in b1 shop.example.com b2 … … some-blog.in bn 
/** Minimal politeness scheduler: one queue per host, min delay between fetches to the same host. */
final class PoliteFrontier {
    private final Map<String, Deque<String>> perHost = new HashMap<>();
    private final PriorityQueue<Map.Entry<String, Long>> ready =      // host → earliest next-fetch time
        new PriorityQueue<>(Map.Entry.comparingByValue());
    private final long delayMs;

    PoliteFrontier(long delayMs) { this.delayMs = delayMs; }

    synchronized void add(String url) {
        String host = java.net.URI.create(url).getHost();
        Deque<String> q = perHost.computeIfAbsent(host, h -> new ArrayDeque<>());
        if (q.isEmpty()) ready.add(Map.entry(host, System.currentTimeMillis()));
        q.addLast(url);
    }

    /** Returns the next URL whose host is allowed to be hit now, or null. */
    synchronized String next() {
        Map.Entry<String, Long> head = ready.peek();
        if (head == null || head.getValue() > System.currentTimeMillis()) return null;
        ready.poll();
        Deque<String> q = perHost.get(head.getKey());
        String url = q.pollFirst();
        if (!q.isEmpty()) ready.add(Map.entry(head.getKey(), System.currentTimeMillis() + delayMs));
        return url;
    }
}

Freshness. Pages change; we must recrawl. Recrawling everything is wasteful, so:

  • Recrawl based on each page's update history (a page that changed in the last 3 visits gets revisited sooner).
  • Recrawl important pages more often.
  • Use HTTP conditional requests (If-Modified-Since / ETag) so unchanged pages cost a tiny 304 Not Modified.

Frontier storage. Hundreds of millions of URLs don't fit in memory, and pure disk is slow. Hybrid: keep most of the frontier on disk, with in-memory buffers for enqueue/dequeue that are flushed/refilled in batches.

docs.title: HTML downloader
docs.text:
robots.txt (Robots Exclusion Protocol) tells crawlers what they may fetch. Fetch it per host before crawling, cache it (refresh daily), and obey it:

User-agent: *
Disallow: /cart/
Disallow: /search
Crawl-delay: 5

User-agent: MyCrawlerBot
Allow: /

Making downloads fast. At ~1,500 pages/s, the downloader spends most of its time waiting, so the wins come from removing waits:

Wait Fix DNS lookups (10–200 ms, often blocking) A local DNS cache refreshed in the background; async resolver Slow or dead servers Aggressive connect/read timeouts (a few seconds) and move on Long network paths Run crawler fleets in several regions; each crawls hosts near it One thread per request Async HTTP clients holding thousands of connections across many hosts One machine's capacity Many crawler machines; partition the URL space by host with consistent hashing, so each host's politeness state lives on exactly one machine

Staying up. Assume crashes, malformed HTML and hostile pages:

Failure Defence A crawler machine dies Its hosts re-hash to neighbours; frontier and seen-sets are checkpointed to durable storage, so work resumes rather than restarts A page crashes the parser Parse in an isolated worker with limits on size and time; catch everything, log, skip Garbage data Validate (content type, encoding, size) before storing

docs.title: Extensibility
docs.text:
Treat everything after the downloader as a set of subscribers to a "page fetched" event. The core loop (parse → dedupe → extract links) is one subscriber; new capabilities are added as more subscribers without touching it. For example, a PDF text extractor that indexes documents, or a structured-data extractor that pulls product prices and ratings out of schema.org markup:

flowchart LR
    DL[Downloader] --> EV[["page-fetched events"]]
    EV --> CORE["Core: parse → dedupe → extract links"]
    EV --> PDF["PDF text extractor<br/>(plug-in)"]
    EV --> SD["schema.org product extractor<br/>(plug-in)"]

docs.title: Dedup in detail
docs.text:
Content seen? Hash each page body (e.g. 64-bit fingerprint) and look it up in a set. Exact hashes catch exact duplicates. For near-duplicates (same article with different ads/timestamps), use SimHash or MinHash: similar documents produce fingerprints that differ in few bits, so you flag pages within a small Hamming distance.

URL seen? Normalise URLs first (lower-case host, remove default ports, sort query params, strip fragments #… and tracking params like utm_*). Then check a Bloom filter: 10 billion URLs × ~10 bits ≈ 12.5 GB of memory, 1% false positives (meaning we occasionally skip a URL we haven't actually seen — acceptable for a crawler).

docs.title: Problematic content
docs.text:
• Redundant content — handled by content dedup.
  • Spider traps — pages that generate infinite URLs, e.g. calendar links (/calendar?month=… forever) or site.in/a/b/c/a/b/c/…. Defences: max URL length, max depth per host, max pages per host per crawl, detecting repetitive path patterns, and manual blacklists for known traps.
  • Data noise — ads, code snippets, spam pages; filter them out where possible.

docs.title: Step 4 · Wrap-up — what else
docs.text:
If time remains, these are the threads worth pulling:

  • JavaScript-heavy sites. Many pages build their links and content in the browser. A pool of headless-browser renderers can handle them, but rendering costs 10–100× a plain fetch — route only sites that need it.
  • Quality over quantity. A spam/low-quality classifier at the filter stage saves storage, bandwidth and index noise.
  • Scaling the stores. The URL store and content store need sharding (by host or URL hash) and replication like any large dataset (Chapters 1 and 6).
  • Operations. Dashboards for pages/s, error rate per host, robots.txt denials, frontier size and freshness lag; alerts when one host's URL count explodes (a trap) or the download rate drops.
  • Being a good citizen. Identify the bot with a clear User-Agent and contact URL, back off on 429/503, and honour site owners' requests.

docs.title: Interviewer follow-ups
docs.text:
How do you make sure two crawler machines don't hit the same host simultaneously?

Partition by host, not by URL: hash(host) → crawler machine (consistent hashing so machines can join/leave). Then all of a host's URLs land on one machine, which keeps one back queue per host and enforces the delay locally — no cross-machine coordination needed.

Your crawler is downloading 1,000 pages/s but CPU is idle. Where's the bottleneck?

Likely I/O waits: DNS lookups (no cache, or a synchronous resolver), slow servers without timeouts, or too few concurrent connections. Fixes: DNS cache + async resolver, aggressive timeouts, async/non-blocking HTTP clients with thousands of concurrent connections across many hosts, and check politeness queues aren't starving workers (too few distinct hosts in the frontier).

How would you prioritise which URLs to crawl first?

Score = f(page importance, change rate, staleness). Importance from link-based rank (PageRank), domain authority and traffic; change rate from past crawl history; staleness = time since last crawl. Map the score to front queues and bias the selector toward high-priority queues.

How do you avoid re-downloading unchanged pages?

Conditional GETs with If-Modified-Since / If-None-Match (ETag) → server answers 304 Not Modified without the body. For servers that don't support it, compare the content fingerprint after download and skip reprocessing.

How do you handle a 'spider trap' you've never seen before?

Generic limits catch most: URL length cap, depth cap per host, page budget per host per crawl cycle, and detection of repeating path segments or query parameters that only change a counter. Alert when one host's discovered-URL count explodes relative to its PageRank — then a human can blacklist the pattern.

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
Practice 1 — Politeness throughput

Your politeness rule is "one request per host every 2 seconds". To sustain 1,500 pages/s, how many distinct hosts must be active in the frontier at any moment?

Solution. Each host contributes at most 0.5 pages/s → need ≥ 1,500 / 0.5 = 3,000 active hosts (more in practice, since downloads take time and some hosts are slow). This is why the frontier must keep many hosts "hot", not just many URLs.

Practice 2 — Bloom filter memory

You expect 5 billion unique URLs and accept 1% false positives. Memory for the Bloom filter?

Solution. ~9.6 bits per element → 5 × 10⁹ × 9.6 ≈ 4.8 × 10¹⁰ bits ≈ 6 GB. Fits in RAM on one machine, or shard it by host alongside the frontier.

Practice 3 — Design a focused crawler

Design a crawler that watches 50,000 e-commerce product pages for price changes every hour. What changes vs a search crawler?

Solution. No discovery (fixed URL list) → no link extraction, no URL-seen set. Frontier = scheduler keyed by next-due time. Politeness still matters (group by host, respect robots and rate limits). Use conditional GETs, extract just the price (selector per site, or headless rendering for JS-heavy pages), store a time series, and alert on changes. 50K/hour ≈ 14 req/s — tiny.

docs.title: Revision checklist
docs.text:
• I can list crawler use cases and the four properties: scalable, robust, polite, extensible.
  • I can estimate QPS, storage and bandwidth for a crawl.
  • I can draw the pipeline and explain each component.
  • I can explain why plain BFS is impolite and unprioritised, and how front/back queues fix it.
  • I know robots.txt, DNS caching, locality, timeouts, and partitioning by host.
  • I can explain content dedup (hash, SimHash) and URL dedup (normalisation + Bloom filter).
  • I can name spider-trap defences and freshness strategies.

Next: 10 · Notification System

docs.title: 10 · Design a Notification System
docs.text:
⏱ 40 min read 🔥 Classic "async pipeline" design Book: Chapter 10

TL;DR

  • Notifications go out through third-party providers: APNs (iOS push), FCM (Android/web push), SMS gateways (Twilio, MSG91…), email services (SES, SendGrid…). We don't deliver to devices ourselves.
  • Services call a notification service (API) that validates, checks user preferences and rate limits, renders a template, and puts the job on a per-channel queue.
  • Workers per channel pull from queues and call providers; failures are retried with backoff; permanent failures go to a dead-letter queue.
  • Guarantees: at-least-once delivery (persist before sending) + dedup by event ID to avoid double-sends. Exactly-once isn't achievable end-to-end.
  • Extras that make it production-grade: device-token lifecycle, opt-outs, quiet hours, priority lanes (OTP ≫ marketing), analytics (sent → delivered → opened → clicked).

docs.title: The intuition: the post office sorting room
docs.text: A company drops all its outgoing mail into a sorting room. Clerks check each letter's address and whether the recipient asked to stop receiving that kind of mail, put it in the right tray — speed post, courier, ordinary post — and the trays are emptied by different delivery partners at their own pace. If a courier can't deliver, the letter comes back to a "retry" tray. Urgent letters (OTPs!) go in a separate tray that's always emptied first.

docs.title: Step 1 · Scope
docs.text:
Clarifying conversation

You: Which channels? — Interviewer: Mobile push, SMS and email. You: Real-time? — I: Soft real-time: OTPs within seconds; other notifications can be a little late under load. You: Devices? — I: iOS, Android, and desktop browsers. You: Who triggers notifications? — I: Our backend services (orders, payments, social) and scheduled marketing campaigns. You: Can users opt out? — I: Yes, per channel and per category; transactional messages (OTP) can't be disabled. You: Volume? — I: ~30M push, ~5M SMS and ~20M emails per day.

Functional: send push/SMS/email; support templates; respect user settings; support immediate and scheduled sends; report delivery status. Non-functional: high reliability (no lost notifications), low latency for critical ones, scalable to spikes (a sale announcement to 50M users), no duplicates where possible.

docs.title: Estimates
docs.text:
Channel Per day Avg/s Peak (campaign bursts) Push 30 M ~350 50K+/s for a broadcast SMS 5 M ~60 ~2K/s (provider-limited) Email 20 M ~230 10K+/s for a newsletter

The averages are tiny; bursts and provider limits drive the design → queues.

docs.title: Step 2 · How each channel works
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph iOS
      P1[Provider<br/>our backend] -->|"device token + payload"| APNS[APNs] --> D1[iPhone]
    end
    subgraph Android
      P2[Provider] -->|"registration token + payload"| FCM[FCM] --> D2[Android phone]
    end
    subgraph SMS
      P3[Provider] --> GW["SMS gateway<br/>(Twilio, MSG91…)"] --> D3[Phone]
    end
    subgraph Email
      P4[Provider] --> ES["Email service<br/>(SES, SendGrid…)"] --> D4[Inbox]
    end

Push (iOS / APNs):

  • Device token — a unique identifier APNs gives an app install; the app sends it to our backend at login/startup.
  • Payload — JSON like:
{
  "aps": {
    "alert": { "title": "Order shipped 📦", "body": "Your kurta is on the way. Track it now." },
    "badge": 1,
    "sound": "default"
  },
  "order_id": "OD-77812"
}
  • Our server authenticates to APNs (token-based JWT or certificate) and sends (device token, payload).

Push (Android / web — FCM): the same idea with an FCM registration token. (In some regions FCM isn't available — e.g. mainland China — and vendors' own push services are used instead.)

SMS: third-party gateways. In India, commercial SMS also needs DLT registration (pre-approved sender IDs and templates) — a real-world constraint that makes templates mandatory.

Email: a commercial email service gives deliverability (SPF/DKIM/DMARC setup, IP reputation, bounce handling) and analytics — much better than running your own SMTP servers.

docs.title: Gathering contact info
docs.text:
At sign-up / app install / login, the app sends phone, email and device tokens to an API that stores them.

users(user_id PK, email, phone_e164, country_code, created_at)
devices(device_id PK, user_id FK, platform /* ios|android|web */, push_token,
        app_version, last_seen_at, is_active)
-- one user ↔ many devices

Tokens change and expire (app reinstall, OS update). When APNs/FCM says a token is invalid, mark it inactive; also refresh tokens on every app start.

docs.title: First draft (and why it's not enough)
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    S1[Order service] --> NS[Notification server]
    S2[Payment service] --> NS
    S3[Campaign scheduler] --> NS
    NS --> APNS[APNs] & FCM[FCM] & SMS[SMS gateway] & EM[Email service]

Problems:

  • Single point of failure — one notification server.
  • Hard to scale — DB, cache and sending all in one box; can't scale them independently.
  • Performance bottleneck — rendering HTML and waiting on slow providers inside the request path blocks everything; a spike overwhelms it.
  • One slow provider stalls all channels (e.g. SMS gateway timeouts back up push too).

docs.title: Improved design
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    S1[Order svc] & S2[Payment svc] & S3[Campaign scheduler] -->|"POST /v1/notifications"| LB{{LB}} --> NS["Notification service<br/>(stateless, many)"]
    NS --> CACHE[(Cache:<br/>users, devices, settings, templates)]
    NS --> DB[(Notification DB:<br/>users, devices, settings, log)]
    NS --> QP[["Queue: push"]] & QS[["Queue: SMS"]] & QE[["Queue: email"]]
    QP --> WP[Push workers] --> APNS[APNs] & FCM[FCM]
    QS --> WS[SMS workers] --> GW[SMS gateway]
    QE --> WE[Email workers] --> ESV[Email service]
    WP & WS & WE -.->|"failed: retry"| QP & QS & QE
    WP & WS & WE --> LOG[(Notification log)]

What changed:

  • Notification service is stateless and horizontally scaled behind a load balancer.
  • DB + cache hold users, devices, settings, templates — cached because every send needs them.
  • One queue per channel — an SMS provider outage only backs up the SMS queue; push and email keep flowing. Queues also absorb bursts.
  • Workers per channel pull jobs and call providers at a rate the provider allows.

docs.title: The flow of one notification
docs.text:
1. A service calls POST /v1/notifications with the user ID(s), template ID, data, and channels/priority.
  2. The notification service authenticates the caller and validates the request.
  3. It fetches user contact info, device tokens and notification settings (cache → DB).
  4. It drops channels the user opted out of, applies rate limits, renders the template.
  5. It writes the notification to the log (status = queued) and publishes an event to each channel queue.
  6. Workers consume events, call APNs/FCM/SMS/email, and update status (sent / failed).
  7. Providers deliver to devices; delivery receipts and opens/clicks flow back as events.
POST /v1/notifications
{
  "event_id": "order-shipped:OD-77812",          ← idempotency key
  "user_ids": [123456],
  "template": "order_shipped",
  "data": { "order_id": "OD-77812", "item": "kurta" },
  "channels": ["push", "email"],
  "priority": "transactional"                      ← vs "promotional"
}

docs.title: Reliability: never lose a notification
docs.text:
Persist before you send. The notification is written to a durable store (the log DB) and a durable queue (Kafka/SQS with replication) before acknowledging the caller. If a worker crashes mid-send, the message is redelivered and retried.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> queued
    queued --> sending: worker picks up
    sending --> sent: provider accepted
    sending --> retrying: timeout / 5xx
    retrying --> sending: after backoff
    retrying --> dead_letter: max attempts
    sent --> delivered: delivery receipt
    delivered --> opened: user opened
    sending --> failed: invalid token / bounced

Retries: exponential backoff with jitter (e.g. 1s, 2s, 4s… up to N attempts). Distinguish retryable (timeouts, 5xx, throttling) from permanent errors (invalid token, unsubscribed, hard bounce) — don't retry the latter, and clean up the bad token/address.

docs.title: Will users get the same notification twice?
docs.text:
With at-least-once delivery, duplicates are possible — e.g. a worker sends the push, then crashes before acking the queue, so the message is redelivered. Exactly-once across a third-party provider is impossible to guarantee, but we can make duplicates rare:

  • Each notification carries an event ID (idempotency key).
  • Before sending, a worker checks a dedup store (e.g. Redis SET event_id:channel:user NX EX 86400). If the key already exists, skip.
  • The API itself is idempotent: the same event_id posted twice creates one notification.
boolean firstTime = redis.set("sent:" + eventId + ":" + channel + ":" + userId, "1",
                              SetParams.setParams().nx().ex(86_400)) != null;
if (!firstTime) return;                 // already handled → skip
provider.send(payload);                 // a crash right here can still cause a rare duplicate

docs.title: Notification templates
docs.text:
Most notifications share a shape. A template with placeholders avoids rebuilding every message, keeps formatting consistent, and (for SMS in India) is legally required anyway.

template: order_shipped (en)
  push.title: "Order shipped 📦"
  push.body : "Your {{item}} is on the way. Track it now."
  email.subject: "Your order {{order_id}} has shipped"
  email.html: <layout> … {{item}} … <a href="{{track_url}}">Track</a> … </layout>
template: order_shipped (hi)
  push.body : "Aapka {{item}} raste mein hai. Abhi track karein."

Store templates with versions and locales; cache rendered pieces.

docs.title: Notification settings (preferences)
docs.text:
Users must control what they get. Store per user, per channel, per category:

notification_settings(
  user_id   BIGINT,
  channel   VARCHAR(10),     -- push | sms | email
  category  VARCHAR(30),     -- transactional | social | promotions | reminders
  opted_in  BOOLEAN,
  quiet_from TIME NULL, quiet_to TIME NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (user_id, channel, category)
)

Check settings before queuing. Transactional messages (OTP, payment alerts) bypass opt-outs but still respect sanity limits; promotional ones respect quiet hours and local regulations.

docs.title: Rate limiting (protect users and providers)
docs.text:
• Per user: e.g. max 3 promotional pushes/day — too many and users disable notifications entirely (or uninstall).
  • Per provider: SMS gateways and APNs/FCM have throughput limits; workers use token buckets (Chapter 4) to stay under them.
  • Per caller service: one buggy service in a loop shouldn't flood users.

docs.title: Priorities
docs.text: OTPs can't wait behind a 50M-user marketing blast. Use separate queues (or topics) per priority: transactional with dedicated workers and capacity, promotional drained with whatever capacity is left.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: Only authenticated internal services (mTLS, service tokens, or appKey/appSecret) may call the notification API. Validate that a caller may send a given template category. Never put secrets or full PII in push payloads — they show on lock screens.

docs.title: Monitoring & tracking
docs.text:
• Queue depth / consumer lag per channel — the key health signal. Growing lag → add workers or check the provider.
  • Provider error rates and latency, invalid-token rates.
  • Funnel analytics: created → sent → delivered → opened → clicked, per template — product teams live on this.
flowchart LR
    W[Workers] -->|"sent / failed"| EV[[Events stream]]
    PR["Providers<br/>(delivery receipts, bounces)"] --> EV
    APP["Apps<br/>(opened, clicked)"] --> EV
    EV --> AN[(Analytics store)] --> DASH[Dashboards / alerts]

docs.title: The final design
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    SV["Internal services<br/>+ campaign scheduler"] -->|"auth'd API calls"| LB{{LB}} --> NS[Notification service]
    NS --> RL{"Rate limiter<br/>+ settings check"}
    RL --> TPL[Template renderer]
    TPL --> LOGW[(Notification log)]
    TPL --> TQ[["transactional queues<br/>push · sms · email"]]
    TPL --> PQ[["promotional queues<br/>push · sms · email"]]
    TQ & PQ --> WK["Channel workers<br/>(dedup check · provider rate limit · retries)"]
    WK --> PROV["APNs · FCM · SMS gateway · Email service"]
    WK -.-> DLQ[["Dead-letter queue"]]
    WK & PROV --> EV[[Tracking events]] --> AN[(Analytics)]
    NS --> C[(Cache)] --> DB[(DB: users, devices,<br/>settings, templates)]

docs.title: Interviewer follow-ups
docs.text:
How would you send one push to 50 million users quickly?

Don't fan out inside the API request. The campaign service creates one campaign job; a fan-out stage reads the target segment in pages (e.g. 10K user IDs per page) and enqueues batched jobs; many workers send in parallel, using provider batch APIs where available (FCM topics/multicast). Throttle to provider limits; spread over minutes rather than seconds if the message isn't urgent; send from the promotional lane so OTPs aren't delayed.

How do you deal with stale device tokens?

Refresh tokens on every app launch/login; store last_seen_at; when APNs/FCM return "unregistered/invalid token", mark the device inactive immediately; periodically purge devices not seen for N months. Sending to dead tokens wastes capacity and can hurt your sender reputation.

Push failed because the phone is offline. Do we retry?

No — APNs/FCM themselves store and forward to offline devices (with a TTL/collapse key you set). Our job ends when the provider accepts the message. We retry only when the provider call fails. Use collapse keys so a phone coming online gets the latest "3 new messages" rather than 3 separate stale pushes.

How do you schedule a reminder for tomorrow 9 AM in each user's time zone?

Store scheduled notifications with an absolute UTC send time computed per user's time zone. A scheduler (time-bucketed table or a delay queue) wakes up each minute, fetches due notifications and pushes them into the normal pipeline. Re-check preferences at send time — the user might have opted out since.

Can we guarantee exactly-once delivery?

Not end-to-end: once we hand a message to APNs or an SMS gateway, a timeout leaves us unsure whether it was delivered. We get at-least-once with dedup — persist first, idempotent API, dedup key per (event, channel, user) — which makes duplicates rare but not impossible. For SMS/OTP, a duplicate is harmless; for money-related emails, include a stable reference so users can recognise repeats.

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
Practice 1 — Size the SMS workers

The SMS gateway allows 500 requests/s per account and each call takes ~200 ms. You must send 1.8M OTP+transactional SMS during a 2-hour peak. How many concurrent worker threads, and is the gateway limit enough?

Solution. Rate needed = 1.8M / 7,200 s = 250 SMS/s — under the 500/s limit ✓. Concurrency = rate × latency = 250 × 0.2 s = 50 in-flight calls; with headroom for 2× bursts, ~100 threads across a few worker instances.

Practice 2 — Design the settings check

A promotional push should go only to users who opted in to promotions on push, aren't in quiet hours locally, and haven't received ≥ 3 promotional pushes today. Write the decision order and data you need.

Solution. (1) settings lookup (cache) for (user, push, promotions) → opted_in? (2) user's time zone + quiet hours → now allowed? if not, schedule for the end of quiet hours; (3) per-user daily counter in Redis promo:push:{user}:{date} → INCR and compare with 3 (atomic); (4) only then enqueue. Do cheap checks first.

Practice 3 — Spot the bug

A worker does: send to provider → mark as sent in DB → ack the queue message. Under what failure do users get duplicates, and how do you reduce it?

Solution. If the worker crashes after sending but before acking, the message is redelivered and sent again. Reduce with a dedup key checked/set before sending (SET NX), and record provider message IDs. A small window remains (crash between provider call and dedup write) — acceptable for notifications.

docs.title: Revision checklist
docs.text:
• I can explain how APNs, FCM, SMS gateways and email services fit in, and what a device token is.
  • I can design the contact-info tables and token lifecycle.
  • I can explain why the first draft fails and how per-channel queues + workers fix it.
  • I can walk a notification through the full flow.
  • I can explain at-least-once + dedup, retries with backoff, and dead-letter queues.
  • I can design templates, user settings, rate limits, priorities, security and tracking.

Next: 11 · News Feed

docs.title: 11 · Design a News Feed System
docs.text:
⏱ 45 min read 🔥 Top-5 most asked; the fan-out trade-off is the whole interview Book: Chapter 11

TL;DR

  • Two flows: publishing (store the post, distribute it to followers' feeds) and retrieval (read the precomputed feed, hydrate it with post/user data).
  • Fan-out on write (push): at post time, insert the post ID into every follower's feed cache → reads are instant; writes explode for accounts with millions of followers.
  • Fan-out on read (pull): build the feed when it's requested by merging recent posts of everyone you follow → cheap writes, slow reads.
  • Hybrid (what real systems do): push for normal accounts, pull for celebrities, merge at read time; skip pushing to inactive users.
  • The feed cache stores only IDs (e.g. a Redis sorted set of the last ~800 post IDs per user); the actual posts and users come from their own caches (hydration). Paginate with cursors, not offsets.

docs.title: The intuition: the newspaper vendor
docs.text:
Two ways a newspaper vendor can serve 1,000 households:

  • Deliver every morning (push): bundle each house's papers at the depot and drop them off. Reading at home is instant — but if one magazine has a million subscribers, the depot drowns every time it publishes.
  • Let people come to the stall (pull): nothing is pre-bundled; each person picks up their selection when they visit. Publishing is free — but every visit takes longer, especially for someone who follows 500 magazines.

A sensible vendor delivers the ordinary papers and keeps the hugely popular magazine at the stall, where everyone grabs a copy when they come by. That's the hybrid.

docs.title: Step 1 · Scope
docs.text:
Clarifying conversation

You: Follow model — mutual friends, or one-way follows? — Interviewer: One-way follows, like Instagram/X. Some accounts have tens of millions of followers. You: What's in the feed? — I: Posts from accounts you follow: text, images, short videos. You: Ordering? — I: Reverse-chronological for now; we may add ranking later. You: Scale? — I: 25M DAU; users follow ~300 accounts on average, max 7,500 follows. You: Platforms? — I: Mobile apps and web. You: How fresh must it be? — I: A new post should appear in followers' feeds within a few seconds; slightly stale is fine.

docs.title: Estimates
docs.text: Quantity Value Posts 25M DAU × 0.5 posts/day = 12.5M/day → ~150/s, peak ~500/s Feed loads 25M × 12 opens/day = 300M/day → ~3.5K/s, peak ~10K/s Fan-out writes (push, avg 300 followers) 150 posts/s × 300 = 45K feed inserts/s average One celebrity post (30M followers) 30M inserts for a single post ← the problem Feed cache 25M users × 800 IDs × ~16 B (ID + score) ≈ 320 GB

docs.title: APIs
docs.text:
POST /v1/me/posts       { "text": "...", "media_ids": ["m_91f"] }      Authorization: Bearer <token>
  → 201 { "post_id": "1849302018273" }

GET  /v1/me/feed?cursor=<opaque>&limit=20                             Authorization: Bearer <token>
  → 200 { "items": [ {post…, author…}, … ], "next_cursor": "..." }

docs.title: Feed publishing
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    U[User] -->|"POST /v1/me/posts"| LB{{LB}} --> WS["Web servers<br/>auth · rate limit"]
    WS --> PS[Post service] --> PDB[(Post DB)] & PC[(Post cache)]
    WS --> FO[Fan-out service] --> FC[(News feed cache)]
    WS --> NS[Notification service]
  • Web servers authenticate the user and rate-limit posting (stops spam).
  • Post service persists the post (DB + cache).
  • Fan-out service pushes the post ID into followers' feeds.
  • Notification service tells followers who opted in (Chapter 10).

docs.title: Feed retrieval
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    U[User] -->|"GET /v1/me/feed"| LB{{LB}} --> WS[Web servers] --> NF[News feed service]
    NF --> FC[(News feed cache:<br/>post IDs)]
    NF --> UC[(User cache)] & PC[(Post cache)]
    U -.->|images / video| CDN[(CDN)]

The news feed service reads the list of post IDs, then hydrates them — author name/avatar, text, media URLs, like counts — and returns JSON. Media itself streams from the CDN.

docs.title: Fan-out on write vs fan-out on read
docs.text:
Fan-out on write (push) Fan-out on read (pull) When work happens At post time At read time Read latency ✅ Very fast — feed is precomputed ❌ Slow — merge N timelines per request Write cost ❌ O(followers) per post; celebrity = millions of writes ✅ O(1) — just store the post Wasted work ❌ Pushes to inactive users who never read ✅ Only active readers pay Freshness Near-real-time Real-time (computed on demand) Best for Normal users, read-heavy apps Celebrities, rarely-active users

Hybrid:

  • Users with ≤ N followers (say 100K): push to followers' feeds.
  • Celebrities (> N followers): don't push. At read time, fetch their recent posts and merge them in.
  • Skip pushing to followers who haven't been active for, say, 30 days; rebuild their feed on their next visit.
  • Consistent hashing (Chapter 5) on user ID spreads feed-cache keys and limits hotspots.

docs.title: The fan-out service in detail
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    PS[Post service] -->|"new post event<br/>(post_id, author_id)"| MQ1[[Queue]]
    MQ1 --> F["Fan-out service"]
    F -->|"1. follower IDs"| G[(Graph DB / follows store)]
    F -->|"2. filter: muted, blocked,<br/>inactive, settings"| UC[(User cache / DB)]
    F -->|"3. batches of 1,000 follower IDs"| MQ2[[Fan-out queue]]
    MQ2 --> W1[Worker] & W2[Worker] & W3[Worker]
    W1 & W2 & W3 -->|"4. ZADD feed:{follower} post_id"| FC[(News feed cache<br/>Redis sorted sets)]
  1. Fetch the author's follower IDs from the follows store (a graph DB, or a sharded follows table keyed by followee_id).
  2. Filter out followers who muted/blocked the author, are inactive, or chose not to see this content.
  3. Split followers into batches and enqueue — so a 50K-follower post becomes 50 independent jobs processed in parallel.
  4. Workers insert post_id into each follower's feed cache.

What's stored per user: only (post_id, score) — not the post. Keep it bounded: the last ~800 entries. Users rarely scroll past that; older items can be rebuilt from the DB if needed.

/** Fan-out worker: push one post into a batch of followers' feeds (Redis sorted sets). */
void fanOut(long postId, long createdAtMs, List<Long> followerIds) {
    try (Pipeline p = jedis.pipelined()) {
        for (long f : followerIds) {
            String key = "feed:" + f;
            p.zadd(key, createdAtMs, Long.toString(postId));   // score = time (or the Snowflake ID itself)
            p.zremrangeByRank(key, 0, -801);                   // keep only the newest 800
        }
        p.sync();
    }
}

Snowflake IDs make great scores

If post IDs are Snowflake IDs (Chapter 7), they're already time-ordered — use the ID as the sort score and as the pagination cursor.

docs.title: Feed retrieval in detail
docs.text:
1. Client calls GET /v1/me/feed?cursor=….
  2. News feed service reads post IDs from feed:{me} with ZREVRANGEBYSCORE feed:{me} (cursor -inf LIMIT 0 20.
  3. Merge celebrity posts: for each celebrity the user follows, fetch their recent post IDs (cached per celebrity — one copy shared by all their followers) and merge by score.
  4. Hydrate: multi-get posts from the post cache and authors from the user cache (fall back to DB on misses).
  5. Filter anything deleted or now-blocked; build the response with next_cursor = score of the last item.
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant NF as News feed service
    participant FC as Feed cache
    participant CC as Celebrity posts cache
    participant PC as Post + user caches
    C->>NF: GET /v1/me/feed?cursor=X
    NF->>FC: ZREVRANGEBYSCORE feed:me (X, 20)
    NF->>CC: recent posts of followed celebrities
    NF->>NF: k-way merge by score, take top 20
    NF->>PC: MGET posts, MGET authors
    NF-->>C: 20 hydrated items + next_cursor

Why cursors, not ?page=3? New posts arrive at the top while you scroll; offset pagination would show duplicates or skip items. A cursor ("everything older than ID X") is stable.

docs.title: The cache layers
docs.text: Layer What it holds Notes News feed Post IDs per user Bounded sorted sets; the output of fan-out Content Post bodies Hot posts in a separate hot tier (a viral post is read millions of times) Social graph Followers / following lists Used by fan-out and by "who do I follow" (celebrity merge) Action Did I like / repost / comment on this post? Needed to render the heart icon correctly Counters Like, comment, repost, follower counts High-write; often approximate and batched (increment in Redis, flush periodically)

docs.title: Edits, deletes and privacy
docs.text:
• Delete: mark the post deleted in the post store; don't chase it through millions of feed caches — hydration simply drops it.
  • Edit: feeds hold only IDs, so the next hydration shows the new text automatically.
  • Unfollow / block: filter at read time immediately; lazily clean the feed cache.
  • Private accounts: fan-out only to approved followers; check permissions again at hydration for safety.

docs.title: Failure handling
docs.text:
• Fan-out is async — a post is "published" once stored; fan-out delays mean feeds lag by seconds, not lost posts. Queues are durable and workers retry.
  • If the feed cache is lost (node failure), rebuild on demand: pull recent posts of followed accounts from the post store (fan-out on read as fallback), then repopulate.
  • Protect the DB from cache-miss storms with request coalescing and rate limits (Chapter 1).

docs.title: Going beyond reverse-chronological
docs.text: Ranked feeds add a stage after candidate generation: gather candidates (the chronological feed + celebrity posts + recommendations), score them with an ML model (predicted engagement), re-rank, then hydrate. The fan-out architecture stays the same — it now produces candidates, not the final order.

docs.title: Step 4 · Wrap-up — scaling the rest
docs.text:
• Database: posts sharded by post_id; follows sharded by user; read replicas; SQL vs NoSQL per access pattern (Chapter 1).
  • Stateless web tier + aggressive caching; CDN for all media.
  • Multiple data centers with the feed caches rebuilt per region from the replicated post store.
  • Decouple with queues (publishing, fan-out, notifications, counters).
  • Monitor: QPS at peak, feed latency p99, fan-out lag (time from post to appearing in feeds), cache hit ratios.

docs.title: Interviewer follow-ups
docs.text:
A celebrity with 40M followers posts. Walk me through what happens.

The post is stored. Because the author is above the celebrity threshold, no fan-out happens; the post ID is appended to the celebrity's own "recent posts" list (cached, replicated, very hot). When any follower loads their feed, the feed service merges their precomputed feed with the recent posts of the celebrities they follow. Cost moves from 40M writes at post time to a cheap cached read per feed load. Notifications to followers who opted in go through the notification pipeline with throttling.

How do you choose the celebrity threshold?

Balance fan-out write cost vs read-time merge cost. Measure: fan-out lag and worker cost per post vs added feed latency from merging K celebrity lists. Typical thresholds are tens to hundreds of thousands of followers. Also consider posting frequency — a 100K-follower account posting 100 times a day costs more than a 1M account posting weekly.

A user follows 7,500 accounts and hasn't opened the app in 3 months. What happens when they return?

We stopped pushing to them after 30 days of inactivity, so their feed cache is stale/empty. On return, run fan-out on read once: fetch recent posts from followed accounts (using per-author recent-post caches), merge, store the result as their feed cache, and resume push fan-out. Show a quick first page while the rest builds.

How would you show 'liked by you' and accurate like counts at scale?

'Liked by you' comes from the action cache keyed by (user, post) (or a Bloom-ish set of the user's recent likes). Counts come from counter caches: increment in Redis on each like, persist asynchronously in batches. Exact counts aren't needed in real time; for huge posts, approximate/batched counters are fine.

Why store only post IDs in the feed cache?

Memory: an ID is ~8 bytes, a hydrated post is kilobytes — 800 posts × 25M users would be terabytes. Also consistency: edits and deletes take effect immediately at hydration time, without rewriting millions of feeds. Content is cached once in the post cache and shared.

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
Practice 1 — Fan-out cost

1M posts/day from normal users with a median of 200 followers (mean 400), and 50 celebrities posting 5 times a day each with 20M followers on average. Compute daily feed inserts with pure push vs hybrid.

Solution. Normal users: 1M × 400 = 400M inserts/day either way. Celebrities with push: 50 × 5 × 20M = 5B/day (12× all normal traffic!). Hybrid: celebrities contribute 0 inserts — instead, followers' reads merge 250 cached posts. Hybrid total 400M/day ≈ 4.6K inserts/s.

Practice 2 — Feed cache memory

40M active users, keep 500 post IDs each in Redis sorted sets. Each entry costs ~64 bytes in Redis (member + score + skiplist overhead). How much memory? How many 64 GB nodes at 70% utilisation?

Solution. 40M × 500 × 64 B = 1.28 TB. Usable per node = 45 GB → ~29 nodes (plus replicas → ~58). Trimming to 300 entries or skipping inactive users cuts this sharply.

Practice 3 — Pagination bug

The app uses GET /feed?page=2&size=20. Users complain about seeing the same post twice while scrolling. Explain and fix.

Solution. Between fetching page 1 and page 2, new posts were inserted at the top, shifting everything down by k positions — so page 2 starts with the last k items of page 1. Use cursor-based pagination: next_cursor = score/ID of the last item; the next request asks for items strictly older than it.

docs.title: Revision checklist
docs.text:
• I can draw the publishing and retrieval flows and name each service.
  • I can compare fan-out on write vs read and explain the hybrid with numbers.
  • I can describe the fan-out service steps and the bounded ID-only feed cache.
  • I can explain hydration, the celebrity merge at read time, and cursor pagination.
  • I can list the five cache layers and what each holds.
  • I can handle deletes, edits, blocks, inactive users and cache loss.

Next: 12 · Chat System

docs.title: 12 · Design a Chat System
docs.text:
⏱ 50 min read 🔥 Top-5 most asked; tests real-time + storage + ordering Book: Chapter 12

TL;DR

  • Clients need server-initiated delivery → use WebSockets (bi-directional, persistent) rather than polling or long polling.
  • Split services: stateless (login, profiles, groups — behind a load balancer), stateful chat servers (hold each user's WebSocket), and third-party push (APNs/FCM for offline users).
  • Service discovery (e.g. ZooKeeper) assigns a user to a healthy, nearby chat server at login.
  • Store messages in a wide-column / key-value store (Cassandra, HBase): huge write volume, reads are "latest N messages in a chat". Key = (chat_id, message_id) with time-sortable IDs.
  • Each device keeps a last_seen_message_id → multi-device sync is "give me everything after X". Presence uses heartbeats + pub/sub to friends.

docs.title: The intuition: a telephone exchange
docs.text:
Old telephone exchanges kept a live line open between two phones for the whole call. Neither side had to keep asking "any news?" — speech flowed both ways the moment someone spoke. If a phone was off the hook somewhere else, the operator took a message and rang later.

A chat server is that exchange: each phone keeps one live line (a WebSocket) to its chat server; messages flow instantly in both directions; if you're offline, a push notification is the operator's call-back, and the message waits in storage until you reconnect.

docs.title: Step 1 · Scope
docs.text:
Clarifying conversation

You: 1:1, groups, or both? — Interviewer: Both. Groups up to 256 members. You: Mobile, web or both? — I: Both; a user can be logged in on several devices at once. You: Scale? — I: 80M DAU. You: Message types? — I: Text only for now (up to 64 KB). Media later. You: Features beyond messaging? — I: Online/last-seen indicator, delivery and read receipts, push notifications when offline. You: History retention? — I: Keep chat history for 2 years. You: End-to-end encryption? — I: Not in scope for the design, but mention it.

docs.title: Estimates
docs.text: Quantity Value DAU 80M; ~25% online at peak → 20M concurrent WebSockets Messages 80M × 40/day = 3.2B/day → ~37K/s, peak ~100K/s Group fan-out avg group 20 members → group messages multiply deliveries ~20× Storage 3.2B × ~150 B ≈ 480 GB/day → 2 years ≈ 350 TB (+ replicas) Chat servers at ~500K connections per tuned server → ~40 servers just for connections (run 2× for headroom)

docs.title: How does the server push a message to the receiver?
docs.text: HTTP is client-initiated. The sender can just POST (or send over its socket). The hard part is the receiver: the server must push to them. Three options:

docs.title: Option 1 · Polling
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Server
    loop every few seconds
        C->>S: any new messages?
        S-->>C: no (most of the time)
    end
Simple, but wasteful: most requests return nothing, and latency = polling interval.

docs.title: Option 2 · Long polling
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Server
    C->>S: any new messages? (hold open)
    Note over S: waits until a message arrives or ~30 s timeout
    S-->>C: message
    C->>S: next long poll
Better latency, but: the server holding the connection may not be the one that receives the sender's message (stateless LB routing); the server can't tell if a client disconnected; inactive users still reconnect every timeout.

docs.title: Option 3 · WebSocket ✅
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Chat server
    C->>S: HTTP GET Upgrade: websocket
    S-->>C: 101 Switching Protocols
    Note over C,S: persistent, bi-directional connection
    S-->>C: message (server-initiated)
    C->>S: message
Starts as HTTP and upgrades; works over ports 80/443 so it passes firewalls; full-duplex. Use it for both sending and receiving — one connection, simpler client.

docs.title: Service architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    U[Users] -->|"HTTP: login, profile, groups"| LB{{Load balancer}}
    LB --> API["Stateless API services<br/>auth · user profile · groups · service discovery"]
    U <-->|"WebSocket"| CS["Stateful chat servers"]
    CS --> PS[Presence servers]
    CS --> IDG[Message ID generator]
    CS --> Q[[Message sync queues]]
    Q --> KV[(Chat KV store)]
    CS --> PN["Push notification service<br/>→ APNs / FCM"]
    API --> SD[(ZooKeeper<br/>chat server registry)]
    API --> DB[(User / group DB + cache)]
Kind Components Notes Stateless Login/auth, user profiles, group management, service discovery Classic request/response behind a LB; scale freely Stateful Chat servers Each client keeps a persistent connection to one chat server; a user only moves server if it fails Third-party Push notifications (APNs/FCM) How offline users learn about new messages (Chapter 10)

Scalability: a single giant server holding 20M connections is a fantasy-level SPOF; we shard connections across many chat servers, and keep everything else stateless.

docs.title: Storage: which database?
docs.text:
Two kinds of data:

  1. Generic data — users, profiles, settings, friend lists, groups. Relational DB with replicas and sharding is fine.
  2. Chat history — the unique part. Its properties:
    • Enormous write volume (tens of billions of messages per day at WhatsApp/Messenger scale).
    • Reads are mostly recent: "open chat → show the latest 50", then scroll back occasionally.
    • Access is by chat and time, rarely by content (search is a separate index).
    • Read:write ratio is near 1:1 for 1:1 chats.

→ A wide-column / key-value store (Cassandra, HBase, ScyllaDB) partitioned by chat. Easy horizontal scaling, very low latency, and battle-tested for chat (Facebook Messenger historically used HBase; Discord uses Cassandra/ScyllaDB).

docs.title: Data model
docs.text:
-- 1:1 messages (partition by the pair, so a conversation lives together)
messages_1to1
  chat_id      (partition key)  = min(user_a, user_b) + ":" + max(user_a, user_b)
  message_id   (clustering key, DESC)   -- time-sortable
  from_user_id
  content
  created_at

-- group messages
messages_group
  group_id     (partition key)
  message_id   (clustering key, DESC)
  from_user_id
  content
  created_at

Message IDs must be unique and sortable by time — ordering in a chat depends on them. created_at alone isn't enough (two messages in the same ms). Options:

  • A global Snowflake ID (Chapter 7) — easy, globally roughly ordered.
  • A per-chat sequence (local ID generator): IDs only need to be ordered within one chat, which is much easier to guarantee (e.g. a counter per chat partition).

docs.title: Service discovery
docs.text:
When a user logs in, which chat server should they connect to? ZooKeeper (or etcd/Consul) keeps a registry of live chat servers with their load and location; the API picks the best one (nearby, least loaded) and returns its address.

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as User A
    participant LB as Load balancer
    participant API as API servers
    participant ZK as Service discovery
    participant CS2 as Chat server 2
    A->>LB: login
    LB->>API: authenticate
    API->>ZK: best chat server for A?
    ZK-->>API: chat-2.ap-south (low load)
    API-->>A: token + ws://chat-2...
    A->>CS2: open WebSocket

A session registry (Redis: user_id → {chat_server, device}) records where each user is currently connected, so other servers can route messages to them.

docs.title: 1:1 message flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as User A
    participant CS1 as Chat server 1
    participant ID as ID generator
    participant Q as Sync queue (B)
    participant KV as KV store
    participant CS2 as Chat server 2
    participant B as User B
    participant PN as Push service
    A->>CS1: send Kal milte hain? to B (client_msg_id c42)
    CS1->>ID: next message_id
    CS1->>Q: enqueue for B
    CS1->>KV: persist message
    CS1-->>A: ack (c42 → message_id)
    alt B is online
        Q->>CS2: deliver
        CS2->>B: push over WebSocket
        B-->>CS2: delivered receipt
    else B is offline
        Q->>PN: send push notification
    end
  1. A sends a message over its WebSocket to chat server 1, with a client-generated ID (c42) for dedup on retries.
  2. Chat server 1 gets a message_id and persists the message (KV store) — the source of truth.
  3. It enqueues the message on B's message sync queue (think: B's inbox).
  4. It acks A (A's UI shows one tick ✓).
  5. If B is online (session registry says chat server 2), the message is delivered over B's WebSocket; B's app acks → delivered (✓✓).
  6. If B is offline, the push notification service sends an APNs/FCM alert; the message waits in storage.

docs.title: Multi-device sync
docs.text:
User B has a phone and a laptop. Each device keeps its own cur_max_message_id — the latest message ID it has seen for each chat. A new message is "new" for a device if:

  • the recipient is the logged-in user, and
  • message_id > cur_max_message_id of that device.

On reconnect, a device asks "everything after cur_max_message_id for my chats", fetches it from the KV store, and updates its pointer. With separate pointers per device, each one catches up independently.

docs.title: Small group chat
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[User A] -->|message to group G| CS[Chat server]
    CS --> QB[["sync queue: B"]] & QC[["sync queue: C"]] & QD[["sync queue: D"]]
    QB --> B[User B]
    QC --> C[User C]
    QD --> D[User D]

For small groups (≤ a few hundred), copy the message (or its ID) into each member's sync queue / inbox. Each recipient then only checks one inbox for everything — simple and fast. The cost is N copies per message, which is fine for groups of 256 but not for channels with 100K members — there, readers pull from the group's own message stream instead (the same push-vs-pull trade-off as Chapter 11).

On the receiving side, one user's inbox gets messages from many senders and groups, merged in order.

docs.title: Online presence
docs.text:
Show a green dot when a friend is online, and "last seen" otherwise.

  • Login: after the WebSocket is established, the presence server sets status = online, last_active_at = now in a KV store.
  • Logout: set status = offline.
  • Disconnects are messy: mobile networks drop constantly (lift, tunnel). Flipping offline/online on every blip is noisy and expensive. Use a heartbeat: the client sends one every ~5 s; if none arrives for ~30 s, mark the user offline.
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant P as Presence server
    C->>P: heartbeat
    Note over P: online
    C->>P: heartbeat (5 s later)
    Note over C: network drops (lift)
    C->>P: heartbeat (reconnected within 30 s)
    Note over P: still online — no flap
    Note over C: app closed
    Note over P: 30 s with no heartbeat → offline, last_seen = t

Fan-out of status changes: use pub/sub — each user has a channel; friends subscribe to it (A→B, A→C…). When A goes offline, the presence server publishes once and subscribers' chat servers push the update. This works for small friend lists/groups; for large groups (say 50K members), don't push presence — fetch it only when a user opens the group or a member's profile.

docs.title: Receipts: sent ✓, delivered ✓✓, read 🔵
docs.text:
• Sent: server persisted the message (ack to sender).
  • Delivered: recipient's device acked receipt → server updates status and notifies the sender.
  • Read: recipient opened the chat → device sends "read up to message_id X" (one event covers many messages). In groups, track per member and aggregate ("read by 12").

docs.title: Failure handling
docs.text:
• Chat server dies: clients notice the closed WebSocket, ask service discovery for a new server, reconnect, and resync from cur_max_message_id — nothing is lost because messages were persisted before acking.
  • Message retry: if the sender gets no ack, it resends with the same client_msg_id; the server dedups → no duplicates.
