  • Ordering: order by message_id within a chat; the client inserts late arrivals into the right position.
  • Queue backlog / slow consumers: sync queues are durable; recipients catch up on reconnect.

docs.title: End-to-end encryption (mention)
docs.text: With E2EE (Signal protocol, used by WhatsApp), messages are encrypted on the sender's device with keys only recipient devices hold. The server stores and forwards ciphertext — it can't read, search, or moderate content, and multi-device sync needs per-device keys. The architecture above still works; only payloads become opaque.

docs.title: Interviewer follow-ups
docs.text:
Why not just use long polling instead of WebSockets?

Long polling works but has drawbacks at our scale: connections are re-established constantly (every message and every timeout), the server holding a client's poll may not be the one receiving the sender's message (needs extra routing), and it's hard to detect disconnects. WebSockets give one persistent full-duplex connection per device — lower latency and overhead for 20M concurrent users.

How do you route a message from chat server 1 to the user connected on chat server 7?

Look up the recipient in the session registry (user_id → chat server(s)), then send via an internal message bus — e.g. each chat server consumes its own queue/topic, or servers talk over internal RPC. Kafka topics partitioned by recipient, or Redis pub/sub channels per chat server, are common choices.

How do you guarantee message order in a chat?

Assign IDs that are strictly increasing within a chat — e.g. a per-chat sequence number from the partition that owns the chat — and have clients sort by it. Global ordering across chats isn't needed. Snowflake IDs are roughly ordered globally but can invert by a few ms across servers; per-chat sequences avoid that.

A group has 100,000 members. What changes?

Stop copying messages into every member's inbox (100K writes per message). Store the message once in the group's stream; members pull recent messages when they open the group, and receive a lightweight notification/badge rather than the full message. Don't fan out presence or typing indicators; rate-limit who can post (announcement-style channels).

How would you add message search?

The KV store is optimised for "latest messages by chat", not text search. Stream messages (asynchronously) into a search index (Elasticsearch/OpenSearch) partitioned by user, and query it per user. With E2EE, server-side search is impossible — search runs on the device over its local copy.

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
Practice 1 — Size the chat-server fleet

35M concurrent connections at peak. A chat server handles 400K connections at 60% CPU. You want N+2 redundancy per region across 3 regions with traffic split 50/30/20. How many servers per region?

Solution. Region connections: 17.5M, 10.5M, 7M → ÷ 400K = 44, 27, 18 servers → +2 each → 46, 29, 20 (95 total). Also plan capacity for one region failing over to the others.

Practice 2 — Multi-device catch-up

B's phone has cur_max_message_id = 9100 and laptop = 9180 for chat X. Messages 9101–9200 exist. The phone reconnects. What's fetched, and what happens to the laptop?

Solution. Phone queries chat X for message_id > 9100 → 100 messages, updates its pointer to 9200. The laptop is unaffected until it reconnects/receives live messages; it would fetch > 9180 → 20 messages. Read receipts are per-user, so if the phone marks "read up to 9200", the laptop's UI can clear unread badges via a sync event.

Practice 3 — Presence traffic

20M online users send a heartbeat every 5 s. What's the heartbeat QPS? How could you cut it?

Solution. 20M / 5 = 4M heartbeats/s — significant. Reduce by: sending heartbeats over the existing WebSocket (no new connections), letting the chat server treat any message as a heartbeat, increasing the interval to 15–30 s with a 60–90 s timeout, and updating the presence store only on state changes (online ↔ offline) rather than on every heartbeat.

docs.title: Revision checklist
docs.text:
• I can compare polling, long polling and WebSockets and justify WebSockets.
  • I can separate stateless, stateful and third-party services and explain service discovery.
  • I can justify a wide-column/KV store for messages and design the 1:1 and group data model.
  • I know why message IDs must be time-sortable and two ways to generate them.
  • I can walk through 1:1 delivery (online/offline), multi-device sync, and small-group fan-out.
  • I can design presence with heartbeats and pub/sub, receipts, and failure recovery.

Next: 13 · Search Autocomplete

docs.title: 13 · Design a Search Autocomplete System
docs.text:
⏱ 40 min read 🔥 Tests data structures + offline/online split Book: Chapter 13

TL;DR

  • Return the top-k most popular queries that start with what the user typed — in < 100 ms, on every keystroke.
  • Core structure: a trie. Make lookups O(prefix length) by (1) capping prefix length and (2) caching the top-k completions at every node.
  • Split into two systems: a data-gathering service (offline: query logs → aggregate → rebuild trie weekly/daily) and a query service (online: read-only trie in memory/cache).
  • Cut traffic with debouncing on the client, browser caching (Cache-Control), and sampling logs.
  • Scale the trie by sharding on prefix, using a shard map that balances uneven letter frequencies. Remove bad suggestions with a filter layer.

docs.title: The intuition: the chaiwala who knows your order
docs.text:
You walk into your regular tea stall and say "ek ad—" and the chaiwala is already pouring adrak chai, because that's what most people who start with "ad" order. He doesn't think through his whole menu each time; he's memorised the most popular finish for each beginning. And he updates that memory slowly — over weeks, as tastes change — not with every single customer.

That's the design: precomputed "most popular completions per prefix", refreshed periodically from history.

docs.title: Step 1 · Scope
docs.text:
Clarifying conversation

You: Match only at the beginning of the query, or anywhere? — Interviewer: Beginning only (prefix match). You: How many suggestions? — I: 10. You: Ranked how? — I: By how often the full query has been searched (popularity). You: Spell correction? Personalisation? — I: Not now; mention as extensions. You: Language? — I: English and Hinglish/Hindi queries in Roman script; design for Unicode later. You: Capitalisation and special characters? — I: Lower-case alphanumerics only. You: Scale? — I: 30M DAU.

Requirements: fast (< 100 ms end-to-end, or typing feels laggy) · relevant (results start with the prefix) · sorted by popularity · scalable · highly available.

docs.title: Estimates
docs.text: Quantity Value Searches 30M DAU × 8 searches/day = 240M/day Requests per search ~6 (a request per keystroke after debounce, avg query ~20 chars) QPS 240M × 6 / 10⁵ ≈ 14,400/s avg, ~30K/s peak New query data 240M × ~25 B = 6 GB/day of logs; ~20% are new unique queries → ~1.2 GB/day of new trie content

docs.title: Step 2 · High-level design
docs.text:
Two independent services:

  • Data gathering service — collects user queries and aggregates them into a frequency table / trie. Offline, batch.
  • Query service — given a prefix, returns the top 10 most frequent queries. Online, read-only, fast.

docs.title: The naive version (to see why it fails)
docs.text:
A frequency table in a relational DB:

query frequency paneer tikka 41,200 paneer butter masala 37,900 pani puri 25,100 pasta 18,700 papad 6,300 
SELECT query FROM frequency_table
WHERE query LIKE 'pa%'
ORDER BY frequency DESC
LIMIT 10;

Fine for thousands of rows. At billions of rows, scanning every LIKE 'pa%' match and sorting on each keystroke is far too slow. We need a structure built for prefix lookups.

docs.title: The trie (prefix tree)
docs.text:
• The root is the empty string.
  • Each node stores one character and has up to 26 (or 36) children.
  • Each node represents a prefix; nodes that complete a real query store its frequency.
flowchart TB
    R(("root")) --> P((p))
    P --> PA((pa))
    PA --> PAN((pan)) & PAS((pas)) & PAP((pap))
    PAN --> PANE((pane)) & PANI(("pani"))
    PANE --> PANEE(("…paneer tikka: 41.2K<br/>…paneer butter masala: 37.9K"))
    PANI --> PANIP(("…pani puri: 25.1K"))
    PAS --> PASTA(("…pasta: 18.7K"))
    PAP --> PAPAD(("…papad: 6.3K"))

Naive top-k lookup:

  1. Walk down to the prefix node — O(p), p = prefix length.
  2. Traverse its whole subtree to collect all completions — O©, c = number of descendant nodes.
  3. Sort and take top k — O(c log c).

Step 2 is the killer: for the prefix "p", the subtree is a large fraction of the whole trie.

Two optimisations make it O(p) ≈ O(1):

  1. Limit the prefix length. People rarely type 50-character prefixes before picking a suggestion. Cap at, say, 50 chars → walking to the node is O(1).
  2. Cache top-k at every node. Each node stores its own precomputed list of the top 10 completions (with frequencies). Lookup = walk to the node, return its list — no subtree traversal.

The cost: more memory (each query string appears in the top-k lists of all its prefixes). Usually worth it — fast responses are the whole point.

Try it — every node in this widget stores its own top-k list:

final class AutocompleteTrie {
    private static final int K = 10;
    private static final class Node {
        final Map<Character, Node> kids = new HashMap<>();
        final List<Map.Entry<String, Long>> topK = new ArrayList<>();   // cached top-k at this prefix
    }
    private final Node root = new Node();

    /** Offline build: called once per (query, frequency) from the aggregated table. */
    void insert(String query, long freq) {
        Node n = root;
        offer(n, query, freq);
        for (char c : query.toCharArray()) {
            n = n.kids.computeIfAbsent(c, x -> new Node());
            offer(n, query, freq);
        }
    }

    private static void offer(Node n, String q, long f) {
        n.topK.add(Map.entry(q, f));
        n.topK.sort((a, b) -> Long.compare(b.getValue(), a.getValue()));
        if (n.topK.size() > K) n.topK.remove(K);
    }

    /** Online: O(prefix length). */
    List<String> suggest(String prefix) {
        Node n = root;
        for (char c : prefix.toCharArray()) { n = n.kids.get(c); if (n == null) return List.of(); }
        return n.topK.stream().map(Map.Entry::getKey).toList();
    }
}

docs.title: Data gathering service
docs.text:
Updating the trie on every search (billions/day) is pointless and expensive: top suggestions barely change minute to minute. Instead, a batch pipeline:

flowchart LR
    LOGS[("Analytics logs<br/>query, timestamp<br/>append-only")] --> AGG["Aggregators<br/>(Spark / MapReduce)<br/>count per query per week"]
    AGG --> AD[("Aggregated data<br/>query · week · frequency")]
    AD --> WK["Workers<br/>build trie"]
    WK --> TDB[("Trie DB<br/>(serialized trie / KV)")]
    TDB --> TC[("Trie cache<br/>(in-memory, read-only)")]
  1. Analytics logs — raw, append-only records of searches (query, timestamp). Not indexed.
  2. Aggregators — periodically roll logs up into (query, time-window, frequency). How often depends on the product: weekly is fine for most search; Twitter-style trending needs near-real-time (see below).
  3. Workers — asynchronously build a fresh trie from aggregated data and store it in the Trie DB.
  4. Trie cache — a distributed cache holding the trie in memory for fast reads; refreshed by snapshotting the DB after each rebuild.

Where to store the trie?

  • Document store — serialise the whole trie (or each shard) as a snapshot blob, e.g. in MongoDB/S3. Simple to swap atomically.
  • Key-value store — map each prefix → node data (top-k list). Every trie node becomes one key: "pa" → ["paneer tikka", …]. Lookups become a single GET. This is also very convenient for sharding and caching.
key (prefix) value (top-k) p paneer tikka, paneer butter masala, pani puri, pasta, … pa paneer tikka, paneer butter masala, pani puri, pasta, papad pan paneer tikka, paneer butter masala, pani puri pas pasta

docs.title: Query service
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser / app
    participant LB as Load balancer
    participant Q as Query service
    participant TC as Trie cache
    participant TDB as Trie DB
    B->>LB: GET /autocomplete?q=pan
    LB->>Q: forward
    Q->>TC: get("pan")
    alt cache hit
        TC-->>Q: [paneer tikka, paneer butter masala, pani puri]
    else miss
        Q->>TDB: get("pan")
        TDB-->>Q: top-k
        Q->>TC: fill
    end
    Q-->>B: suggestions (Cache-Control: max-age=3600)

Making it lightning fast:

  • AJAX / fetch from the page — no full-page reloads.
  • Debounce on the client: wait ~100–150 ms after the last keystroke before sending, and cancel in-flight requests that are now stale.
  • Browser caching: suggestions for a prefix change slowly, so respond with Cache-Control: private, max-age=3600 — the browser answers repeat prefixes itself (Google does something similar).
  • Data sampling: logging every query at full scale costs a lot of processing; logging 1 in N still captures popularity accurately.

docs.title: Trie operations
docs.text:
• Create — workers build it from aggregated data.
  • Update — either (1) rebuild periodically and swap the new trie in (preferred), or (2) update individual nodes in place — and then every ancestor's top-k list must be updated too (expensive; fine only for small tries).
  • Delete — hateful, violent, sexually explicit or dangerous suggestions must disappear immediately, not at the next weekly rebuild. Put a filter layer in front of the trie cache that drops blocklisted results; remove them physically from the trie at the next rebuild.
flowchart LR
    API[Query service] --> F{{"Filter layer<br/>(blocklist rules)"}} --> TC[(Trie cache)]

docs.title: Scaling the storage
docs.text:
When the trie outgrows one server, shard by prefix:

  • Naive: 2 shards a–m and n–z; 26 shards = one per first letter; beyond 26, shard on the second letter (aa–ag, ah–an, …).
  • Problem: letters aren't evenly used — far more English words start with s than with x. Equal-letter ranges create hot, uneven shards.
  • Fix: analyse historical distribution and use a shard map manager (a lookup DB) that maps ranges to shards so each holds a similar load — e.g. s alone gets a shard, while u–z share one.
flowchart LR
    Q[Query service] -->|"which shard for 'pan'?"| SM[(Shard map manager)]
    SM -->|"shard 7"| Q
    Q --> S7[(Trie shard 7)]

docs.title: Step 4 · Wrap-up — extensions
docs.text:
How do you support multiple languages (Hindi, Tamil, Japanese…)?

Store Unicode characters in trie nodes instead of a 26-letter alphabet (children become a map, not an array). Normalise input (Unicode NFC, lower-casing where it applies). For Roman-script Hinglish, transliteration variants ("paneer"/"panir") may need to be merged as synonyms.

Different top queries per country?

Build separate tries per country/region from region-filtered logs, and store them in CDNs/edges near those users. Route requests by user locale.

How do you support trending (real-time) queries — e.g. breaking news?

Weekly rebuilds can't catch a query that exploded 10 minutes ago. Options: a streaming pipeline (Kafka → Flink/Spark Streaming) counting recent queries in sliding windows; give recent queries more weight (time-decayed scores); keep a small real-time "trending" trie that's merged with the main trie's results at query time. Reduce the working set by sharding.

How would you add personalisation?

Blend global suggestions with the user's own recent searches (stored per user, small) and context (location, time of day). The query service fetches both and re-ranks — the global trie stays the same.

What about typos — 'panner' should still suggest 'paneer'?

Prefix tries are exact-match. Add fuzzy matching: query the trie with prefixes within edit distance 1–2 (bounded search over the trie), or maintain a spelling-correction model that rewrites the prefix first. Costlier — apply only when the exact prefix returns few results.

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
Practice 1 — Memory of top-k caching

A trie has 50M nodes. Each node caches its top 10 completions as 8-byte query IDs plus 8-byte frequencies. How much memory do the cached lists add?

Solution. 50M × 10 × 16 B = 8 GB — plus the query-ID → string dictionary stored once. Manageable, and sharding splits it further. (Storing full strings in each list instead could be 5–10× more.)

Practice 2 — Browser cache savings

Users type on average 6 prefixes per search, and 40% of prefixes repeat a prefix that user requested within the last hour. With a 1-hour browser cache, how much does server QPS drop?

Solution. 40% of requests are served by the browser → server QPS drops from ~14.4K to ~8.6K/s average. Combined with debouncing (e.g. 6 → 4 requests per search), QPS can fall to ~5.8K/s.

Practice 3 — Uneven shards

You have 6 shards and this traffic share by first letter: s 12%, c 9%, p 8%, m 7%, b 6%, t 6%, a 6%, d 5%, others 41% spread evenly over 18 letters. Propose a balanced split.

Solution. Target ≈ 16.7% per shard. One assignment: S1 = {s, a} 18%; S2 = {c, p} 17%; S3 = {m, b, i, l} 7+6+2.3+2.3 ≈ 17.6%; S4 = {t, d, f, g, h, k} 6+5+2.3×4 ≈ 20%; S5 and S6 split the remaining 12 letters (~27% → ~13.7% each). Not perfect — S4 runs hot, so move one of its small letters to S5 — then tune with real data. The shard map manager stores whatever ranges you end up with.

docs.title: Revision checklist
docs.text:
• I can state the requirements and estimate QPS for per-keystroke requests.
  • I can explain why the SQL LIKE approach fails and how a trie works.
  • I can apply the two optimisations (prefix cap + cached top-k) and state the resulting complexity.
  • I can draw the data-gathering pipeline and the query service, and explain why updates are batched.
  • I know trie storage options (snapshot vs prefix→top-k KV), update/delete strategies and the filter layer.
  • I can shard by prefix with a shard map, and discuss languages, regions, trending and typos.

Next: 14 · YouTube

docs.title: 14 · Design YouTube
docs.text:
⏱ 50 min read 🔥 Big, open-ended — focus on upload pipeline + CDN cost Book: Chapter 14

TL;DR

  • Two big flows: upload (client → object storage → transcoding pipeline → CDN + metadata) and streaming (client ← nearest CDN edge, adaptive bitrate).
  • Upload straight to blob storage with a pre-signed URL; split large files into chunks for parallel, resumable uploads.
  • Transcoding is a DAG of tasks (inspect, encode to many resolutions/codecs, thumbnails, watermark, audio) scheduled onto workers via queues.
  • Stream with HLS/DASH: video is cut into few-second segments at several bitrates; the player switches quality as bandwidth changes.
  • The biggest bill is CDN egress. Serve only popular videos from the CDN, the long tail from your own storage; encode rarely-watched videos lazily; place content regionally.

docs.title: The intuition: a film distributor
docs.text:
A filmmaker delivers one master print to a distributor. The distributor makes copies in different formats (IMAX, 2K, a dubbed version, a trailer, a poster), checks the print for damage, and ships copies to cinemas close to audiences. Blockbusters go to every cinema; an art-house film only to a few, and is fetched from the warehouse when someone asks for it.

Uploading = delivering the master print. Transcoding = making all the formats. CDN = the cinemas. Cost control = not shipping art-house films to every multiplex.

docs.title: Step 1 · Scope
docs.text:
Clarifying conversation

You: Long-form, short vertical clips, or live? — Interviewer: Long-form and short clips. Live is out of scope. You: Where are viewers, and on what networks? — I: Mostly India and South-East Asia, a lot of it on patchy mobile data. You: How big is it? — I: 20M daily viewers watching ~40 minutes each; about 2% upload something on a given day. You: What do creators upload? — I: Phone and camera files in most formats, up to 4 GB. You: What quality do we stream? — I: 144p to 1080p for now. You: Build or buy storage and CDN? — I: Use cloud object storage and a commercial CDN. You: Paid/premium content? — I: Some — mention how you'd protect it.

Focus: fast uploads, smooth streaming, quality switching, low infrastructure cost, high availability, scalability, reliability.

docs.title: Estimates
docs.text:
Quantity Value Uploads 2% of DAU upload 1 video/day → 400K videos/day (~5/s) Raw upload size avg 400 MB → 160 TB/day of originals Stored renditions ~1.5× original across all resolutions → ~240 TB/day more Watch volume 20M × 40 min = 800M minutes/day; at ~2.5 Mbps ≈ 19 MB/min → ~15 PB/day egress CDN cost at $0.01–0.02 per GB → $150K–300K per day ← the dominant cost

Those numbers already tell you where the deep dive should go: the transcoding pipeline (correctness + throughput) and CDN cost.

docs.title: Step 2 · High-level design
docs.text:
Lean on cloud building blocks:

  • Blob/object storage (S3/GCS) for original and transcoded videos.
  • CDN for streaming.
  • Our own: API servers, metadata DB + cache, transcoding pipeline.
flowchart LR
    C["Client<br/>(phone · browser · TV)"] -->|"stream video"| CDN[(CDN)]
    C -->|"everything else:<br/>feed, upload URL, metadata,<br/>sign-in, likes"| API[API servers]
    API --> MDB[(Metadata DB)] & MC[(Metadata cache)]

docs.title: Upload flow
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    U[User] -->|"1. request upload URL"| API[API servers]
    API -->|"2. pre-signed URL"| U
    U -->|"3. upload bytes (chunked, resumable)"| OS[(Original storage)]
    U -->|"4. title, description, tags"| API --> MDB[(Metadata DB + cache)]
    OS -->|"5. new upload event"| TP["Transcoding pipeline"]
    TP --> TS[(Transcoded storage)]
    TS --> CDN[(CDN)]
    TP -->|"6. done event"| CQ[[Completion queue]] --> CH["Completion handler"]
    CH -->|"status = ready,<br/>rendition URLs"| MDB
    CH -.-> N["Notify uploader"]

Two things happen in parallel:

a) Uploading the actual video

  1. The client asks the API for an upload URL. The API returns a pre-signed URL — a time-limited URL that grants permission to write one specific object directly to object storage. Our API servers never touch the gigabytes.
  2. The client uploads to original storage.
  3. A "new upload" event triggers the transcoding pipeline: the video is converted to multiple formats/resolutions.
  4. Transcoded files land in transcoded storage and are distributed to / pulled by the CDN.
  5. When transcoding finishes, an event goes onto the completion queue; completion handlers update the metadata DB/cache (status = ready, rendition URLs, duration, thumbnails) and notify the uploader.

b) Updating metadata

While the file uploads, the client sends the title, description, tags, visibility, etc. to the API, which writes them to the metadata DB and cache.

docs.title: Streaming flow
docs.text:
Streaming means the player starts after downloading a few seconds and keeps fetching while you watch — no full download first. It relies on streaming protocols:

Protocol Notes HLS (HTTP Live Streaming, Apple) Most widely supported; .m3u8 playlists + segments MPEG-DASH Open standard; similar idea, .mpd manifest Microsoft Smooth Streaming, Adobe HDS Older / niche

How adaptive bitrate (ABR) streaming works:

sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Player
    participant CDN as CDN edge (nearest)
    P->>CDN: GET master.m3u8
    CDN-->>P: renditions: 240p@400kbps, 480p@1Mbps, 720p@2.5Mbps, 1080p@5Mbps
    P->>CDN: GET 720p/segment_001.ts (4 s)
    P->>CDN: GET 720p/segment_002.ts
    Note over P: bandwidth drops (train enters tunnel)
    P->>CDN: GET 240p/segment_003.ts
    Note over P: bandwidth recovers
    P->>CDN: GET 720p/segment_004.ts

Videos are cut into 2–6 second segments per resolution; a manifest lists them. The player measures throughput and buffer level and picks the bitrate for the next segment — that's why quality changes mid-video instead of buffering. Segments are plain HTTP files → perfect for CDNs.

docs.title: Why transcode at all?
docs.text:
• Raw video is enormous — an hour of high-bitrate camera footage can be hundreds of GB.
  • Devices and browsers support different formats/codecs.
  • Networks differ — someone on 4G in a moving train needs 360p; someone on fibre wants 1080p+.
  • Mobile conditions change mid-video → you need several bitrates to switch between.

Terms: a video file is a container (.mp4, .webm, .mov, .mkv) holding streams encoded with codecs (video: H.264/AVC, H.265/HEVC, VP9, AV1; audio: AAC, Opus). Newer codecs (VP9, AV1) give similar quality at 30–50% fewer bits — saving CDN money — but cost more CPU to encode and need device support.

docs.title: The transcoding DAG
docs.text:
Different creators need different processing (thumbnails, watermarks, HD vs SD only…). Model the work as a directed acyclic graph of tasks (Facebook's SVE and Netflix's pipelines use this idea):

flowchart LR
    O[Original video] --> SPLIT[Split: video · audio · metadata]
    SPLIT --> INS[Inspect<br/>quality, corruption]
    INS --> E1[Encode 1080p] & E2[Encode 720p] & E3[Encode 480p] & E4[Encode 240p]
    INS --> TH[Thumbnails]
    INS --> WM[Watermark]
    SPLIT --> AE[Encode audio<br/>AAC / Opus]
    SPLIT --> MD[Extract metadata<br/>duration, size, codec]
    E1 & E2 & E3 & E4 & AE --> PKG["Package<br/>HLS/DASH segments + manifest"]
    PKG --> ASM[Assemble + publish]
    TH & WM & MD --> ASM
  • Inspect — make sure the video is valid and not malformed.
  • Encode — produce each resolution/codec/bitrate rendition.
  • Thumbnails — auto-generated or uploaded by the user.
  • Watermark — overlay identifying info.

docs.title: Running the DAG at scale
docs.text:
Think of the pipeline as four roles. Different companies name them differently; what matters is the job each does.

flowchart LR
    OS[(Original storage)] --> PL["① Planner<br/>chunk the video,<br/>pick the DAG"]
    PL --> OR["② Orchestrator<br/>track which tasks<br/>are ready"]
    OR --> DQ[["③ Dispatch queues<br/>by priority & task type"]]
    DQ --> W1[Encoder pool] & W2[Thumbnail pool] & W3[Packager pool]
    W1 & W2 & W3 --> SCR[(Scratch storage)]
    W3 --> OUT[(Transcoded storage)]
    W1 & W2 & W3 -.->|"task finished"| OR

① Planner. Reads the upload, cuts it into GOP-aligned chunks (a GOP — group of pictures — is a run of frames that starts with a keyframe and can be decoded on its own, so each chunk can be encoded independently). It also chooses which DAG to run from configuration: a 15-second clip from a new creator might get a small DAG (360p + 720p + thumbnail); a premium upload gets the full ladder, two codecs and a watermark. Chunks and metadata go to scratch storage so any task can be retried without re-reading the original.

② Orchestrator. Holds the DAG's state: which tasks are done, which are waiting on inputs, which are ready. When a task finishes it marks dependents ready and hands them to dispatch. Because every chunk of every rendition is its own task, a 10-minute video can fan out into hundreds of small parallel jobs.

③ Dispatch. Ready tasks wait in queues split by priority (a paying creator's upload before a bulk re-encode) and by task type (encode tasks need big CPU/GPU boxes; thumbnails are cheap). Workers pull from the queues they're built for — pull-based dispatch naturally balances load: an idle worker just takes the next task.

④ Worker pools. Stateless processes (encoders, thumbnailers, watermarkers, packagers) that read inputs from scratch storage and write outputs back. They're ideal for spot/preemptible machines: if one disappears, its task times out and another worker picks it up.

/** Run a transcoding DAG: tasks become runnable when all their dependencies have finished. */
void runDag(Map<String, List<String>> deps, ExecutorService workers) throws InterruptedException {
    Map<String, Integer> pending = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    Map<String, List<String>> dependents = new HashMap<>();
    deps.forEach((task, ds) -> {
        pending.put(task, ds.size());
        ds.forEach(d -> dependents.computeIfAbsent(d, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(task));
    });
    CountDownLatch done = new CountDownLatch(deps.size());
    Consumer<String>[] submit = new Consumer[1];
    submit[0] = task -> workers.submit(() -> {
        execute(task);                                   // encode / thumbnail / watermark …
        for (String next : dependents.getOrDefault(task, List.of()))
            if (pending.merge(next, -1, Integer::sum) == 0) submit[0].accept(next);
        done.countDown();
    });
    pending.forEach((t, n) -> { if (n == 0) submit[0].accept(t); });   // no dependencies → start now
    done.await();
}

docs.title: Making uploads and processing fast
docs.text: Bottleneck What we do Why it works One big upload over a weak link Client splits the file into parts, uploads several at once, retries only failed parts, resumes after a crash A dropped connection costs one part, not the whole file Distance to the upload endpoint Regional upload endpoints (often CDN POPs) accept the bytes, then forward to storage over the backbone The slow "last mile" leg is short Stages waiting on each other A queue between every stage (fetch → encode → package → publish) Each stage scales on its own; a slow stage builds a backlog instead of stalling everyone Time-to-first-play Publish a small rendition set first, add the rest later Viewers can watch within minutes of upload

docs.title: Protecting uploads and content
docs.text:
• Who can upload what: the API signs a short-lived URL for exactly one object key, tied to the authenticated user — nobody can overwrite someone else's video.
  • Who can watch what: private and paid videos are served through signed CDN URLs/cookies that expire.
  • Stopping copying of premium content: encrypt segments (AES) and deliver keys through a DRM system (Widevine on Android/Chrome, FairPlay on Apple, PlayReady on Windows/TVs); add visible or forensic watermarks so leaks can be traced.

docs.title: Where the money goes — and how to spend less
docs.text:
Egress is the bill. Views follow a long tail, so treat popular and unpopular videos differently:

Lever Saving Trade-off Keep only the head (popular videos) on CDN edges; serve the tail from origin storage Big — most bytes are head bytes, most videos are tail First viewer of a tail video gets slower start Produce extra renditions lazily, when a video starts getting views Encoding CPU and storage for videos nobody watches Short delay before HD exists for a sudden hit Distribute by region of popularity Don't pay to pre-position a regional hit worldwide Need per-region analytics Efficient codecs (VP9/AV1) for popular videos 30–50% fewer bytes on every view Encoding is several times more expensive; device support varies Own edge caches inside ISPs (at very large scale) Cheaper bandwidth, lower latency A major infrastructure programme

All of these depend on good analytics: what's watched, where, and how quickly views are growing.

docs.title: When things fail
docs.text:
Separate failures you can retry from ones you can't:

  • Retry (idempotent, chunk-level): a part upload that timed out; an encode task whose worker vanished; a write to scratch storage that failed. Because tasks work on chunks and write to deterministic paths, rerunning them is safe.
  • Don't retry: a corrupt or unsupported file, or a video that fails policy checks — mark the upload failed with a clear reason and tell the creator.
  • Lose a planner/orchestrator instance: its state (the DAG and task status) lives in a durable store, so another instance resumes it.
  • Serving path: API servers are stateless behind a load balancer; the metadata cache and DB are replicated with automatic failover (Chapters 1 and 6); if an edge cache misses or fails, the CDN falls back to origin.

docs.title: Step 4 · Wrap-up — what else
docs.text:
• Scale the API tier — stateless, horizontal.
  • Scale the metadata DB — replication + sharding (by video ID).
  • Live streaming — same building blocks (encode, package, CDN) but much lower latency targets, so you need different protocols (low-latency HLS, WebRTC), smaller segments, less parallelism in processing, and different failure handling (you can't "retry" a live moment).
  • Takedowns — copyright/abuse removals must delete or block content from storage and invalidate CDN caches.
  • Recommendations, comments, view counts — separate systems; view counts are high-write counters (batched, approximate in real time).

docs.title: Interviewer follow-ups
docs.text:
Why use a pre-signed URL rather than uploading through the API servers?

Uploads are huge (GBs) and slow. Routing them through API servers would tie up their bandwidth, memory and connections for minutes each. A pre-signed URL lets the client write directly to object storage (which is built for this), while the API still controls who may upload what and until when.

A user uploads a 4 GB video over a flaky mobile network. How do you make it work?

Chunked, resumable uploads (e.g. 8 MB parts via S3 multipart or the tus protocol). The client uploads parts in parallel, retries only failed parts, and after an app restart asks the server which parts already arrived and continues. The server assembles the parts when all have arrived (or the pipeline processes GOP chunks directly).

How many renditions should you produce, and when?

A typical ladder: 144p/240p/360p/480p/720p/1080p (+4K for capable sources), in one or two codecs. For a new upload produce a small fast set first (e.g. 360p + 720p H.264) so the video goes live quickly; add the rest asynchronously, and add AV1/VP9 only once a video proves popular.

How do you decide which videos go on the CDN?

Use view-count predictions and recent popularity per region: push/keep the top N% of videos on edges, let the rest be fetched from origin (pull-through with short TTLs). Re-evaluate continuously; viral videos get promoted quickly based on view velocity.

How does the player know which quality to pick?

The player downloads the manifest listing all renditions, then for each segment uses estimated bandwidth and current buffer to pick a bitrate (ABR algorithms like throughput-based or buffer-based/BOLA). It starts low for a fast start and climbs as the buffer grows.

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
Practice 1 — Transcoding fleet

400K uploads/day, average length 8 minutes. Encoding all renditions takes ~2 CPU-minutes per minute of video. How many 32-core machines do you need at steady state, at 70% utilisation?

Solution. Video minutes/day = 3.2M. CPU-minutes = 6.4M/day ÷ 1,440 = ~4,444 cores busy on average. At 70% of 32 cores (22.4 usable) → ~200 machines average; peaks need more (or a queue that absorbs the burst). Spot/preemptible instances fit well because tasks are retryable.

Practice 2 — CDN vs origin split

15 PB/day egress. 80% of views go to the top 10% of videos. CDN costs $0.02/GB, serving from origin costs $0.008/GB but only works for the long tail. What's the daily saving vs serving everything from CDN?

Solution. All CDN: 15M GB × $0.02 = $300K/day. Split: 12 PB via CDN = $240K; 3 PB from origin = $24K → $264K/day. Saving ≈ $36K/day (~$13M/year).

Practice 3 — Segment maths

A 10-minute video, 6 renditions, 4-second segments. How many segment files? If the player picks a new bitrate every segment, how often can quality change?

Solution. 600 s / 4 s = 150 segments × 6 = 900 files (+ 7 playlists). Quality can change every 4 seconds.

docs.title: Revision checklist
docs.text:
• I can estimate storage and CDN egress and explain why CDN cost dominates.
  • I can draw the upload flow (pre-signed URL, original storage, pipeline, completion queue, metadata) and the streaming flow.
  • I can explain containers vs codecs and why we transcode into several renditions.
  • I can explain HLS/DASH and adaptive bitrate with segments and manifests.
  • I can describe the transcoding DAG and the planner → orchestrator → dispatch queues → worker pools roles.
  • I know the speed, security and cost optimisations and how to handle errors.

Next: 15 · Google Drive

docs.title: 15 · Design Google Drive
docs.text:
⏱ 45 min read 🔥 Tests sync, consistency and storage efficiency Book: Chapter 15

TL;DR

  • Files are split into blocks (e.g. 4 MB), each identified by its content hash. Upload/download only blocks that changed → delta sync; identical blocks are stored once → dedup.
  • Bytes live in object storage (S3) via block servers; everything else — users, devices, files, versions, block lists — lives in a strongly consistent metadata DB (relational, ACID).
  • When a file changes, notification service (long polling) tells the user's other devices; they fetch the new block list and download only missing blocks. Offline devices catch up from an offline backup queue / change log.
  • Conflicts: the first version to commit wins; the other becomes a "conflicted copy" the user resolves.
  • Control cost with dedup, limited version history (and thinning old versions), and cold storage for rarely accessed data.

docs.title: The intuition: a shared almirah with a register
docs.text:
Imagine a family almirah where everyone keeps documents, and a register at the front lists every document, its pages, and who changed it last. To update a 100-page file where only page 37 changed, you don't replace the whole file — you swap page 37 and update the register. If two people edit the same page at once, whoever writes in the register first wins; the other's version is kept as "copy 2". Family members in other cities get a phone call: "register updated" — and they fetch only the new page.

Pages = blocks. Register = metadata DB. Phone call = notification service.

docs.title: Step 1 · Scope
docs.text:
Clarifying conversation

You: Is this personal storage, team storage, or both? — Interviewer: Personal first, with folder sharing. You: What must "sync" mean — every device always mirrors the cloud? — I: Yes, desktop clients keep a local mirror; phones fetch on demand. You: How big can files get? — I: Up to 5 GB. You: Free quota? — I: 10 GB per user. You: How many users? — I: 40M registered, 8M active daily. You: Do we keep old versions? — I: Yes, users must be able to restore earlier versions. You: Security expectations? — I: Encrypted in transit and at rest.

Out of scope (mention only): real-time collaborative editing (that's Google Docs — operational transforms/CRDTs, a different problem).

Non-functional: reliability (never lose data — the #1 requirement), fast sync, low bandwidth (mobile data is expensive), scalability, high availability.

docs.title: Estimates
docs.text: Quantity Value Allocated storage 40M × 10 GB = 400 PB allocated (actual use maybe 30–40% → ~140 PB) Uploads 8M DAU × 3 files/day = 24M/day → ~280/s, peak ~600/s Average file ~1 MB → ~24 TB/day of new data before dedup Metadata reads sync checks, listing folders: ~10× uploads → ~3K/s

docs.title: Start simple: one server
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    C[Client] -->|"upload / download / revisions"| WS["Web server<br/>(Apache)"] --> DB[(MySQL metadata)]
    WS --> FS[("Local disk<br/>/drive/{namespace}/…")]

APIs:

POST /files/upload?uploadType=resumable      # start a resumable upload → returns upload session URL
PUT  <session URL>  (bytes, Content-Range)   # send data; resume after failures
GET  /files/download?path=/docs/resume.pdf
GET  /files/list_revisions?path=/docs/resume.pdf&limit=20
  • Simple upload for small files; resumable upload for large ones — survive a dropped connection without restarting.
  • All endpoints require auth (OAuth tokens) over HTTPS.

It works until the disk fills up. Now scale it.

docs.title: Scaling out
docs.text:
• Storage → move files to object storage (S3): replicated within a region; enable cross-region replication so a regional disaster doesn't lose data.
  • Load balancer + many stateless web/API servers.
  • Metadata DB → separate, replicated (and later sharded) relational DB.
  • Block servers split files into blocks before upload to storage.

docs.title: The full design
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    U["Clients<br/>desktop · mobile · web"] -->|"API: metadata"| LB{{Load balancer}} --> API[API servers]
    U -->|"blocks"| BS["Block servers<br/>split · compress · encrypt"]
    BS --> S3[(Cloud storage<br/>S3)]
    S3 -.->|"rarely used"| COLD[(Cold storage)]
    API --> MC[(Metadata cache)] --> MDB[(Metadata DB<br/>strongly consistent)]
    API --> NS["Notification service<br/>(long polling)"]
    NS <-->|"long poll"| U
    API --> OQ[["Offline backup queue"]]
Component Role Block servers Split files into blocks, compress, encrypt, and upload to cloud storage; on download, reassemble. Each block has an ID = hash of its content. Cloud storage Holds the blocks (immutable objects). Cold storage Cheaper tier for inactive files (e.g. S3 Glacier). API servers Everything except bytes: auth, profiles, file metadata, sharing, versions. Metadata DB Users, devices, files, versions, block lists, sharing. Strong consistency. Metadata cache Hot metadata for fast reads. Notification service Publishes "something changed" to clients (long polling). Offline backup queue Stores changes for devices that are offline, so they can sync later.

docs.title: Block servers: delta sync and compression
docs.text:
Uploading a whole 2 GB file because one paragraph changed wastes bandwidth. So:

  1. Split the file into blocks (Dropbox famously used 4 MB max).
  2. Hash each block (SHA-256) → block ID.
  3. Ask the server which block IDs it already has; upload only the missing ones (delta sync).
  4. Compress each block (gzip/zstd for text; images/video are already compressed) and encrypt it before sending.
flowchart LR
    F["resume.pdf (v2)"] --> SPLIT["split into blocks<br/>b1 b2 b3 b4"]
    SPLIT --> H["hash each block"]
    H --> CMP{"server already<br/>has block?"}
    CMP -->|"b1, b2, b4: yes"| SKIP[skip]
    CMP -->|"b3: no (changed)"| UP["compress → encrypt → upload b3"]

Fixed vs content-defined chunking. With fixed-size blocks, inserting one byte at the start shifts every block boundary → every block hash changes. Content-defined chunking (rolling hash, e.g. Rabin fingerprints) cuts blocks where the content itself has certain patterns, so an insertion only changes the block around it.

/** Fixed-size chunking with SHA-256 block IDs (content-defined chunking would replace the split rule). */
static List<String> blockIds(Path file, int blockSize) throws Exception {
    List<String> ids = new ArrayList<>();
    MessageDigest sha = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256");
    try (InputStream in = Files.newInputStream(file)) {
        byte[] buf = new byte[blockSize];
        int n;
        while ((n = in.readNBytes(buf, 0, blockSize)) > 0) {
            ids.add(HexFormat.of().formatHex(sha.digest(Arrays.copyOf(buf, n))));
        }
    }
    return ids;   // the file's version = this ordered list of block IDs
}

docs.title: Why strong consistency for metadata
docs.text:
If two devices see different versions of the same file's block list, they'll show different content — or worse, overwrite each other. The metadata must be strongly consistent (any read after a commit sees the commit), even if that costs some availability.

  • Use a relational DB with ACID transactions — committing a new version (insert version row + block list + update "latest" pointer) is one transaction.
  • Caches must be kept consistent: replicas of the cache agree with the master; invalidate the cache on every metadata write.
  • Many NoSQL stores default to eventual consistency → would need extra care. The bytes (blocks) don't need this — they're immutable and content-addressed, so they can never be "inconsistent".

docs.title: Metadata schema
docs.text:
erDiagram
    USER ||--o{ DEVICE : has
    USER ||--o{ NAMESPACE : owns
    NAMESPACE ||--o{ FILE : contains
    FILE ||--o{ FILE_VERSION : has
    FILE_VERSION ||--o{ VERSION_BLOCK : "ordered list of"
    BLOCK ||--o{ VERSION_BLOCK : "used by"
    USER {
        bigint user_id PK
        string email
        bigint quota_used
    }
    DEVICE {
        uuid device_id PK
        bigint user_id FK
        bigint last_synced_change
        timestamp last_seen
    }
    NAMESPACE {
        bigint namespace_id PK
        bigint owner_id FK
    }
    FILE {
        bigint file_id PK
        bigint namespace_id FK
        string path
        int latest_version
        bool is_deleted
        string checksum
    }
    FILE_VERSION {
        bigint file_id FK
        int version_no
        uuid device_id
        timestamp created_at
    }
    BLOCK {
        string block_hash PK
        int size
        int ref_count
    }
    VERSION_BLOCK {
        bigint file_id FK
        int version_no FK
        int position
        string block_hash FK
    }
  • Namespace = a user's root folder (or a shared folder).
  • File versions are immutable rows — never updated, only appended → full history for "restore previous version".
  • A version is an ordered list of block hashes. Blocks have a ref_count for dedup and garbage collection.

docs.title: Upload flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C1 as Client 1 (laptop)
    participant API as API servers
    participant MDB as Metadata DB
    participant BS as Block servers
    participant S3 as Cloud storage
    participant NS as Notification service
    participant C2 as Client 2 (phone)
    par metadata
        C1->>API: new version of report.xlsx (block list)
        API->>MDB: status = uploading, record pending version
        API->>NS: notify: report.xlsx uploading
        NS->>C2: change event
    and bytes
        C1->>BS: missing blocks only
        BS->>S3: store blocks (compressed, encrypted)
        S3-->>API: upload-complete callback
        API->>MDB: commit version, status = uploaded
        API->>NS: notify: report.xlsx updated
        NS->>C2: change event
    end

Two requests in parallel: (1) add file metadata (status pending/uploading), and (2) upload blocks. When storage confirms all blocks, the version is committed (status uploaded) and other devices are notified.

docs.title: Download / sync flow
docs.text:
How does a device learn something changed?

  • Online: the notification service tells it.
  • Offline: changes accumulate (in the offline backup queue / change log); on reconnect it asks "what changed since change #N?" (last_synced_change).
sequenceDiagram
    participant NS as Notification service
    participant C2 as Client 2
    participant API as API servers
    participant MDB as Metadata DB
    participant BS as Block servers
    participant S3 as Cloud storage
    NS->>C2: report.xlsx changed
    C2->>API: get changes since #N
    API->>MDB: fetch new version + block list
    MDB-->>API: blocks [b1,b2,b7,b4]
    API-->>C2: block list
    C2->>C2: compare with local blocks → need b7
    C2->>BS: download b7
    BS->>S3: get b7
    S3-->>BS: b7
    BS-->>C2: b7 (decrypt, decompress)
    C2->>C2: reassemble file, update last_synced_change

docs.title: Notification service: why long polling?
docs.text:
Long polling WebSocket Direction needed Server → client only, infrequent Bi-directional, frequent Fit for Drive ✅ changes are occasional bursts; client then calls normal APIs Overkill Fit for chat (Ch. 12) Weaker ✅

Each client holds a long-poll connection; when a change arrives (or the poll times out), the server responds; the client fetches metadata changes and reconnects. Connections are cheap to hold but numerous — millions per cluster. If a notification server dies, clients reconnect to another one (they can't lose data — they'll fetch the change log).

docs.title: Conflicts
docs.text:
Two devices edit the same file before syncing. The first version to commit wins; the second is saved as a conflicted copy (report (Asha's laptop's conflicted copy 2026-11-17).xlsx) and the user merges manually. (Automatic merging only works for formats with structure — that's collaborative editing, out of scope.)

Implement "first wins" with optimistic concurrency: a commit says "new version based on version 7"; if latest is no longer 7, the commit is rejected as a conflict.

docs.title: Saving storage space
docs.text:
Storage grows forever unless you design against it. Four levers, from biggest to smallest win in a typical deployment:

  1. Content-addressed blocks give dedup for free. Same hash → same object; just increment ref_count. Per-account dedup is safe; global dedup across users saves more but can reveal whether some other user already holds a file, so apply it carefully.
  2. Versions are cheap but not free. Because a new version only adds the changed blocks, history costs little — but an app that auto-saves every few seconds can still create thousands of versions. Thin history as it ages (dense recent versions, sparse old ones) and cap retention per plan.
  3. Tiering. Data nobody has opened for months moves to an archive tier at a fraction of the price; restoring it is slower, which users rarely notice for old files.
  4. Garbage collection. When versions expire or files are deleted, blocks whose ref_count hits zero are removed — after a grace period, in case of bugs or restores.

docs.title: Failure handling
docs.text:
Sort failures by what's at risk:

Could we lose data? This is the one that matters most.

  • Blocks are written to object storage that replicates within a region, and we replicate to a second region; a version is only committed after all its blocks are durably stored — so a crash mid-upload leaves an uncommitted version, never a corrupt file.
  • The metadata DB runs with synchronous replicas and automatic leader failover; regular backups and point-in-time recovery protect against bad writes (bugs, accidental mass deletes).

Could sync stall?

  • If a notification server dies, its clients' long polls drop; they reconnect elsewhere and ask "what changed since my last sync?" — the change log makes missed notifications harmless.
  • Change events for offline devices sit in replicated queues/logs, so a broker failure delays sync but loses nothing.

Could requests fail?

  • API servers and block servers are stateless behind redundant load balancers; an unfinished block job is simply retried by another server (block uploads are idempotent — same hash, same object).
  • The metadata cache is replicated; a lost node only means more DB reads until it's replaced.

docs.title: Step 4 · Wrap-up — other directions
docs.text:
• Where should chunking happen? We put splitting/compression/encryption in block servers so the logic lives in one trusted place. The alternative — clients upload blocks straight to object storage with signed URLs — removes a hop and server cost, but every client platform (Windows, macOS, iOS, Android, web) must implement the same chunking and crypto correctly, and a buggy or tampered client can upload bad data. Many real systems do a hybrid: clients chunk and hash, servers verify.
  • Selective sync / on-demand files. Desktop clients show placeholders and download content only when opened — essential once users have more cloud data than laptop disk.
  • Sharing and permissions. ACLs per namespace/file, expiring share links, and permission checks on every metadata and block request.
  • Search. Index file names (and optionally contents) asynchronously into a search service, respecting permissions.
  • Presence. If other features need "who's online", split it out of the notification service into its own service.

docs.title: Interviewer follow-ups
docs.text:
A user changes 1 byte in a 1 GB file. What gets uploaded?

With 4 MB fixed blocks, the block containing that byte changes → upload ~4 MB (compressed), not 1 GB. If bytes were inserted (not modified), fixed chunking would shift every later block; content-defined chunking keeps the change local, so still only one or two blocks are uploaded.

Why not use eventual consistency for metadata, like Dynamo?

Because divergent metadata means devices disagree on which blocks make up a file — users would see different content or silently overwrite each other's changes. Sync correctness needs a single, linearizable view of "latest version" and atomic commits; we accept the availability/latency cost for metadata while keeping the bulky, immutable blocks in a highly available store.

How do you make the upload resumable?

The client first registers the upload (gets a session ID and the list of blocks the server still needs). Each block is uploaded independently and acknowledged. After a crash or disconnect, the client asks the session which blocks are still missing and sends only those. The version commits only when all blocks are confirmed.

How does a phone that was offline for a week catch up efficiently?

It sends last_synced_change = N; the server returns the change log entries since N (file IDs and their latest versions — not every intermediate version). The phone downloads only block lists for those files and only blocks it doesn't have. For huge backlogs, it can sync folders the user actually opens first (selective sync).

How would you implement sharing a folder with another user?

Shared folders are namespaces with an ACL (owner, editors, viewers). The recipient's device subscribes to notifications for that namespace; metadata queries include all namespaces the user can access. Permission checks happen in the API servers and block servers (signed, scoped block URLs) on every access.

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
Practice 1 — Delta sync bandwidth

A designer saves a 200 MB PSD 30 times a day; each save changes ~5% of the file, scattered across ~6 blocks of 4 MB. How much is uploaded per day with full-file upload vs block-level delta sync?

Solution. Full: 30 × 200 MB = 6 GB/day. Delta: 30 × 6 × 4 MB = 720 MB/day (≈ 8× less, before compression).

Practice 2 — Dedup savings

A company has 10,000 employees; each has the same 300 MB onboarding folder in their Drive. Storage with and without per-company dedup?

Solution. Without: 10,000 × 300 MB = 3 TB. With dedup: 300 MB (+ metadata and ref counts). This is why block-level, content-addressed storage is so effective in workplaces.

Practice 3 — Version thinning

A file is auto-saved every 30 seconds for 8 hours a day, every day. Design a retention policy that keeps the last hour minute-by-minute, the last week hourly, and older history daily up to 30 days. How many versions are kept at most?

Solution. Last hour: 60; last week (excluding last hour): ~7 × 24 = 168; days 8–30: 23 → ~251 versions instead of 960/day × 30 = 28,800.

docs.title: Revision checklist
docs.text:
• I can state requirements and estimate storage and upload QPS.
  • I can evolve the single-server design into the full architecture and explain each component.
  • I can explain block splitting, hashing, delta sync, compression, encryption — and content-defined chunking.
  • I can justify strong consistency for metadata and design the metadata schema.
  • I can walk through the upload and download/sync flows, including offline devices.
  • I can explain long polling for notifications, conflict handling, storage savings and failure handling.

Next: 16 · Revision Cheat Sheet

docs.title: 01 · Scale from Zero to Millions of Users
docs.text:
⏱ 45 min read 🔥 Foundation for every other chapter Book: Chapter 1

TL;DR

  • Start with one server, then peel pieces off it as each one becomes the bottleneck: database → web tier → cache → static files → sessions → data centers → async work → the database again.
  • Scale out, not up: add more machines behind a load balancer and keep the web tier stateless so any server can handle any request.
  • Replicate the database (one leader for writes, many followers for reads), put a cache in front of it, and push static files to a CDN.
  • Use message queues to decouple slow work, and multiple data centers with geo-routing for availability.
  • When one database can't hold the data any more, shard it — choosing the shard key is the most important decision, and hotspots/resharding/joins are the price.

docs.title: The intuition: a dhaba that becomes a chain
docs.text:
Picture a roadside dhaba run by one person. They take orders, cook, serve and handle cash. That's a single server. It works until the lunch rush.

  • First they hire a separate cook so the person at the counter only takes orders → separate the database from the web server.
  • Then they open more counters and put a person at the door saying "go to counter 3" → load balancer + more web servers.
  • The cook writes the recipe book once and gives copies to helpers who can only read it → database replication.
  • The most popular dishes are pre-cooked and kept warm → cache.
  • Packaged drinks are sold from stalls near each colony instead of the main kitchen → CDN.
  • Order slips go on a rail and cooks pick them up when free → message queue.
  • Eventually there are branches in different cities → multiple data centers, and the menu is split across specialised kitchens → sharding.

Every technique in this chapter is just that story, told with computers.

docs.title: Stage 0 · A single server
docs.text:
Everything — the web app, the database, the cache — runs on one machine. Let's trace one request, because every later design is a variation of this flow.

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User (browser / app)
    participant D as DNS
    participant S as Web server
    U->>D: Where is shop.example.in?
    D-->>U: 203.0.113.42
    U->>S: GET /products/42 (HTTP)
    S->>S: run business logic, read DB
    S-->>U: 200 OK + JSON / HTML
  1. The user types a domain. DNS (usually a paid third-party service like Route 53 or Cloudflare) translates it to an IP address.
  2. The client sends an HTTP request straight to that IP.
  3. The server returns HTML (for browsers) or JSON (for mobile apps and SPAs).

Traffic comes from two kinds of clients: web apps (server-side code in Java/Python/Go plus HTML/JS in the browser) and mobile apps (talk to the server over HTTP, usually exchanging JSON, e.g. GET /products/42 → {"id":42,"name":"Kurta","price":899}).

Why this can't last

One machine = one single point of failure (SPOF). If it reboots, the product is down. And CPU, RAM and disk are shared by the web app and the database, so they fight each other.

docs.title: Stage 1 · Separate the database
docs.text:
Move the database onto its own machine. Now the web tier (handles requests) and the data tier (stores data) can be scaled independently — you'll soon want 20 web servers but still 1 primary database.

flowchart LR
    U[Users] --> W[Web server]
    W -->|read / write| DB[(Database)]

docs.title: Which database? SQL vs NoSQL
docs.text:
This is a decision you'll make in every design, so let's do it properly.

Relational (SQL) Non-relational (NoSQL) Examples MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle Cassandra, DynamoDB, MongoDB, HBase, Redis, Neo4j Data model Tables, rows, fixed schema Key-value, document, wide-column, graph Joins Yes, powerful SQL Usually no (you denormalise instead) Transactions Full ACID across rows/tables Often limited to one key / one partition Scaling writes Hard beyond one primary (needs sharding) Built to partition across many nodes Best for Money, orders, inventory, anything relational with integrity rules Huge volume, simple access patterns, flexible schema, low latency

Default to SQL. It has decades of tooling and correctness guarantees. Reach for NoSQL when one of these is true:

  • You need very low latency at very high scale for simple lookups (e.g. session store, feature flags).
  • Your data is unstructured / semi-structured or the schema changes often (product catalogs with wildly different attributes).
  • You mostly serialise and deserialise blobs (JSON documents) by key.
  • You must store a massive amount of data (billions of rows, petabytes) and write throughput matters more than joins.

The four NoSQL families, with one sentence each:

Family Mental model Example use Key-value A giant distributed HashMap<String, byte[]> Sessions, carts, caches (Redis, DynamoDB) Document Key → JSON document you can query inside User profiles, catalogs (MongoDB) Wide-column Row key → sorted map of columns, built for heavy writes Chat messages, time series (Cassandra, HBase) Graph Nodes + edges with fast traversal Social graph, recommendations (Neo4j)

In an interview

Don't say "NoSQL because it scales". Say what access pattern you have and why that store fits it: "Messages are written constantly and read by (channel, time range), so a wide-column store like Cassandra partitioned by channel_id and clustered by message_id fits perfectly."

docs.title: Stage 2 · Vertical vs horizontal scaling
docs.text:
Vertical ("scale up") Horizontal ("scale out") What Bigger machine: more CPU, RAM, faster disk More machines sharing the load Pros Dead simple, no code changes, no distributed-systems problems Practically unlimited, failure of one machine is survivable Cons Hard ceiling; cost grows super-linearly; still one SPOF; upgrades need downtime Needs load balancing, stateless servers, data partitioning Use when Traffic is low/moderate, or for the database early on Large scale, high availability required

Vertical scaling is not "bad" — it's often the right first move for a database (a single big Postgres box goes surprisingly far). But for the web tier you want horizontal scaling from early on, and that needs a load balancer.

docs.title: Stage 3 · Load balancer
docs.text:
A load balancer (LB) sits in front of a pool of web servers and spreads requests across them.

flowchart LR
    U[Users] -->|public IP| LB{{Load balancer}}
    LB -->|private IP| W1[Web server 1]
    LB -->|private IP| W2[Web server 2]
    W1 --> DB[(Database)]
    W2 --> DB
  • Users only know the LB's public IP. Servers sit on private IPs (reachable inside the network, not from the internet) — better security.
  • If server 1 dies, the LB's health checks notice and send everything to server 2 → failover.
  • If traffic grows, add server 3, 4, 5 to the pool → the LB starts using them automatically.

docs.title: How does the LB pick a server?
docs.text: Algorithm How Good for Round robin 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3… Identical servers, similar requests Weighted round robin Bigger servers get more turns Mixed hardware Least connections Send to the server with fewest active connections Long-lived or uneven requests (WebSockets, uploads) Least response time Fastest-responding healthy server Latency-sensitive APIs IP hash / consistent hashing hash(client IP or key) → server Stickiness, cache locality

docs.title: L4 vs L7 load balancing
docs.text:
• Layer 4 (transport): routes on IP + port only, never reads the HTTP request. Extremely fast, protocol-agnostic. Example: AWS NLB.
  • Layer 7 (application): reads the HTTP request — path, headers, cookies — so it can route /api/* to API servers and /static/* elsewhere, terminate TLS, do auth, rate limiting. Example: NGINX, Envoy, AWS ALB.

\"Isn't the load balancer itself a single point of failure?\"

Yes, if there's only one. Real setups run LBs in pairs (active-passive with a floating/virtual IP, or active-active), and DNS can return multiple LB IPs. Managed cloud LBs are already replicated across availability zones.

docs.title: Stage 4 · Database replication
docs.text:
The web tier now survives failures. The database doesn't. Replication keeps copies of the data on several servers.

The classic setup is leader–follower (the book uses the older master–slave terms):

  • The leader (primary) accepts all writes — INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE.
  • Followers (replicas) receive a copy of every change and serve reads.
  • Most apps read far more than they write (often 10:1 to 100:1), so you run one leader, many followers.
flowchart TB
    W[Web servers] -->|writes| L[(Leader DB)]
    W -->|reads| F1[(Follower 1)]
    W -->|reads| F2[(Follower 2)]
    W -->|reads| F3[(Follower 3)]
    L -. replication log .-> F1
    L -. replication log .-> F2
    L -. replication log .-> F3

What you gain

  • Performance — reads are spread over many machines and run in parallel.
  • Reliability — data survives a disk failure, even a whole data center burning down, if replicas are elsewhere.
  • Availability — if one DB machine is down, others still answer.

What happens when something fails

  • A follower dies → reads go to other followers (or temporarily to the leader); a new follower is created from a snapshot + the log.
  • The leader dies → a follower is promoted to leader (failover). The hard part: that follower may be slightly behind, so the last few writes can be missing. Production systems use consensus (e.g. Raft in etcd, Orchestrator for MySQL) and careful recovery to decide who's freshest.

docs.title: Going deeper: sync vs async replication and lag
docs.text:
Mode Leader waits for… Upside Downside Synchronous Follower to confirm before telling client "OK" Follower is never behind One slow follower slows every write Asynchronous Nothing — replies immediately Fast writes Replication lag: followers can be seconds behind Semi-sync At least one follower Good compromise Slightly slower writes

Replication lag causes real bugs. Classic example — read-your-own-writes:

Riya updates her profile photo (write → leader). The page reloads and reads from a follower that hasn't received the change yet. She sees her old photo and thinks the upload failed.

Fixes: read the user's own data from the leader for a short time after they write; or track the replication position and only read from followers that have caught up; or route by user so a user sticks to one replica.

Beyond leader–follower

Multi-leader (several DCs accept writes, then sync) and leaderless (Dynamo-style, any node accepts writes, quorums decide) exist. They trade simplicity for availability and bring write conflicts. Chapter 6 (Key-Value Store) goes deep on leaderless replication.

docs.title: Stage 5 · Cache
docs.text:
Every page load hits the database several times. A cache keeps the results of expensive or frequent reads in memory, which is roughly 100–1000× faster than going to a database on disk.

flowchart LR
    W[Web server] -->|1. get key| C[(Cache<br/>Redis / Memcached)]
    C -->|2a. hit: return| W
    W -->|2b. miss: query| DB[(Database)]
    DB -->|3. rows| W
    W -->|4. set key, TTL| C

The flow above — check cache, on a miss read the DB and fill the cache — is the most common pattern. The book calls it a read-through cache; many engineers call this exact flow cache-aside (the application does the filling). Here it is in Java:

public User getUser(long id) {
    String key = "user:" + id;
    User cached = cache.get(key);              // 1. try the cache
    if (cached != null) return cached;         // 2a. hit

    User fromDb = userRepository.findById(id); // 2b. miss → database
    if (fromDb != null) {
        cache.set(key, fromDb, Duration.ofMinutes(10)); // 3. populate with a TTL
    }
    return fromDb;
}

public void updateUser(User u) {
    userRepository.save(u);         // write the source of truth first
    cache.delete("user:" + u.id()); // then invalidate (don't update) the cached copy
}

docs.title: Caching strategies — the full menu
docs.text: Strategy Read path Write path Use when Cache-aside (lazy loading) App checks cache, on miss loads from DB and fills App writes DB, deletes cache key Default for read-heavy apps Read-through Cache library itself loads from DB on a miss — You want loading logic in the cache layer Write-through — Write cache and DB synchronously Data must be in cache right after write Write-behind (write-back) — Write cache now, flush to DB later in batches Very write-heavy, can tolerate small loss (counters, likes) Write-around — Write DB only; cache filled on next read Data written once, rarely re-read

docs.title: Things to think about before adding a cache
docs.text:
1. When to cache. Data that's read often, changed rarely. Never treat the cache as the only copy — it lives in volatile memory and a restart wipes it.
  2. Expiration (TTL). Without one, stale data lives forever and memory fills up. Too short → you hammer the DB reloading; too long → users see stale data. Minutes to hours is typical; tune per data type.
  3. Consistency. The DB write and the cache update are not one transaction, so they can drift (especially across regions). Deleting the key on write (as above) is safer than updating it, because two concurrent updates can't leave the wrong value behind. Facebook's Scaling Memcache paper is the classic reference on how hard this gets.
  4. Failure. One cache server is a SPOF. Run several (across zones / DCs) and over-provision memory so a node loss or growth spike doesn't cause mass eviction.
  5. Eviction policy. When memory is full, something must go:
    • LRU (least recently used) — the usual default.
    • LFU (least frequently used) — better when popularity is stable.
    • FIFO — simplest, rarely the best.

Cache stampede (thundering herd)

A hot key (say, the home-page feed) expires. 10,000 requests miss at the same instant and all hit the database together, which falls over. Fixes: let only one request rebuild the key (a lock or single-flight), serve the stale value while one worker refreshes it, and add random jitter to TTLs so keys don't all expire at the same second.

docs.title: Stage 6 · Content Delivery Network (CDN)
docs.text:
Images, videos, CSS and JS are static — the same bytes for every user. Serving them from your web servers wastes their CPU and bandwidth and is slow for far-away users. A CDN is a network of servers spread around the world (edge locations) that cache static content close to users.

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as User A (Mumbai)
    participant E as CDN edge (Mumbai)
    participant O as Origin (S3 / web server)
    participant B as User B (Pune)
    A->>E: GET cdn.example.in/logo.png
    E->>O: miss → fetch logo.png
    O-->>E: logo.png + Cache-Control TTL
    E-->>A: logo.png (now cached at edge)
    B->>E: GET cdn.example.in/logo.png
    E-->>B: hit → served from Mumbai, origin untouched
  • The URL points at the CDN's domain (e.g. cdn.example.in/... mapped to the CDN provider).
  • On a miss, the edge fetches from the origin (your server or S3), caches it for the TTL the origin specifies, and returns it.
  • Every later request in that region is a hit until the TTL expires.

Pull vs push CDN. Pull (above) fetches lazily on first request — easy, good for most sites. Push means you upload content to the CDN ahead of time — useful for big files you know will be popular (a new movie release).

Things to think about

  • Cost — you pay per GB transferred. Don't put rarely-accessed files on the CDN.
  • Expiry — time-sensitive content needs a sensible TTL.
  • CDN outage — the client/app should be able to fall back to the origin.
  • Invalidation — to remove a file early, call the vendor's invalidation API, or better, use versioned URLs (app.css?v=42 or app.3f9a1c.css). A new URL is a new object, so there's nothing to invalidate.

After stages 5 and 6, the web servers no longer serve static files, and the DB is protected by the cache.

docs.title: Stage 7 · Stateless web tier
docs.text:
To add and remove web servers freely (auto-scaling), no web server may hold user state like session data.

Stateful — user A's session lives in server 1's memory. Every request from A must reach server 1. LBs can do this with sticky sessions, but then adding/removing servers or losing a server breaks sessions, and load spreads unevenly.

Stateless — session data lives in a shared store (Redis, a NoSQL DB, or an RDBMS). Any server can handle any request; servers are interchangeable "cattle", not "pets".

flowchart LR
    U[Users] --> LB{{Load balancer}}
    LB --> W1[Web 1]
    LB --> W2[Web 2]
    LB --> W3[Web 3]
    W1 & W2 & W3 --> S[(Shared session store<br/>Redis / NoSQL)]

Now auto-scaling is trivial: a rule like "if average CPU > 70% for 5 minutes, add 2 servers" just works, because a new server needs nothing from the old ones.

Going deeper: tokens instead of sessions

Another way to be stateless is to put the state in the client: a signed token (e.g. a JWT) that each server can verify with a shared key, without any lookup. Trade-off: you can't easily revoke a token before it expires, so it's often combined with short expiry + a small revocation list.

docs.title: Stage 8 · Multiple data centers
docs.text:
As users spread across the world, one data center means high latency for distant users and a total outage if that DC fails. So we run two or more.

flowchart TB
    U[Users] --> G{{GeoDNS}}
    G -->|"x% (nearest)"| DC1
    G -->|"(100-x)%"| DC2
    subgraph DC1[Data center: US-East]
      LB1{{LB}} --> W1[Web tier] --> C1[(Cache)] & D1[(DB)]
    end
    subgraph DC2[Data center: US-West]
      LB2{{LB}} --> W2[Web tier] --> C2[(Cache)] & D2[(DB)]
    end
    D1 <-. async replication .-> D2
  • GeoDNS resolves the domain to a different IP depending on where the user is, sending them to the nearest DC.
  • If DC2 goes down, DNS sends 100% of traffic to DC1.

What makes this hard:

  1. Traffic redirection — tools (GeoDNS, anycast, global LBs) to steer users and to fail over quickly. DNS caching means failover isn't instant; keep TTLs low.
  2. Data synchronisation — after failover, users land in a DC that must already have their data. Data is replicated across DCs, usually asynchronously (so a few seconds of writes can be lost in a disaster). Netflix's active-active multi-region setup is the well-known example.
  3. Testing and deployment — every DC must run the same code and config. Automated deployment is mandatory.

Active-passive vs active-active: in active-passive, the second DC is a warm standby. In active-active, both serve live traffic — better utilisation and faster failover, but you must handle concurrent writes to the same data in two places.

docs.title: Stage 9 · Message queue
docs.text:
Some work is slow (resizing images, sending emails, transcoding video) and shouldn't block the user's request. A message queue is a durable buffer between services that enables asynchronous communication.

  • Producers publish messages to the queue.
  • Consumers pull messages and do the work.
  • Neither needs the other to be up at the same moment → decoupling.
flowchart LR
    W[Web servers<br/>producers] -->|"publish job: crop photo 123"| Q[[Message queue]]
    Q --> P1[Photo worker 1]
    Q --> P2[Photo worker 2]
    Q --> P3[Photo worker 3]
    P1 & P2 & P3 --> S[(Object storage)]

Example: a photo app lets users crop, sharpen and blur. The web server just drops a job in the queue and replies "processing…" immediately. Workers pick jobs up at their own pace. If the queue grows, add workers; if it's usually empty, remove some. Producers and consumers scale independently.

docs.title: Going deeper
docs.text:
• Delivery guarantees. At-most-once (may lose messages), at-least-once (may duplicate — the common default), exactly-once (expensive, limited). With at-least-once, make consumers idempotent: processing the same message twice must be harmless (e.g. dedupe by message ID).
  • Queue vs log. RabbitMQ/SQS-style queues delete a message once consumed. Kafka is a log: messages are retained, consumers track an offset, many consumer groups can replay the same stream.
  • Backpressure. Queue depth is a key metric — growing depth means consumers can't keep up. It's also a natural auto-scaling signal.
  • Dead-letter queue (DLQ). Messages that keep failing are moved aside instead of blocking everything.

docs.title: Stage 10 · Logging, metrics, automation
docs.text:
At a few servers these are nice-to-haves. At this scale they're mandatory.

  • Logging — collect error logs from every server into one searchable place (ELK / OpenSearch, Loki, Cloud Logging).
  • Metrics at three levels:
    • Host: CPU, memory, disk I/O, network.
    • Aggregated/service: DB tier latency, cache hit ratio, queue depth, error rate.
    • Business: daily active users, retention, revenue, sign-ups.
  • Automation — CI (every commit is built and tested automatically), CD (automated, repeatable deploys), infrastructure as code.

The four golden signals

For any service, watch latency, traffic, errors and saturation. If you mention these by name in an interview, you sound like someone who has run production systems.

docs.title: Stage 11 · Scaling the database: sharding
docs.text:
Data keeps growing, and the single leader is overloaded. Two options again.

Vertical: buy a monster database server. Cloud providers offer machines with terabytes of RAM, and Stack Overflow famously ran on a single primary database for years with ~10M monthly visitors. But: hard hardware limits, still a SPOF, and very expensive.

Horizontal = sharding: split the data across many databases (shards). Every shard has the same schema but holds a different subset of rows.

flowchart TB
    A[App] --> R{"shard = user_id % 4"}
    R -->|0| S0[(Shard 0<br/>users 0,4,8…)]
    R -->|1| S1[(Shard 1<br/>users 1,5,9…)]
    R -->|2| S2[(Shard 2<br/>users 2,6,10…)]
    R -->|3| S3[(Shard 3<br/>users 3,7,11…)]

docs.title: Choosing the shard key (the most important decision)
docs.text:
The shard key (partition key) decides which shard a row lives on. A good key:

  1. Spreads data evenly (high cardinality, no skew).
  2. Matches the main query — the common request should hit one shard, not all of them.
  3. Rarely changes — moving a row between shards is expensive.

Common sharding strategies:

Strategy How Pro Con Hash-based hash(key) % N (or consistent hashing) Even spread Range queries hit all shards; changing N moves most data Range-based A–F → shard 1, G–M → shard 2 … or by date Range scans are cheap Hotspots (all new data lands on the latest shard) Directory / lookup A table maps key → shard Flexible, easy to rebalance The lookup service is extra infra + possible SPOF Geo-based Users in India → shard IN Data locality, data-residency laws Uneven sizes

docs.title: The new problems sharding brings
docs.text:
1. Resharding. A shard fills up (growth) or some shards fill faster (skew) → you must change the sharding function and move data. With % N, changing N relocates almost everything. Consistent hashing (Chapter 5) fixes this by moving only ~1/N of the keys.
  2. The celebrity / hotspot problem. If Virat Kohli, Shah Rukh Khan and Taylor Swift land on the same shard, it melts under reads. Fixes: give hot keys dedicated shards, split a hot key further (e.g. celebrity_id#1..#10), and cache aggressively.
  3. Joins and transactions across shards. A SQL join across shards is slow or impossible, and cross-shard transactions need two-phase commit. Common workaround: denormalise — store data so each query can be answered from one table on one shard.

Finally, move workloads that don't need relational features (e.g. activity logs, session data, counters) into NoSQL stores to take load off the relational database.

docs.title: The final picture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    U["Users (web + mobile)"] --> DNS{{GeoDNS}}
    U --> CDN[(CDN<br/>static assets)]
    DNS --> LB{{Load balancer}}
    subgraph DC["Data center (×2 or more)"]
      LB --> W1[Web 1] & W2[Web 2] & W3[Web N]
      W1 & W2 & W3 --> CACHE[(Cache cluster)]
      W1 & W2 & W3 --> SESS[(Session store / NoSQL)]
      W1 & W2 & W3 --> SH0[(Shard 0<br/>leader + followers)] & SH1[(Shard 1<br/>leader + followers)]
      W1 & W2 & W3 --> MQ[[Message queue]] --> WK[Workers]
      MON[Logging · Metrics · Automation]
    end

The scaling checklist (memorise this — it's your vocabulary for every later chapter):
