  • Web tier is stateless; state lives in shared stores.
  • Redundancy at every tier — nothing important runs on exactly one machine.
  • Cache reads aggressively; put static assets on a CDN.
  • Replicate databases; shard them when one leader isn't enough.
  • Multiple data centers with geo-routing and failover.
  • Decouple with queues; split big apps into independent services.
  • Monitor everything and automate builds, tests and deploys.

docs.title: Trade-offs at a glance
docs.text: Technique You gain You pay Load balancer Availability, horizontal scale Extra hop; LB must itself be redundant Replication Read scale, durability, failover Replication lag, failover complexity Cache Latency, DB offload Staleness, invalidation bugs, stampedes CDN Global latency, origin offload Cost per GB, invalidation Stateless tier Easy auto-scaling, resilience A shared state store to run Multi-DC Disaster tolerance, lower global latency Cross-DC sync, possible data loss on failover, ops cost Message queue Decoupling, smoothing spikes Eventual results, duplicates, another system to run Sharding Write + storage scale Resharding, hotspots, no cross-shard joins/transactions

docs.title: Interviewer follow-ups
docs.text:
Your read replicas are 5 seconds behind. A user edits a post and immediately sees the old version. What do you do?

This is a read-your-own-writes problem caused by async replication lag. Options: (1) for a few seconds after a user writes, route that user's reads to the leader; (2) record the leader's log position at write time and only read from replicas that have reached it; (3) update the client-side state optimistically so the UI shows the new version anyway. Mention that making replication synchronous would also fix it but would hurt write latency and availability.

The cache goes down completely. What happens and how do you protect the database?

Every read becomes a DB read — the DB may get 10–50× its normal load and fall over (a cascading failure). Protections: run the cache as a replicated cluster across zones; put a circuit breaker / rate limit on the path to the DB; warm a new cache before sending full traffic; serve degraded responses (e.g. a slightly stale feed) rather than failing completely.

Why delete the cache key on update instead of writing the new value into it?

Two concurrent writers can interleave: A writes DB=1, B writes DB=2, B sets cache=2, A sets cache=1 → the cache now holds a stale value with no expiry in sight. Deleting is idempotent and order-insensitive: the next reader reloads the true value. (There's still a small race with a concurrent reader; TTLs bound the damage.)

How would you pick a shard key for an e-commerce orders table?

Look at the dominant queries: "show my orders" (by user_id) and "get order X" (by order_id). Sharding by user_id keeps all of a user's orders on one shard (fast history page, no scatter-gather). Then embed the shard in the order ID (or keep a small order_id → user_id lookup) so direct lookups also hit one shard. Watch for skew from huge B2B customers — they may need their own shard.

When would you NOT add a cache?

When data is write-heavy or changes on almost every read (low hit ratio), when strong consistency is required and staleness is unacceptable (account balance during a transfer), or when the DB already meets the latency target — a cache adds an extra system to run and a new class of bugs.

Sticky sessions vs a shared session store — which and why?

Shared store. Sticky sessions break on server failure (users get logged out), make scale-in painful, and skew load. A shared store (Redis cluster) adds ~1 ms per request but makes servers interchangeable. Sticky sessions are acceptable only for short-lived, rebuildable state or as a cache-locality optimisation.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
Avoid these

  • Jumping straight to "microservices + Kafka + Cassandra" for a system with 1,000 users. Scale to the stated requirements.
  • Adding a cache without saying what is cached, the TTL, and how it's invalidated.
  • Saying "add replicas" without mentioning replication lag and what it breaks.
  • Sharding without naming the shard key and justifying it with the main query.
  • Forgetting that the load balancer, cache and queue also need redundancy.
  • Treating the cache as a database (data only in memory).

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
Practice 1 — Order the steps

A startup's single server is at 90% CPU. The database and app share the box, all images are served by the app, and sessions are stored in server memory. List the first four changes you'd make, in order, and why.

Solution. 1. Move the DB to its own machine — biggest immediate relief; app and DB stop competing. 2. Put static images on a CDN / object storage — removes a large share of bandwidth and CPU from the app. 3. Move sessions to Redis — makes the web tier stateless, which is a prerequisite for… 4. Add a load balancer + a second web server — horizontal scale and no single point of failure in the web tier. (Then: add a cache in front of the DB, then read replicas.)

Practice 2 — Cache sizing

A product catalog has 50M products, average 2 KB each. 80% of traffic hits the top 10% of products. How much memory to cache the hot set? How many 64 GB cache nodes (keep 30% headroom)?

Solution. Hot set = 10% × 50M = 5M products × 2 KB = 10 GB. With overhead (keys, data-structure metadata, fragmentation ~1.5×) ≈ 15 GB. With 30% headroom → ~21 GB. One 64 GB node fits it, but run at least 2–3 nodes (replicas / across zones) so a node failure doesn't send everything to the DB.

Practice 3 — Hot shard

You shard tweets by user_id. A celebrity with 100M followers posts and their shard's CPU hits 100% from reads. Give three mitigations.

Solution. (1) Cache the celebrity's recent tweets in a replicated cache tier so reads rarely reach the shard. (2) Add read replicas for that hot shard specifically. (3) Split the hot key — move the celebrity to a dedicated shard, or salt the key (user_id#0..#9) to spread their data across several shards and fan-in on read. (Bonus: for feeds, use a fan-out-on-read path for celebrities — see Chapter 11.)

Practice 4 — Availability maths

Your app needs the LB, web tier and DB to all be up. Each is 99.9% available. What's the overall availability? What changes if you run two independent DB replicas with automatic failover?

Solution. In series: 0.999³ ≈ 99.7% (~26 h downtime/year). Two DBs in parallel: 1 − (0.001)² = 99.9999%, so total ≈ 0.999 × 0.999 × 0.999999 ≈ 99.8%. Redundancy at every tier is what moves the number — try it in the widget in Chapter 2.

docs.title: Revision checklist
docs.text:
• I can trace a request from DNS lookup to JSON response.
  • I can explain SQL vs NoSQL with access patterns, not buzzwords, and name the four NoSQL families.
  • I know why vertical scaling hits a wall and what horizontal scaling requires.
  • I can name 4 load-balancing algorithms and explain L4 vs L7.
  • I can explain leader–follower replication, failover, and replication lag with an example.
  • I can write cache-aside code and compare 5 caching strategies; I know TTL, eviction, and stampede fixes.
  • I know how a CDN serves content, pull vs push, and why versioned URLs beat invalidation.
  • I can explain why the web tier must be stateless.
  • I can describe a multi-DC setup and its three hard problems.
  • I know what a message queue gives you, delivery guarantees, and why consumers must be idempotent.
  • I can compare sharding strategies, pick a shard key, and explain resharding, hotspots and joins.

Next: 02 · Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation

docs.title: 02 · Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation
docs.text:
⏱ 35 min read 🔥 Asked in almost every design round Book: Chapter 2

TL;DR

  • Estimation isn't about the exact answer — it's about showing a clear process and landing within the right order of magnitude (10× matters, 20% doesn't).
  • Know three tables cold: powers of two (KB→PB), latency numbers (memory ≈ 100 ns, SSD ≈ 100 µs, cross-continent ≈ 150 ms), and availability nines (99.9% ≈ 8.8 h/year down).
  • Core recipe: DAU × actions per user ÷ 86,400 = average QPS, × 2–3 for peak. Storage = writes/day × size × retention × replicas.
  • Round aggressively (86,400 ≈ 10⁵), write assumptions down, and always label units.
  • Use the numbers to make decisions: "40K QPS of reads → needs a cache", "55 PB → needs object storage, not a DB".

docs.title: The intuition: why estimate at all?
docs.text:
When a civil engineer plans a bridge, they don't start by choosing the paint. They first ask: how many trucks, how heavy, how often? The answer decides whether you need a footbridge or a steel suspension bridge.

Estimation does the same for software. "Design Twitter" could need 3 servers or 3,000 — and those are completely different designs. Five minutes of arithmetic tells you which one you're building, and it tells the interviewer that you design from requirements, not from buzzwords.

docs.title: Table 1 · Powers of two
docs.text:
Data sizes are powers of 2, but for estimation treat them as powers of 10 — the error is under 10%.

Power Exact value ≈ Name Short 2¹⁰ 1,024 1 thousand Kilobyte KB 2²⁰ 1,048,576 1 million Megabyte MB 2³⁰ 1,073,741,824 1 billion Gigabyte GB 2⁴⁰ ≈ 1.1 × 10¹² 1 trillion Terabyte TB 2⁵⁰ ≈ 1.1 × 10¹⁵ 1 quadrillion Petabyte PB

Size of everyday things (memorise roughly):

Thing Size 1 ASCII character 1 byte A long / a Snowflake ID / a timestamp 8 bytes A UUID 16 bytes (36 as a string) A tweet-length text (280 chars) ~300 bytes A typical DB row of metadata 100 B – 1 KB A compressed photo 200 KB – 2 MB 1 minute of 1080p video ~50–100 MB raw upload, ~10–20 MB per streamed rendition

docs.title: Table 2 · Latency numbers every programmer should know
docs.text:
These come from Jeff Dean's famous list (circa 2010, with modern approximations). Exact values drift as hardware improves; the ratios are what matter.

Operation Approx. time Think of it as… L1 cache reference 0.5–1 ns — Branch mispredict 3–5 ns — L2 cache reference 4–7 ns — Mutex lock/unlock ~25 ns — Main memory reference ~100 ns baseline "fast" Compress 1 KB (Snappy/zstd) ~2–3 µs cheap — compress before sending! Send 1 KB over 1 Gbps network ~10 µs — Random read from SSD ~16–100 µs ~1,000× slower than memory Read 1 MB sequentially from memory ~5–10 µs — Round trip within same data center ~0.5 ms — Read 1 MB sequentially from SSD ~50 µs – 1 ms — Disk (HDD) seek ~2–10 ms avoid random seeks! Read 1 MB sequentially from HDD ~1–5 ms — Packet round trip CA → Netherlands → CA ~150 ms the speed of light is the limit

Units: 1 ns = 10⁻⁹ s · 1 µs = 1,000 ns · 1 ms = 1,000 µs = 10⁶ ns.

Scaled to human time — if a memory reference took 1 second: an SSD read takes about 1–2 days, a disk seek about 3 months, and a cross-continent round trip about 5 years. That's why caches and data locality matter so much.

Takeaways you should say out loud in interviews:

  1. Memory is fast, disk is slow → cache hot data in RAM.
  2. Avoid disk seeks → prefer sequential I/O (this is why LSM-trees and append-only logs exist — Chapter 6).
  3. Compression is cheap → compress before sending over the network.
  4. Cross-region calls are expensive (~100+ ms) → keep chatty calls inside one data center; replicate data closer to users.

docs.title: Table 3 · Availability numbers ("the nines")
docs.text:
Availability = fraction of time a system is operational. A Service Level Agreement (SLA) is the promise a provider makes to customers (AWS, GCP and Azure set most compute SLAs at 99.9% or higher). Related terms: an SLO is your internal target, an SLI is the actual measured value.

Availability Downtime / day Downtime / week Downtime / month Downtime / year 99% ("two nines") 14.4 min 1.68 h 7.31 h 3.65 days 99.9% ("three nines") 1.44 min 10.1 min 43.8 min 8.77 h 99.99% ("four nines") 8.64 s 1.01 min 4.38 min 52.6 min 99.999% ("five nines") 864 ms 6.05 s 26.3 s 5.26 min 99.9999% ("six nines") 86.4 ms 605 ms 2.63 s 31.6 s

Composing availability:

  • In series (all parts needed): multiply. Three 99.9% parts → 0.999³ ≈ 99.7%. Every dependency lowers availability.
  • In parallel (any one is enough): 1 − (1 − a)ⁿ. Two 99% replicas → 1 − 0.01² = 99.99%. Redundancy raises it.

Try it:

docs.title: Handy conversions
docs.text: Fact Use this Seconds in a day = 86,400 ≈ 10⁵ (makes division trivial) Seconds in a month ≈ 2.5 × 10⁶ Seconds in a year ≈ 3 × 10⁷ 1 million requests/day ≈ 12 QPS 1 billion requests/day ≈ 12,000 QPS 1 request/sec sustained ≈ 86K/day ≈ 2.6M/month

docs.title: The core recipes
docs.text:
DAU                = MAU × (fraction active daily)
Average QPS        = DAU × (requests per user per day) / 86,400
Peak QPS           = Average QPS × (2 … 5)          ← traffic isn't flat
Read vs write QPS  = split by read:write ratio
Storage per day    = (writes per day) × (bytes per write)
Total storage      = storage per day × 365 × years × replication factor
Bandwidth          = QPS × bytes per request          (ingress for writes, egress for reads)
Cache memory       = ~20% of daily read data          (80/20 rule: 20% of items get 80% of reads)
Servers            = Peak QPS / (QPS one server can handle)  + headroom

Rule-of-thumb capacities (very rough, for a single commodity server):

Component Ballpark Stateless web/app server 1K – 10K simple requests/sec Relational DB (single primary) ~1K – 10K writes/sec, more reads with good indexes Redis / Memcached node ~100K+ ops/sec Kafka broker ~100K+ messages/sec Commodity server RAM 64 – 512 GB

docs.title: Interactive calculator
docs.text: Change any input and the whole chain recomputes. The defaults match Worked Example 1 below (100 KB is the average write: 20% of posts × 500 KB image).

docs.title: Worked example 1 · A microblogging service
docs.text:
(Numbers are invented for practice.)

Assumptions — write these on the board first:

  • 400 M monthly active users, 40% use it daily.
  • Each daily user publishes 3 posts and reads ~80 posts (timeline loads).
  • 20% of posts carry an image of ~500 KB (ignore video for now).
  • Keep everything for 7 years.

QPS

  • DAU = 400 M × 40% = 160 M
  • Write QPS = 160 M × 3 / 86,400 ≈ 480 M / 10⁵ ≈ 4,800 posts/sec; peak (×2) ≈ ~10,000
  • Read QPS = 160 M × 80 / 10⁵ ≈ 128,000 post reads/sec → read-heavy (~27:1) → caching and precomputed timelines are mandatory (Chapter 11).

Storage

  • Text + metadata per post: id 8 B + author id 8 B + text ~300 B + timestamps/counters ~100 B ≈ ~0.5 KB
  • Text/day = 480 M posts × 0.5 KB = 240 GB/day → ×365×7 ≈ ~0.6 PB (before replication)
  • Media/day = 480 M × 20% × 500 KB = 48 TB/day → ×365×7 ≈ ~123 PB

What the numbers tell us: media outweighs text by ~200×. Text belongs in a sharded database; media belongs in object storage (S3) + CDN. That single observation shapes the whole architecture.

docs.title: Worked example 2 · WhatsApp-style chat
docs.text:
Assumptions: 2 B MAU, 50% daily → 1 B DAU; each sends 40 messages/day; average message ~100 bytes; messages stored on server for 30 days (until delivered/backed up).

  • Messages/day = 1 B × 40 = 40 B/day
  • Average write QPS = 40 B / 10⁵ = 400,000 msgs/sec; peak ×3 ≈ 1.2 M/sec
  • Storage/day = 40 B × 100 B = 4 TB/day → 30 days ≈ 120 TB, ×3 replicas ≈ 360 TB
  • Connections: if 30% of DAU are online at peak → 300 M concurrent WebSocket connections. At ~1 M connections per well-tuned server → ~300+ chat servers just to hold connections (plus headroom).

Decision: the bottleneck isn't storage, it's concurrent connections and message fan-out → stateful chat servers + a key-value store optimised for writes (Chapter 12).

docs.title: Worked example 3 · YouTube-style video
docs.text:
Assumptions: 2 B MAU, 50% daily → 1 B DAU; each watches 5 videos/day; 1% of users upload 1 video/day; average upload 300 MB (raw); we store ~4 renditions totalling ~1.5× the raw size.

  • View QPS = 1 B × 5 / 10⁵ = 50,000 views/sec
  • Uploads/day = 1 B × 1% = 10 M videos/day → ~115 uploads/sec
  • Storage/day = 10 M × 300 MB × 1.5 ≈ 4.5 PB/day (!)
  • Egress: if an average view streams 100 MB → 5 B views × 100 MB = 500 PB/day served — only a CDN can do this.

Decision: cost is dominated by CDN egress and storage. Optimisations — serve only popular videos from CDN, compress better, store fewer renditions for unpopular videos — become first-class design topics (Chapter 14).

docs.title: Worked example 4 · URL shortener
docs.text:
Assumptions: 40 M new short links/day; each link is opened ~50 times over its life (read:write = 50:1); keep links for 15 years; ~250 bytes per record (long URL + code + owner + timestamps).

  • Write QPS = 40 M / 10⁵ ≈ 400/sec (precisely ~460)
  • Read QPS = ×50 ≈ 20,000–23,000/sec; peak ×2 ≈ ~45K/sec
  • Records over 15 years = 40 M × 365 × 15 ≈ 219 B records
  • Storage = 219 B × 250 B ≈ 55 TB (before replication)
  • Short-code length: need ≥ 219 B unique codes. Base-62: 62⁶ ≈ 57 B (too few), 62⁷ ≈ 3.5 T ✓ → 7 characters.

Decision: small records, huge count, reads ≫ writes → a sharded key-value store plus an aggressive cache for hot links. (Full design in Chapter 8.)

docs.title: Worked example 5 · Instagram-style photos — cache & servers
docs.text:
Assumptions: 500 M DAU; each views 50 photos/day; uploads 0.2 photos/day at 2 MB; metadata 1 KB per photo; a server handles 2,000 QPS.

  • Read QPS = 500 M × 50 / 10⁵ = 250,000/sec; peak ×2 = 500K/sec
  • Write QPS = 500 M × 0.2 / 10⁵ = 1,000 uploads/sec
  • Photo storage/day = 100 M × 2 MB = 200 TB/day
  • Metadata cache: daily reads = 25 B photo views; but unique photos viewed are far fewer. If the hot set is ~20% of the last 30 days of photos: 100 M × 30 × 20% × 1 KB ≈ 600 GB → ~10 cache nodes of 64 GB (with headroom/replicas).
  • API servers: 500K / 2,000 = 250 servers at peak, + ~30% headroom ≈ 325.

docs.title: Tips that impress interviewers
docs.text:
How to estimate in an interview

  1. State assumptions first, and confirm them: "I'll assume 100 M DAU — does that sound right?"
  2. Round ruthlessly. 48,213 × 6.8 → 50,000 × 7 = 350,000. Nobody expects decimal precision.
  3. Label every unit. "5" is meaningless; "5 MB/s" isn't.
  4. Separate reads from writes — they lead to different components (cache vs. write-optimised storage).
  5. Translate numbers into decisions — "so a single DB can handle the writes, but reads need a cache".
  6. Sanity-check with something you know: "1.2 M msgs/sec is plausible for a global chat app."
  7. Don't over-spend time. 3–5 minutes, then move to the design.

Commonly asked estimates

QPS and peak QPS · storage over N years · bandwidth (ingress/egress) · cache memory · number of servers / connections · ID space (how many bits / characters).

docs.title: Interviewer follow-ups
docs.text:
Why multiply by 2–5 for peak? Isn't that arbitrary?

Traffic follows daily cycles (evening peaks), weekly cycles and events (cricket finals, New Year, a sale). A peak-to-average ratio of 2–3× is common for consumer apps; event-driven spikes can be 10×+. The point is to design for peak, not average — and to say why you chose the multiplier ("India-heavy user base, so evening peak").

Your storage estimate is 55 PB. What does that change in the design?

No database will hold that economically. Use object storage (S3/GCS/HDFS) for blobs, keep only metadata (URLs, owners, sizes) in a database, tier old data to cold storage (cheaper, slower), deduplicate identical uploads, and push reads through a CDN.

How do you estimate how much cache you need?

Use the 80/20 rule: ~20% of objects get ~80% of reads. Cache memory ≈ 20% × (daily unique objects read) × object size. Then add overhead (~1.3–1.5× for keys and metadata) and replicas. Validate later with real hit-ratio metrics.

1 B requests/day — is that a lot?

It's ~12K QPS average, maybe 30K at peak — large, but very manageable: a few dozen stateless servers, a cache cluster, and a sharded/replicated DB. Converting "per day" to "per second" is the fastest way to calibrate how scary a number really is.

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
Practice 1 — Food delivery

A food-delivery app in India: 20 M DAU, each opens the app 4 times/day and each open triggers 10 API calls. Orders: 3 M/day. Each order writes 5 KB. Keep 3 years. Peak at dinner is 4× average. Compute API peak QPS, order write QPS, and order storage with 3× replication.

Solution. API: 20 M × 4 × 10 = 800 M/day → 800 M / 10⁵ = 8K QPS avg, ×4 = 32K peak. Orders: 3 M / 10⁵ ≈ 35/sec avg (~140 peak) — tiny for a DB. Storage: 3 M × 5 KB = 15 GB/day × 365 × 3 ≈ 16.4 TB × 3 replicas ≈ ~50 TB. Takeaway: the API read path (menus, restaurant lists) needs caching; order writes are easy.

Practice 2 — Snowflake bits

How many years of IDs does a 41-bit millisecond timestamp give you?

Solution. 2⁴¹ ms ≈ 2.2 × 10¹² ms ≈ 2.2 × 10⁹ s ≈ 2.2 × 10⁹ / 3.15 × 10⁷ ≈ ~69.7 years (Chapter 7).

Practice 3 — Bandwidth

A video platform serves 50K concurrent streams at 5 Mbps each. What's the egress?

Solution. 50,000 × 5 Mbps = 250,000 Mbps = 250 Gbps ≈ 31 GB/s. Over a day ≈ 2.7 PB. You need a CDN.

Practice 4 — Connections

A multiplayer game has 10 M DAU; 10% are online at peak, each holding one WebSocket. A gateway server holds 200K connections. How many gateway servers?

Solution. 10 M × 10% = 1 M connections / 200K = 5 servers; with N+2 redundancy and headroom → 7–8.

docs.title: Revision checklist
docs.text:
• I can write the powers-of-two table from KB to PB.
  • I can recall memory ≈ 100 ns, SSD ≈ 100 µs, HDD seek ≈ 10 ms, cross-continent ≈ 150 ms — and the 4 takeaways.
  • I know downtime/year for 99%, 99.9%, 99.99%, 99.999%, and how to combine series vs parallel.
  • I can convert per-day to per-second instantly (÷ 10⁵) and know 1 M/day ≈ 12 QPS.
  • I can estimate QPS, peak, storage, bandwidth, cache size and server count with labelled units.
  • I can turn each number into a design decision.

Next: 03 · The Interview Framework

docs.title: 03 · A Framework for System Design Interviews
docs.text:
⏱ 35 min read 🔥 The method you'll reuse in every case study Book: Chapter 3

TL;DR

  • The interview simulates two colleagues solving a vague problem together. The process matters more than the final diagram.
  • Use 4 steps: (1) understand & scope (~5–8 min) → (2) high-level design + buy-in (~10–15 min) → (3) deep dive (~15–20 min) → (4) wrap up (~3–5 min).
  • Never jump to a solution. Ask about features, users, scale, growth, constraints. Write the answers down.
  • Let the interviewer steer the deep dive, but come prepared with the 2–3 hardest parts of the problem.
  • Red flags: over-engineering, silence, stubbornness, ignoring trade-offs, getting lost in trivia.

docs.title: What the interviewer is really evaluating
docs.text:
Nobody expects you to design YouTube in 45 minutes — thousands of engineers took years. So what is being tested?

Signal What it looks like when you're strong Handling ambiguity You turn "design a chat app" into a crisp, agreed scope with numbers. Asking good questions Your questions change the design ("1:1 only, or groups of 500?"). Technical design Sensible components, clear data flow, correct use of caches/queues/DBs. Trade-off thinking You name alternatives and say why you picked one — and what it costs. Depth When pushed on one component, you can go 2–3 levels deeper. Communication & collaboration You think out loud, check in, take hints gracefully. Pragmatism You design for the stated scale, not for Google-scale by default.

Red flags interviewers write down

  • Over-engineering — 12 microservices and Kafka for 10K users. Complexity has real, compounding costs.
  • Jumping to a solution before understanding the problem.
  • Narrow-mindedness / stubbornness — defending a choice after a clear counter-argument.
  • Long silences — the interviewer can't score what they can't hear.
  • Buzzword soup — "we'll use microservices and NoSQL for scalability" with no reason.

docs.title: The 4-step framework
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    S1["① Understand<br/>& scope<br/>5–8 min"] --> S2["② High-level<br/>design + buy-in<br/>10–15 min"]
    S2 --> S3["③ Deep dive<br/>15–20 min"]
    S3 --> S4["④ Wrap up<br/>3–5 min"]
    S2 -. feedback .-> S1
    S3 -. feedback .-> S2

Times assume a 45-minute session. The arrows going back matter: you'll often revise the scope or the high-level design as you learn more — that's normal and good.

docs.title: Step 1 · Understand the problem and establish scope
docs.text:
Don't be the student who blurts out the answer first. In a design interview, speed without understanding is a negative signal. Slow down, ask, and write the answers on the board.

When you ask, the interviewer either answers or says "you decide". If it's the latter, state an assumption and write it down — you'll refer back to it.

docs.title: The question bank
docs.text:
Pick the relevant ones — don't machine-gun all of them.

Features (functional)ScaleQuality (non-functional)Constraints
  • What are the core features we must build? What's explicitly out of scope?
  • Who are the users — consumers, businesses, internal teams? Web, mobile, or both?
  • What's the most important user journey? (e.g. "post a photo" and "see my feed")
  • Any special requirements: search? notifications? analytics? edits/deletes?
  • How many users (MAU/DAU)? How many are concurrent?
  • Read:write ratio? Size of a typical object?
  • How fast are we growing? Expected scale in 3 / 6 / 12 months?
  • Is traffic spiky (sales, live events) or smooth? Global or one region?
  • Latency target? (e.g. p99 < 200 ms for reads)
  • Availability target? Is it OK to be briefly down, or briefly stale?
  • Consistency — must every read see the latest write? (bank balance vs like count)
  • Durability — can we ever lose data? How long do we keep it?
  • Existing tech stack or services we can reuse (auth, payments, a blob store)?
  • Budget / cost sensitivity? On-prem or cloud?
  • Legal: data residency, privacy (GDPR / DPDP), content moderation?

docs.title: Turn answers into a requirements sheet
docs.text:
Here's how a short scoping conversation for "design a photo-sharing app" might go — notice that each answer deletes a branch of the design:

A good scoping conversation (photo sharing)

You: Who's posting — anyone, or verified creators only? — Interviewer: Anyone. You: Core actions? — I: Upload a photo with a caption, follow people, scroll a home feed. You: Is the home feed ranked or chronological? — I: Chronological for now. You: How big? — I: 50M DAU; a typical user uploads every few days but opens the feed ~8 times a day. You: Max photo size, and do we keep originals? — I: Up to 10 MB; keep originals plus resized versions. You: Any users with huge followings? — I: Yes, some accounts have tens of millions of followers.

"Chronological" removes a ranking service. "Tens of millions of followers" warns you that pure fan-out-on-write will hurt. "Keep originals + resized" means an async image-processing pipeline, object storage and a CDN.

Write the result on the board — it's your contract with the interviewer:

FUNCTIONAL
  1. Upload photo (≤10 MB) + caption
  2. Follow / unfollow
  3. Home feed of followed accounts, newest first
NON-FUNCTIONAL
  - 50M DAU; feed p99 < 300 ms; uploads may take a few seconds to appear
  - Availability over consistency for the feed; never lose an uploaded photo
OUT OF SCOPE
  - Ranking, stories, DMs, ads
ESTIMATES (Ch. 2)
  - Feed loads ≈ 50M × 8 / 10^5 = 4K QPS avg, ~10K peak
  - Uploads ≈ 50M × 0.3 / 10^5 = 150/s; 15M/day × ~3 MB stored (orig + sizes) ≈ 45 TB/day

docs.title: Step 2 · Propose a high-level design and get buy-in
docs.text:
Goal: a blueprint both of you agree on before going deep.

  1. Sketch the boxes: clients → (DNS/CDN) → load balancer → services → cache → databases → queues/workers → object storage.
  2. Walk a request through it — "a user uploads: the app gets a pre-signed URL, uploads straight to blob storage, then calls POST /photos…" Concrete use cases expose missing pieces.
  3. Sanity-check against your estimates — "10K QPS of feed reads at peak — fine for a cache-backed feed service."
  4. Ask for feedback — "Does this direction make sense before I go deeper?" Treat the interviewer as a teammate.

docs.title: APIs and data model — include them?
docs.text:
Depends on the problem. For "design web search" it's too low-level. For "design a URL shortener" or "a multiplayer game backend", the API and schema are the design. When in doubt, sketch the 2–4 core APIs:

POST /v1/photos/upload-url  → 200 { upload_url, photo_id }     # pre-signed URL to object storage
POST /v1/photos             { photo_id, caption }  → 201
GET  /v1/feed?cursor=...    → 200 { items[], next_cursor }

and the 2–3 core tables:

users(user_id PK, handle, ...)
photos(photo_id PK, owner_id, caption, storage_key, created_at)
follows(follower_id, followee_id, created_at)   PK(follower_id, followee_id)

docs.title: Example: the photo-sharing high-level design
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    C[Client] -->|1. get upload URL| API[API servers]
    C -->|2. PUT bytes| OBJ[(Object storage)]
    C -->|3. POST /photos| API
    API --> META[(Photo + follow DB)]
    API -->|new photo event| Q[[Queue]]
    Q --> IMG[Resize workers] --> OBJ
    Q --> FAN[Feed builder] --> FC[(Feed cache)]
    C -->|read feed| API --> FC
    OBJ --> CDN[(CDN)] --> C

The upload path and the feed path are separate, and heavy work (resizing, feed building) happens asynchronously behind a queue. That's enough detail to get agreement — Chapter 11 goes deep on feeds.

docs.title: Step 3 · Design deep dive
docs.text:
By now you've agreed on scope, drawn the blueprint, and received feedback. Now go deep where it matters.

How to choose what to dive into:

  1. Follow the interviewer's lead. If they ask "how would the fan-out work for a celebrity?", that's your deep dive.
  2. Otherwise, pick what's unique to this problem — the part that makes it this system and not a generic CRUD app:
Problem Typical deep dives URL shortener Hash/encode function, collisions, 301 vs 302, cache Rate limiter Algorithm choice, distributed counters, race conditions Chat WebSockets, message ordering/IDs, online presence, multi-device sync News feed Fan-out on write vs read, celebrity problem, feed cache Web crawler URL frontier (politeness + priority), dedup, traps YouTube Upload + transcoding pipeline, CDN cost, streaming protocols Google Drive Block-level sync, conflict resolution, consistency, notifications
  1. Seniority changes the focus. Junior: correct components and data flow. Senior: bottlenecks, capacity numbers, failure modes, operational concerns, cost.

Time management: it's easy to burn 10 minutes on something that shows nothing (e.g. explaining a ranking algorithm's maths in detail). Keep asking yourself: does this demonstrate that I can design a scalable system?

docs.title: Step 4 · Wrap up
docs.text:
The interviewer may ask open-ended follow-ups or let you choose. Use these to show breadth:

  • Bottlenecks & improvements — "The single fan-out queue is the bottleneck; I'd partition it by user_id." Never claim the design is perfect.
  • Recap — 30 seconds summarising the design and the key trade-offs. Especially valuable if you went down several paths.
  • Failure cases — server crash, network partition, cache loss, DC outage. What degrades, what's lost?
  • Operations — metrics, logging, alerting, deployment/rollback.
  • Next 10× of scale — "At 100M DAU I'd shard the post DB by post_id and add a second region."
  • Other refinements — security, abuse/rate limiting, cost.

docs.title: Habits that score well — and ones that cost you
docs.text:
Habits that score

  • Treat every assumption as a question until the interviewer confirms it.
  • Say the requirements back before drawing anything.
  • Remember the "right" design depends on context — a 5-person startup and a hyperscaler make different calls.
  • Narrate your reasoning; the interviewer grades what they hear.
  • When there's a real fork, name both paths, pick one, and say what it costs.
  • Once the blueprint is agreed, spend time on the riskiest component first.
  • Use the interviewer as a collaborator — their hints are free signal.
  • Keep going when stuck; reasoning out loud still earns credit.

Habits that cost you

  • Showing up without having practised the common problems.
  • Drawing before asking.
  • Polishing one box in detail while the rest of the system is still blank.
  • Sitting stuck in silence instead of asking for a nudge.
  • Treating the first diagram as "done" — keep checking in until the interviewer closes the session.

docs.title: A full mock walkthrough: "Design Pastebin"
docs.text:
A compressed example of all four steps, so you can hear the rhythm.

Step 1 — Scope (6 min)

You: Users paste text and get a shareable link — is that the core? Do we need accounts, editing, syntax highlighting? I: Core is paste + share link. Optional expiry. No editing. Accounts optional. You: Size limit per paste? — I: 1 MB max, most are a few KB. You: Scale? — I: 5M new pastes/day, reads 10× writes. You: Must links work forever? — I: Default expiry 1 year, user can choose shorter.

Board: FR: create paste (≤1 MB, optional expiry), read by link. NFR: high read availability, low read latency, pastes are immutable. Estimates: writes 5M/10⁵ ≈ 60 QPS; reads ≈ 600 QPS (peak ~1.5K). Storage: 5M × 10 KB avg = 50 GB/day → 18 TB/year.

Step 2 — High-level design (12 min) 

flowchart LR
    C[Client] --> LB{{LB}} --> API[Paste service]
    API -->|metadata| DB[(Metadata DB<br/>id, s3_key, expiry, owner)]
    API -->|content| S3[(Object storage)]
    API --> R[(Cache: hot pastes)]
    CL[Cleanup job] --> DB & S3
POST /pastes {content, expiry} → generate a 7-char ID (base-62 of a unique ID — see Ch. ⅞), store content in object storage, metadata in DB, return the link. GET /{id} → cache → DB → object storage. Immutable data = trivially cacheable; put popular pastes behind a CDN. You: "Does this look right? I'd like to dive into ID generation and expiry next."

Step 3 — Deep dive (18 min)
  • ID generation: random 7-char base-62 has 3.5 T space; with 1.8 B IDs/year, collision chance per insert is tiny but non-zero → use a unique numeric ID (Snowflake/ticket range) then base-62 encode → no collisions, no DB check.
  • Expiry: store expires_at; reads check it (lazy delete); a daily batch job deletes expired rows and S3 objects. Use S3 lifecycle rules for bulk cleanup.
  • Hot pastes: a paste shared on social media gets 100K hits in minutes → CDN with Cache-Control: max-age set to min(remaining expiry, 1 day).
  • Abuse: rate limit creates per IP (Ch. 4); size limit at the LB.
Step 4 — Wrap up (4 min)

"To recap: stateless paste service, metadata in a sharded KV/SQL store keyed by paste_id, content in object storage, cache + CDN for reads. Bottleneck at 10× would be metadata writes → shard by paste_id. Failure: if object storage is slow, we serve from cache/CDN; we'd monitor p99 read latency, 4xx/5xx, cache hit ratio. Next I'd add analytics via an async event stream."

docs.title: Phrases that help
docs.text: Situation Say something like Starting "Before designing, I'd like to clarify a few requirements." Assuming "I'll assume X — let me write that down; tell me if it's off." Choosing "Two options here: A and B. A gives us…, costs us…; given our read-heavy load I'd pick A." Checking in "Does this level of detail work, or should I go deeper somewhere?" Stuck "I'm not sure about the best approach here — let me reason through it out loud." Taking a hint "Good point — that changes things. Let me revise this part." Wrapping up "Let me recap the design and the main trade-offs, then talk about bottlenecks."

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
Practice 1 — Write the scope

Prompt: "Design a parking-lot reservation system for a city." Write 6 clarifying questions and a requirements sheet (FR, NFR, out of scope) with assumed numbers.

Sample answer. Questions: Which users — drivers, lot operators, both? Reserve ahead or only real-time? How many lots/spots? Peak times? Payments in scope? Must a reserved spot be guaranteed (no double booking)? FR: search spots by location/time, reserve, cancel, pay; operators manage inventory. NFR: strong consistency on booking (no double-booking), search can be slightly stale, p99 search < 300 ms. Out: dynamic pricing, navigation. Numbers: 2,000 lots × 200 spots = 400K spots; 1M reservations/day → ~12 writes/sec avg, peaks 10× at office hours.

Practice 2 — Spot the red flags

A candidate, given "design a URL shortener for an internal company tool (5K employees)", proposes Kafka, Cassandra, Kubernetes with 20 microservices, and a multi-region active-active setup. What feedback would you give?

Answer. Over-engineering for the stated scale (5K users → a few QPS). A single service + Postgres + a small cache is enough, with backups. Complexity adds cost and failure modes. They should have estimated first and scaled the design to the numbers, while mentioning how they'd evolve it if usage grew.

Practice 3 — Choose the deep dives

For "design a ticket-booking system for concerts (like BookMyShow)", which 2–3 areas would you deep dive and why?

Answer. (1) Seat inventory & concurrency — preventing double booking (row locks / optimistic concurrency / temporary holds with expiry). (2) Flash-sale traffic — a virtual waiting room / queue and rate limiting when a big concert opens. (3) Payment flow & idempotency — hold → pay → confirm, with timeouts that release the hold.

docs.title: Revision checklist
docs.text:
• I can list what interviewers evaluate and the top 5 red flags.
  • I can recite the 4 steps with rough time budgets for a 45-min round.
  • I have a mental question bank across features, scale, quality and constraints.
  • I write requirements (FR / NFR / out of scope / estimates) on the board before designing.
  • I know how to choose deep-dive topics and how seniority changes them.
  • I can wrap up with bottlenecks, failures, monitoring, and the next 10× of scale.

docs.title: 16 · Revision Cheat Sheet
docs.text:
⏱ 15 min read 🔥 Read this the night before

How to use this page

Cover the right-hand column of each table and say the answer out loud. Anything you can't explain in one breath, go back to that chapter.

docs.title: The method (Chapter 3)
docs.text:
Step Time (45 min) Must produce ① Understand & scope 5–8 min Functional reqs · non-functional reqs · out of scope · numbers ② High-level design 10–15 min Boxes + arrows, 2–4 APIs, core tables, one request walked through, interviewer buy-in ③ Deep dive 15–20 min The 2–3 parts unique to this problem, with trade-offs ④ Wrap up 3–5 min Bottlenecks, failures, monitoring, next 10×

Red flags: jumping to a solution · over-engineering · silence · stubbornness · buzzwords without reasons.

docs.title: Numbers (Chapter 2)
docs.text:
Fact Value Seconds/day 86,400 ≈ 10⁵ 1M requests/day ≈ 12 QPS 1B requests/day ≈ 12K QPS Memory read / SSD read / HDD seek / cross-continent RTT ~100 ns / ~100 µs / ~10 ms / ~150 ms 99.9% / 99.99% / 99.999% 8.77 h / 52.6 min / 5.26 min down per year 2¹⁰ / 2²⁰ / 2³⁰ / 2⁴⁰ / 2⁵⁰ KB / MB / GB / TB / PB Snowflake 41-bit ms timestamp ~69 years Base-62, 7 chars 62⁷ ≈ 3.5 trillion Bloom filter at 1% FP ~10 bits per key 
QPS      = DAU × actions/day ÷ 10^5          peak = ×2…5
Storage  = writes/day × size × days × replicas
Cache    ≈ 20% of daily hot data (80/20)
Servers  = peak QPS ÷ per-server QPS (+30% headroom)

docs.title: Scaling toolbox (Chapter 1)
docs.text: Problem Reach for Watch out for One server overloaded Separate DB; horizontal web tier behind a load balancer LB itself must be redundant DB reads too slow Read replicas, cache (cache-aside + TTL) Replication lag, invalidation, stampedes Static files slow far away CDN with versioned URLs Cost per GB Can't auto-scale web tier Stateless servers, sessions in Redis — Slow work in request path Message queue + workers At-least-once → idempotent consumers Region outage Multi-DC + GeoDNS + async replication Data loss window on failover DB writes / size too big Sharding (pick the key by the main query) Hotspots, resharding, cross-shard joins

docs.title: Building blocks (Chapters 4–7)
docs.text: Topic Key idea Say this in the interview Rate limiter Counters per (key, rule) in Redis; 429 + headers Token bucket allows bursts; sliding-window counter is the cheap accurate default; Lua for atomicity; fail open Consistent hashing Servers and keys on a ring; first server clockwise Moves only ~k/n keys; virtual nodes fix uneven arcs; TreeMap.ceilingEntry KV store AP + tunable consistency N/W/R with W+R>N; vector clocks; gossip; sloppy quorum + hinted handoff; Merkle trees; LSM + Bloom filters Unique IDs Snowflake 1/41/5/5/12 Time-sortable, 64-bit, no coordination; clock going backwards is the risk; UUIDv7 if 128 bits is OK

docs.title: Rate-limiting algorithms in one line each
docs.text: Algorithm One line Token bucket Refill at rate r up to capacity C; each request takes a token — bursts OK Leaky bucket FIFO queue drained at a fixed rate — smooth output Fixed window Counter per calendar window — 2× burst at edges Sliding log Timestamps per request — exact, memory-heavy Sliding window counter curr + prev × overlap — approximate, O(1)

docs.title: Quorum quick reference (N = 3)
docs.text: W, R Result 2, 2 Strong (overlap), balanced 1, 3 Fast writes 3, 1 Fast reads 1, 1 Eventual, fastest

docs.title: Case studies (Chapters 8–15)
docs.text: System Core idea Main data store The hard part to deep-dive URL shortener code → long URL map; 301/302 Sharded KV by code + Redis cache Code generation: hash+check vs ID→base-62 (permuted) vs key service Web crawler BFS loop with a smart frontier Blob store for pages, Bloom filter for URLs Frontier: priority front queues + per-host politeness back queues; traps Notification API → per-channel queues → workers → APNs/FCM/SMS/email Relational (users, devices, settings) + log At-least-once + dedup, retries/DLQ, preferences, rate limits, priority lanes News feed Publish → fan-out; read precomputed IDs → hydrate Redis sorted sets (feed), post DB, graph store Fan-out on write vs read; hybrid for celebrities; cursor pagination Chat WebSockets to stateful chat servers Wide-column (Cassandra/HBase) keyed by chat Routing between servers, per-chat ordered IDs, multi-device sync, presence Autocomplete Trie with cached top-k per node Prefix → top-k KV, in-memory cache Offline rebuild pipeline, browser caching, shard map, filter layer YouTube Pre-signed upload → transcoding DAG → CDN; HLS/DASH Object storage + metadata DB DAG scheduling, parallel/resumable upload, CDN cost (long tail) Google Drive Blocks + hashes; delta sync Object storage for blocks; strongly consistent relational metadata Sync flows, long-poll notifications, conflicts, dedup & version thinning

docs.title: Classic follow-ups — 10-second answers
docs.text: Question Answer "What if the cache dies?" Replicated cache; circuit breaker/rate limit to the DB; warm before full traffic; serve degraded "Replica lag shows stale data?" Read-your-writes from leader for that user briefly, or track replication position "Hot key / celebrity?" Cache in front, replicate the hot key, split it, or pull instead of push "Exactly-once?" Not end-to-end; at-least-once + idempotency keys / dedup "How to choose a shard key?" High cardinality, matches the main query, rarely changes "Why not SQL?" / "Why not NoSQL?" Name the access pattern, transactions/joins needed, scale of writes "How to delete in an eventually consistent store?" Tombstones + grace period before compaction "Clock went backwards (Snowflake)?" Detect; wait for small drift; refuse + alert for large "How do you monitor this?" Latency, traffic, errors, saturation + the system-specific lag metric (queue lag, fan-out lag, freshness)

docs.title: The final 60-second self-check
docs.text:
• I can draw the "millions of users" architecture from memory.
  • I can estimate QPS and storage for any prompt in under 3 minutes.
  • For each case study, I can name the APIs, the data store, and the hardest part.
  • For every component I add, I can say what it costs.

docs.text:
⏱ Reference Use the search box (top right) to jump to a term

Terms are grouped by theme. The Ch. column says where it's explained in depth.

docs.title: Scaling & infrastructure
docs.text: Term Meaning Ch. Availability Fraction of time a system answers correctly; measured in "nines" 1, 2 Auto-scaling Adding/removing servers automatically based on load 1 CDN Network of edge servers caching content near users 1, 14 Edge location / POP A CDN site close to users 1, 14 Failover Switching to a standby component when the primary fails 1 GeoDNS DNS that answers with different IPs depending on user location 1 Health check Periodic probe a load balancer uses to detect dead servers 1 Horizontal scaling Adding more machines ("scale out") 1 Vertical scaling Using a bigger machine ("scale up") 1 Load balancer (L4/L7) Spreads requests across servers; L4 by IP/port, L7 by HTTP content 1 Latency Time taken by one request 2 Throughput Requests handled per unit time 2 QPS Queries (requests) per second 2 Peak QPS Highest expected QPS (typically 2–5× average) 2 SLA / SLO / SLI Promise to customers / internal target / measured value 2 SPOF Single point of failure — one part whose failure stops the whole system 1 Stateless server Keeps no client state between requests; any server can serve anyone 1 Sticky session LB keeps sending a client to the same server 1 Multi-DC / multi-region Running in several data centers for latency and disaster tolerance 1 Active-active / active-passive Both sites serve traffic / one is a standby 1 Four golden signals Latency, traffic, errors, saturation 1 Back-of-the-envelope Quick order-of-magnitude estimation 2 p99 latency 99% of requests are faster than this value 2

docs.title: Data & databases
docs.text: Term Meaning Ch. ACID Atomic, consistent, isolated, durable transactions 1, 15 RDBMS / SQL Tables, schemas, joins, transactions (MySQL, Postgres) 1 NoSQL Non-relational stores: key-value, document, wide-column, graph 1 Key-value store A distributed Map<key, value> 6 Wide-column store Row key → sorted columns; built for heavy writes (Cassandra, HBase) 6, 12 Document store Stores JSON-like documents (MongoDB) 1 Graph DB Nodes + edges, fast traversals (Neo4j) 1, 11 Replication Keeping copies of data on several nodes 1, 6 Leader / follower Writes go to the leader; followers copy and serve reads 1 Replication lag How far a follower is behind the leader 1 Read-your-writes A user always sees their own latest write 1 Sharding / partitioning Splitting data so each node holds a subset 1, 6 Shard / partition key The field deciding which shard a row lives on 1 Resharding Changing the partitioning and moving data 1, 5 Hotspot / celebrity problem One key or shard gets disproportionate traffic 1, 11 Denormalisation Duplicating data to avoid joins 1 Index (B-tree) Sorted structure that speeds up lookups by a column 7 Object / blob storage Stores large immutable files (S3, GCS) 14, 15 Cold storage Cheap, slow storage tier for rarely accessed data 15 Tombstone A deletion marker that replicates like a write 6 Compaction Merging storage files and dropping old/deleted entries 6 Commit log / WAL Append-only log written before applying changes, for crash recovery 6 Memtable In-memory sorted buffer of recent writes 6 SSTable Immutable, sorted on-disk file of key-value pairs 6 LSM tree Storage design: log + memtable + SSTables + compaction 6

docs.title: Caching
docs.text: Term Meaning Ch. Cache hit / miss Found / not found in cache 1 Cache-aside App reads cache, on miss loads DB and fills cache 1 Read-through The cache library loads from DB on a miss 1 Write-through Write to cache and DB together 1 Write-behind (write-back) Write to cache now, DB later in batches 1 Write-around Write only to DB; cache fills on next read 1 TTL Time-to-live before an entry expires 1 Eviction (LRU, LFU, FIFO) Policy for what to drop when the cache is full 1 Cache stampede Many requests miss at once and overload the DB 1 Cache invalidation Removing/updating stale cached entries 1

docs.title: Distributed systems
docs.text: Term Meaning Ch. CAP theorem During a partition, choose consistency or availability 6 PACELC Else (no partition), trade latency vs consistency 6 Network partition Nodes can't communicate with each other 6 Strong consistency Reads always return the latest write 6, 15 Eventual consistency Replicas converge if writes stop 6 Quorum (N, W, R) Replicas / write acks / read responses; W+R>N → overlap 6 Coordinator Node that proxies a request to replicas 6 Preference list The N servers responsible for a key 6 Vector clock [server, counter] list to detect concurrent versions 6 Last-write-wins (LWW) Keep the version with the latest timestamp 6 CRDT Data type whose replicas merge automatically 6 Gossip protocol Nodes share membership/heartbeat info with random peers 6 Heartbeat Periodic "I'm alive" signal 6, 12 Sloppy quorum Use the first healthy nodes, not the designated ones 6 Hinted handoff Temporarily store another node's writes, hand back later 6 Anti-entropy Background process that syncs diverged replicas 6 Merkle tree Hash tree to find differing data ranges cheaply 6 Read repair Fix stale replicas during a read 6 Consensus (Raft, Paxos) Agreement among nodes, e.g. for leader election 6 Service discovery Registry to find healthy service instances (ZooKeeper, etcd) 12 Idempotency Repeating an operation has the same effect as doing it once 1, 10 Bloom filter Probabilistic set: "definitely not" or "probably yes" 6, 9

Next: 18 · The Learning Continues

docs.title: 18 · The Learning Continues
docs.text:
⏱ 15 min read Book: Chapter 16

Finishing fifteen designs is a start, not the end. Real systems knowledge comes from three things: reading how real companies built things, practising new problems out loud, and going one level deeper into the distributed-systems ideas you met here.

docs.title: 1 · Read the papers behind the chapters
docs.text:
Most designs in this site are simplified versions of systems described in public papers. Reading even the introduction and architecture sections is worth it.

Paper (year) What it teaches Chapters Dynamo — Amazon (2007) Consistent hashing, quorums, vector clocks, sloppy quorum, Merkle trees 5, 6 Bigtable — Google (2006) Wide-column model, SSTables, memtables, tablets 6, 12 Cassandra — Facebook (2009) Dynamo-style distribution + Bigtable-style storage 6, 12 GFS — Google (2003) Chunked file storage, single master + replicas 15 MapReduce — Google (2004) Batch processing at scale — the "aggregator" in autocomplete 13 Scaling Memcache at Facebook (2013) Cache invalidation, leases, regional caches 1, 11 TAO — Facebook (2013) Social-graph storage and caching 11 Kafka — LinkedIn (2011) The log as a message queue 1, 10 Chubby (2006) / ZooKeeper (2010) Coordination, locks, service discovery 7, 12 Raft (2014) Understandable consensus and leader election 1, 6 Spanner — Google (2012) Globally consistent transactions with synchronised clocks 6, 7 Borg — Google (2015) Cluster scheduling — the ancestor of Kubernetes 14

docs.title: 2 · Books for the next level
docs.text: Book Why Designing Data-Intensive Applications — Martin Kleppmann The best single book on replication, partitioning, transactions, consistency and stream processing. Read it after this site. System Design Interview Volume 2 — Alex Xu & Sahn Lam 13 more problems (see the list below) in the same style. Understanding Distributed Systems — Roberto Vitillo Short, practical bridge between interview designs and production reality. Database Internals — Alex Petrov B-trees, LSM trees, replication and consensus from the inside. Site Reliability Engineering — Google How large systems are actually run: SLOs, monitoring, incident response.

docs.title: 3 · Engineering blogs worth following
docs.text:
Search for these companies' engineering blogs; read posts about architecture, migrations and outages (post-mortems teach the most):

  • Global: Netflix, Uber, Meta, Google, Amazon (AWS Architecture), Discord, Cloudflare, Stripe, Shopify, Slack, Dropbox, Pinterest, Airbnb, LinkedIn, Figma.
  • India: Flipkart, Swiggy, Zomato, Razorpay, PhonePe, Zerodha, Hotstar/JioCinema (live-streaming scale stories), CRED.

How to read an engineering blog post

For each post, write three lines: the problem (with numbers), the design choice, and what they gave up. That's exactly the shape of a good interview answer.

docs.title: 4 · More problems to practise
docs.text:
Use the 4-step framework and a 35-minute timer. Hints are deliberately short — expand only after you've tried.

Proximity service (nearby restaurants / Yelp)

Read-heavy; static-ish data. Index locations with geohash or a quadtree; cache popular areas; search neighbouring cells.

Nearby friends (live locations)

Frequent location updates over WebSockets; pub/sub channel per user; only fan out to friends within radius; TTL on stale locations.

Google Maps

Map tiles pre-rendered and served via CDN; routing on a graph partitioned into tiles; ETA from historical + live traffic.

Distributed message queue (Kafka-like)

Partitioned append-only logs on disk; consumer groups with offsets; replication with leader/followers and in-sync replicas.

Metrics monitoring & alerting

Time-series DB; push vs pull collection; downsampling and retention tiers; alert rules evaluated on streams.

Ad click aggregation

Stream processing with windows (Flink); exactly-once-ish via idempotent sinks; reconcile with batch for accuracy.

Hotel / ticket reservation

Strong consistency on inventory; prevent double booking (row locks / optimistic concurrency); idempotent payments; holds that expire.

Distributed email service

SMTP ingestion, spam filtering, per-user mailbox storage, search index, attachments in object storage.

S3-like object storage

Separate metadata service from data nodes; erasure coding vs replication; multipart upload; versioning.

Real-time gaming leaderboard

Redis sorted sets per leaderboard; shard by game/region; periodic snapshots to durable storage.

Payment system & digital wallet

Double-entry ledger; idempotency keys everywhere; reconciliation with the payment provider; exactly-once effects via state machines.

Stock exchange

Single-threaded matching engine per symbol for determinism; sequencer; extreme low latency; replay from an event log.

Collaborative document editing (Google Docs)

Operational transformation or CRDTs; per-document session server; presence cursors; snapshots + operation log.

Ride-hailing (driver matching)

Driver locations in a geo index (geohash cells in Redis); matching service per city; surge pricing from supply/demand per cell.

docs.title: 5 · A 30-day practice plan
docs.text: Days Do this 1–3 Re-draw Chapter 1's architecture from memory; redo all Chapter 2 practice problems without looking. 4–7 Building blocks: implement the token bucket, consistent hash ring and Snowflake in Java from scratch. 8–15 One case study per day, timed, out loud. Compare with the chapter; write down what you missed. 16–25 One new problem per day from the list above. Record yourself; listen back for silences and hand-waving. 26–28 Two mock interviews with a friend (swap roles — interviewing teaches as much as being interviewed). 29–30 Read the Cheat Sheet; re-attempt your two weakest problems.

docs.title: 6 · Beyond high-level design
docs.text:
• Low-level design (LLD) / object-oriented design — class diagrams, design patterns (strategy, observer, factory…), SOLID, concurrency. Many interviews include an LLD round (parking lot, elevator, rate limiter class design).
  • Hands-on — run Redis, Kafka and Postgres locally with Docker; build a tiny URL shortener with a cache and a load test; watch what breaks.
  • Operate what you build — set up monitoring (Prometheus + Grafana) on something you run and practise reading its graphs.

docs.title: Closing thought
docs.text:
Every chapter here came down to the same few questions: what's the access pattern, what are the numbers, what breaks first, and what are we willing to give up? If you can ask those calmly and reason through the answers out loud, you're ready for the interview — and, more importantly, for the job.

docs.text:

Is site ke baare mein

docs.title: Yahan se shuru karo
docs.text: ⏱ 10 min read Sabse pehle yeh padho

docs.title: System design asal mein hai kya?
docs.text:
Code likhna ek problem ko ek request ke liye solve karta hai. System design wahi problem millions of requests ke liye, ek saath solve karta hai — jab machines fail ho rahi hain, network slow ho raha hai, aur data roz badh raha hai.

Toh ek system design question asal mein chaar sawaal ek ke upar ek rakhe hue hain:

  1. System ko karna kya hai? (functional requirements — "user URL short kar sake")
  2. Kitna achha karna hai? (non-functional — latency, availability, consistency, cost)
  3. Kitna bada hai? (scale — users, requests per second, kitne bytes store honge)
  4. Sabse pehle kya tootega, aur tab kya karenge? (bottlenecks, failures, trade-offs)

Is site ka har chapter yahi chaar sawaal ek system ya ek component ke liye answer karta hai.

flowchart LR
    A[Vague problem<br/>'YouTube design karo'] --> B[Scope clear karo<br/>features + scale]
    B --> C[Estimate karo<br/>QPS, storage, bandwidth]
    C --> D[High-level design<br/>boxes + arrows]
    D --> E[Deep dive<br/>2-3 mushkil hisse]
    E --> F[Trade-offs,<br/>failures, wrap-up]

docs.title: Is site ko use kaise karein
docs.text:
3-pass method

  1. Pass 1 — samjho. Chapter upar se neeche tak padho. Har diagram ko dhyaan se dekhne se pehle khud paper pe banane ki koshish karo. Jahan interactive widgets hain, unse khelo.
  2. Pass 2 — dobara banao. Page band karo. 35 minute ka timer lagao aur system ko scratch se design karo — whiteboard ya paper pe, bol-bol ke. Phir chapter se compare karo.
  3. Pass 3 — defend karo. Interviewer follow-ups section kholo aur har sawaal ka jawab answer expand karne se pehle zor se bolo.

English ya Hinglish? Dono versions mein same depth hai. Jo tumhe sochne mein help kare, wahi use karo. Ek kaam ka trick: intuition banane ke liye Hinglish mein padho, phir English version dobara padho taaki interview mein fluently bol sako.

docs.title: 4-week plan
docs.text:
Week Chapters Goal 1 01 Scale · 02 Estimation · 03 Framework Vocabulary + method. "Millions of users" waala architecture yaad se bana pao, aur QPS/storage 3 minute ke andar estimate kar pao. 2 04 Rate Limiter · 05 Consistent Hashing · 06 KV Store · 07 Unique IDs Building blocks. Yeh baad ke har design ke andar aate hain — jaldi mat karna. 3 08 URL Shortener · 09 Crawler · 10 Notifications · 11 News Feed Pehli chaar case studies. Har ek ko kam se kam ek baar timed (pass 2) karo. 4 12 Chat · 13 Autocomplete · 14 YouTube · 15 Google Drive · 16 Cheat Sheet Last chaar case studies + revision. End mein do full mock interviews.

Agar sirf ek hafta hai: 01, 02, 03 poore karo, 05 aur 06 skim karo, phir 08, 11, 12 aur 14 timed karo.

docs.title: Pehle din se chahiye yeh vocabulary
docs.text:
Yeh words baar-baar aayenge. Har ek ka proper explanation baad mein hai, abhi ke liye one-liner. Glossary mein 100+ aur hain.

Term Ek line mein Latency Ek request mein kitna time lagta hai (ms). Throughput / QPS System ek second mein kitni requests handle karta hai. Availability Kitne % time system chalu hai aur jawab de raha hai (99.9% = saal mein ~8.8 ghante down). Scalability Resources add karke zyada load sambhalne ki capacity. Horizontal vs vertical scaling Zyada machines vs ek badi machine. Replication Same data ki copies kai machines pe rakhna. Sharding / partitioning Data ko tod dena taaki har machine pe sirf ek hissa ho. Cache Chhota, tez, temporary store jo hot data rakhta hai taaki slow kaam na karna pade. Load balancer Aane wali requests ko kai servers mein baant-ta hai. Message queue Ek buffer jisse producer aur consumer alag-alag speed pe kaam kar sakein. Consistency Kya har reader ko latest write dikhta hai? Idempotency Same operation do baar karo toh effect ek hi baar jaisa ho.

docs.title: Java code ke baare mein
docs.text: Code samples Java mein hain (interviews ki sabse common language). Yeh readable aur correct hone ke liye likhe gaye hain, production-hardened nahi — inhe "chalne waale explanations" samjho.

docs.title: Credits
docs.text:
Yeh site Alex Xu, System Design Interview – An Insider's Guide (2nd ed.) ka companion hai. Chapter order book ke hisaab se hai. Yahan ka saara text, diagrams, code aur examples original hain; book se kuch copy nahi kiya. Book khareedna — worth it hai.

Chapter 1 shuru karo

docs.title: 04 · Rate Limiter Design karo
docs.text:
⏱ 50 min read 🔥 Standalone question bhi, aur har doosre design ke andar bhi Book: Chapter 4

TL;DR

  • Rate limiter ek client (user, IP, API key, device) ki ek time window mein requests ki limit lagata hai; extra requests ko HTTP 429 Too Many Requests milta hai.
  • Ise server side rakho, aam taur pe middleware / API gateway mein — client pe kabhi bharosa mat karo.
  • Paanch algorithms: token bucket (bursts chalenge, sabse popular), leaky bucket (smooth fixed outflow), fixed window (simple, par window edges pe 2× burst), sliding log (exact, memory khaata hai), sliding window counter (approximate, sasta — aksar best choice).
  • Counters Redis mein (in-memory, INCR + EXPIRE), aur race conditions se bachne ke liye check-and-update ko Lua script se atomic banao.
  • Rules config files mein (limiter cache karta hai); clients ko X-RateLimit-* / Retry-After headers se quota batao; limiter khud toote toh fail open.

docs.title: Intuition: metro ka turnstile
docs.text:
Bheed waale metro station pe turnstiles ek-ek karke logon ko andar jaane dete hain. Jab platform bhar jaata hai, staff kuch gates band kar deta hai taaki overflow na ho — log wait karte hain ya doosra raasta lete hain. Andar wale logon ko bahar ki bheed se koi nuksaan nahi hota.

Rate limiter tumhari API ka wahi turnstile hai. Rules ke examples:

  • Ek user 1 second mein max 2 posts kar sakta hai.
  • Ek IP address se ghante mein max 5 sign-ups.
  • Ek device hafte mein max 5 baar reward claim kar sakta hai.
  • Ek phone number pe 10 minute mein max 3 OTP.

docs.title: Kyun chahiye?
docs.text:
1. Resource starvation / DoS rokna — galti se (retry loop mein phansa buggy client) ya jaan-bujh ke. Lagbhag har public API (GitHub, Twitter/X, Google APIs, Stripe) limits lagata hai.
  2. Cost control — kam servers; aur sabse important, paid third-party APIs (credit check, SMS, payments, LLM calls) jo har request ka paisa lete hain, unki raksha.
  3. Overload rokna — bots aur badtameez users ko filter karo taaki genuine traffic tez rahe.
  4. Fairness — multi-tenant system mein ek bhaari tenant baaki sab ko slow na kare.

docs.title: Step 1 · Problem scope karo
docs.text:
Clarifying baatcheet

Tum: Hum apni HTTP APIs bacha rahe hain, ya kisi aur ko jaane waali calls limit kar rahe hain? — Interviewer: Apni public APIs. Tum: Client ki pehchaan kaise — API key, user, IP? — I: Sab; alag endpoints alag keys use karte hain. Tum: Traffic roughly kitna? — I: Peak pe kuch lakh requests per second. Tum: Ek server ya load balancer ke peeche poori fleet? — I: Badi fleet, do regions mein. Tum: Strict limits, ya thoda overshoot chalega? — I: Zyada tar endpoints pe thoda overshoot theek; login strict hona chahiye. Tum: Kya clients ko bacha hua quota pata chalna chahiye? — I: Haan, response mein bhejo.

Requirements

Functional Non-functional Configurable key (user, IP, API key, endpoint) pe requests limit karo Low latency — requests noticeably slow na hon (< 1–2 ms extra) Ek saath kai rules (per endpoint, per tier) Accurate — zyada excess andar na aaye; genuine users block na hon Throttled clients ko saaf batao (429 + headers) Memory-efficient — millions of keys Distributed — saare API servers / processes mein shared Fault-tolerant — limiter ka cache mar jaaye toh bhi API chalti rahe

docs.title: Step 2 · Rate limiter rehta kahan hai?
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph A["Option 1 · client side"]
      c1[Client with limiter] --> s1[API servers]
    end
    subgraph B["Option 2 · har API server ke andar"]
      c2[Client] --> s2["API servers<br/>(code mein limiter)"]
    end
    subgraph C["Option 3 · middleware / API gateway"]
      c3[Client] --> g["Rate limiter<br/>middleware / gateway"] --> s3[API servers]
    end
  • Client side — bharosemand nahi: koi bhi client requests modify ya forge kar sakta hai, aur aksar client tumhare control mein nahi hota. (SDKs ka khud-throttle karna achhi baat hai, par uspe depend mat karo.)
  • API server ke andar — poora control, par har service khud implement karegi, aur state share na ho toh limits per-process ho jaati hain.
  • Middleware / API gateway — common answer. Gateways (Kong, Envoy, NGINX, AWS API Gateway, Apigee) pehle se auth, TLS termination, IP allow-lists karte hain — rate limiting yahan naturally fit hoti hai.

Example: limit = 2 req/s. Client ek second mein 3 requests bhejta hai → middleware pehli do aage bhej deta hai aur teesri ko khud 429 Too Many Requests de deta hai.

Kaise decide karein — judgement call hai, toh batao kya tumhe kis taraf le jaayega:

  • Auth/TLS ke liye pehle se gateway chal raha hai? Toh wahi natural ghar hai — ek hop, ek config.
  • Koi unusual algorithm ya per-request cost weighting chahiye? Khud banana (library ya sidecar) poora control deta hai; off-the-shelf gateways ka menu fixed hota hai.
  • Hot-path cost — check har request pe chalta hai, toh tumhare runtime mein sasta hona chahiye (DC ke andar Redis round trip ≈ 0.5–1 ms).
  • Team size — chhoti team ke liye managed gateway aksar sahi hai; apna banana aur chalana asli kaam hai.

docs.title: Paanch algorithms
docs.text: Theory padhne se pehle sabse popular waale ko mehsoos karo:

docs.title: 1 · Token bucket
docs.text:
Ek bucket mein max capacity tokens aa sakte hain. Ek refiller fixed refill rate pe tokens daalta hai; bucket full ho toh extra tokens bah jaate hain. Har request ek token leti hai; bucket khaali ho toh request reject.

flowchart LR
    R["Refiller<br/>+r tokens/sec"] --> B[("Bucket<br/>capacity = C")]
    Q[Request] --> D{token hai?}
    B --- D
    D -->|haan: 1 lo| OK[API ko bhejo]
    D -->|nahi| X[Drop → 429]

Worked trace — capacity 5, har 2 second mein 1 token (:02, :04, :06 … pe add hota hai), bucket 10:00:00 pe full:

Time Event Pehle tokens Decision Baad mein tokens 10:00:00 4 requests (page load) 5 ✅✅✅✅ 1 10:00:01 2 requests 1 ✅ ❌ 0 10:00:02 +1 refill, 1 request 0 → 1 ✅ 0 10:00:03 1 request 0 ❌ 429 0 10:00:12 +5 refills (5 pe cap) 0 → 5 — 5 10:00:12 5 requests 5 ✅✅✅✅✅ 0

10:00:00 ka burst aaram se nikal gaya (capacity ka yahi matlab hai), par lagatar rate kabhi 2 second mein 1 request se zyada nahi ho sakta.

Asal mein background "refiller" ki zaroorat nahi. tokens aur lastRefillTime store karo, aur har request pe beete time ke hisaab se lazily refill karo:

public final class TokenBucket {
    private final long capacity;
    private final double refillPerNano;     // har nanosecond mein kitne tokens
    private double tokens;
    private long lastRefill;

    public TokenBucket(long capacity, double tokensPerSecond) {
        this.capacity = capacity;
        this.refillPerNano = tokensPerSecond / 1_000_000_000.0;
        this.tokens = capacity;             // full se shuru: shuruaati burst allowed
        this.lastRefill = System.nanoTime();
    }

    public synchronized boolean tryAcquire() {
        long now = System.nanoTime();
        tokens = Math.min(capacity, tokens + (now - lastRefill) * refillPerNano);
        lastRefill = now;
        if (tokens >= 1) { tokens -= 1; return true; }
        return false;
    }
}

Parameters: bucket size (max burst) aur refill rate (lagatar rate).

Kitne buckets? Har (key, rule) ka ek:

  • Per-endpoint rules: "1 post/sec, 150 friend-adds/din, 5 likes/sec" → har user ke 3 buckets.
  • Per-IP throttling → har IP ka ek bucket.
  • Global cap ("total 10,000 req/s") → ek shared global bucket.
✅ Fayde ❌ Nuksaan Simple, memory-efficient (har key ke 2 numbers) Do parameters jinhe tune karna tricky ho sakta hai Chhote bursts chalte hain (capacity tak) jabki average rate enforce hota hai Agar downstream ko smooth load chahiye toh bursts problem hain

Kaun use karta hai: AWS API Gateway, Stripe (aur bahut saare).

docs.title: 2 · Leaky bucket
docs.text:
Jaise chhed waali baalti: requests ek fixed size ki FIFO queue mein aati hain; ek worker use fixed outflow rate pe khaali karta hai. Queue full ho toh nayi requests drop.

flowchart LR
    Q[Aati hui requests] --> F{queue full?}
    F -->|nahi| QU[["FIFO queue (size N)"]]
    F -->|haan| X[Drop → 429]
    QU -->|"fixed rate: r req/sec"| P[Processor / API]

Parameters: bucket (queue) size aur outflow rate.

✅ Fayde ❌ Nuksaan Memory bounded (queue size) Burst queue ko purani requests se bhar deta hai; nayi drop hoti hain chahe zyada important hon Ekdum smooth output — jab downstream ko stable rate chahiye (jaise payment provider jo exactly 100 TPS allow karta hai) Queueing latency badhti hai; do parameters tune karne hain

Kaun use karta hai: Shopify ki API (leaky-bucket style). Networking mein traffic shaping ka classic algorithm bhi yahi hai.

Token vs leaky bucket ek line mein

Token bucket average rate limit karta hai aur bursts allow karta hai. Leaky bucket constant output rate enforce karta hai aur bursts ko queue mein sokh leta hai.

docs.title: 3 · Fixed window counter
docs.text:
Time ko fixed windows mein baant do (jaise har calendar second ya minute). Har window ka ek counter; har request use badhati hai; limit pe pahunche toh agli window shuru hone tak reject.

// Redis-style: key = "rl:{user}:{epochMinute}"
long window = System.currentTimeMillis() / 60_000;
String key = "rl:" + userId + ":" + window;
long count = redis.incr(key);
if (count == 1) redis.expire(key, 60);   // window ki pehli hit TTL set karti hai
boolean allowed = count <= LIMIT;

Edge problem. Limit = 100 per minute, windows round minutes pe shuru hoti hain. Ek script 9:14:50 se 9:14:59 ke beech 100 requests bhejti hai, phir 9:15:00 se 9:15:09 ke beech 100 aur. Har window ko exactly 100 dikhti hain — sab allowed. Par boundary ke aas-paas ke 20 seconds mein 200 requests nikal gayi: per-minute limit ka double.

9:14:00 9:15:00 9:16:00 window 1: 100 req ✓ window 2: 100 req ✓ boundary ke aas-paas 20 s → 200 requests (limit ka 2×)

Window boundary ke dono taraf bursts limit ka double andar aane dete hain. ✅ Fayde ❌ Nuksaan Bahut memory-efficient (har key ka 1 counter) Window edges pe limit ka 2× tak Samajhna aur banana aasaan Sabka quota ek hi pal mein reset → thundering herd Round time units pe reset kuch products ke liye fit hai ("1,000 calls/din")

docs.title: 4 · Sliding window log
docs.text:
Edge problem ko exactly fix karta hai. Har key ke liye request timestamps ka log rakho (jaise Redis sorted set, score = timestamp). Har request pe:

  1. now − window se purane timestamps hatao.
  2. Nayi request ka timestamp jodo.
  3. Log size ≤ limit → allow; warna reject.

Trace — limit 10 second mein 3 requests (log har request store karta hai, accept ho ya na ho):

Aayi Cleanup + insert ke baad log Size Decision 12:00:01 [:01] 1 ✅ 12:00:03 [:01, :03] 2 ✅ 12:00:04 [:01, :03, :04] 3 ✅ 12:00:07 [:01, :03, :04, :07] 4 ❌ (timestamp phir bhi store) 12:00:12 window (12:00:02, 12:00:12] → :01 hata → [:03, :04, :07, :12] 4 ❌ 12:00:15 :03, :04 hate → [:07, :12, :15] 3 ✅ 
public boolean allow(String key, long nowMs) {
    Deque<Long> log = logs.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ArrayDeque<>());
    synchronized (log) {
        while (!log.isEmpty() && log.peekFirst() <= nowMs - WINDOW_MS) log.pollFirst();
        log.addLast(nowMs);                 // is variant mein rejected requests bhi log hoti hain
        return log.size() <= LIMIT;
    }
}

Step 2 mein chhupa ek design choice

Upar waala variant rejected requests ko bhi log karta hai — toh jo client lagatar thok raha hai woh blocked hi rehta hai (retry karne ki saza). Bahut implementations sirf accepted requests log karti hain, jisse purani requests expire hote hi client wapas aa sakta hai. Batao tum kaunsa chun rahe ho.

✅ Fayde ❌ Nuksaan Exact — koi bhi rolling window limit cross nahi karti Memory khaata hai: har request ki ek entry (100 req/min limit × 1M users = 100M timestamps) Har request pe cleanup ka kaam

docs.title: 5 · Sliding window counter (hybrid)
docs.text:
Sirf do fixed-window counters rakho — current aur previous — aur rolling count ka estimate lagao yeh maan ke ki previous window ki requests barabar phaili thi:

estimated = current_count + previous_count × (rolling window ka previous window ke saath overlap)

Example: limit 10/min. Pichle minute mein 8 requests thi; current minute mein ab tak 4. Ek nayi request current minute ke 40% pe aati hai → rolling window ab bhi pichle minute ke aakhri 60% ko cover karti hai.

estimated = 4 + 8 × 0.6 = 8.8 → 8.8 < 10 → allow (current 5 ho gaya). Usi pal do aur requests aayein toh estimate 10.8 pahunchega → doosri reject. (Raw estimate compare karo ya round up/down — policy choice hai; round down thoda zyada lenient hai.)

pichla minute: 8 requests current minute: ab tak 4 rolling 1-minute window pichle ka 60% current mein 40% abhi

estimate = 4 + 8 × 0.6 = 8.8 requests pichle ek minute mein. 
public synchronized boolean allow(String key, long nowMs) {
    long window = nowMs / WINDOW_MS;
    double elapsedFraction = (nowMs % WINDOW_MS) / (double) WINDOW_MS;
    long curr = counters.getOrDefault(key + ":" + window, 0L);
    long prev = counters.getOrDefault(key + ":" + (window - 1), 0L);
    double estimated = curr + prev * (1.0 - elapsedFraction);
    if (estimated >= LIMIT) return false;
    counters.merge(key + ":" + window, 1L, Long::sum);  // (Redis mein purani windows TTL se expire)
    return true;
}
✅ Fayde ❌ Nuksaan Edge spikes smooth karta hai (previous window ka average use karta hai) Approximate — maanta hai previous window uniform thi Memory-efficient — har key ke 2 counters Jahan har request pe strict limit chahiye wahan nahi chalega

Practice mein approximation kitna bura hai? Cloudflare ne 40 crore requests pe naapa: sirf 0.003% galti se allow ya rate-limit hui. Isliye yeh aksar best default hai.

docs.title: Algorithm comparison
docs.text: Algorithm Memory / key Accuracy Bursts Kab best Token bucket O(1) — tokens + timestamp Achhi ✅ capacity tak General APIs; bursts theek hain Leaky bucket O(queue size) Achhi ❌ queue mein smooth Downstream ko constant rate chahiye Fixed window O(1) — 1 counter ❌ edges pe 2× ⚠ edge bursts Simple quotas ("1,000/din") Sliding log O(limit) timestamps ✅ exact ❌ Chhoti limits jo exact honi chahiye (OTP, login attempts) Sliding window counter O(1) — 2 counters ≈ (99.997%) Smooth High-volume APIs — usual best pick

docs.title: High-level architecture
docs.text:
Saare algorithms ko ek hi primitive chahiye: har key ka tez, shared counter with expiry. Database bahut slow hai (disk). Redis jaisa in-memory store ideal hai: tez hai aur time-based expiry support karta hai.

  • INCR key — counter ko atomically badhao (na ho toh 1 se bana do).
  • EXPIRE key seconds — timeout ke baad key apne aap delete.
flowchart LR
    C[Client] --> M{{Rate limiter<br/>middleware}}
    M <-->|"counter lao / badhao"| R[(Redis)]
    M -->|limit ke andar| API[API servers]
    M -->|limit ke bahar| X["429 Too Many Requests"]
  1. Client request rate-limiter middleware ko bhejta hai.
  2. Middleware Redis se sahi bucket ka counter laata hai aur limit check karta hai.
  3. Limit cross → reject (429). Andar → API servers ko forward aur counter increment.

docs.title: Rules: kahan rehte hain aur dikhte kaise hain
docs.text:
Rules aam taur pe config files (YAML) mein likhe jaate hain aur disk / config service mein store hote hain. Ek illustrative format, Envoy ki open-source rate-limit service ke descriptor-based config jaisa:

domain: public_api
descriptors:
  - key: plan
    value: free
    rate_limit: { unit: minute, requests_per_unit: 60 }     # free tier: har API key 60 calls/min
  - key: plan
    value: pro
    rate_limit: { unit: minute, requests_per_unit: 1000 }   # paid tier
---
domain: otp
descriptors:
  - key: phone_number
    rate_limit: { unit: hour, requests_per_unit: 5 }        # har phone pe ghante mein max 5 OTP

Workers samay-samay pe disk/config service se rules kheench ke rate limiter ke andar local cache mein rakhte hain, taaki hot path pe rule lookup ka kharcha zero ho.

docs.title: Clients ko batana ki woh throttle hue
docs.text:
HTTP 429 Too Many Requests headers ke saath return karo taaki samajhdaar clients ruk sakein:

Header Matlab X-RateLimit-Limit Client ek window mein kitni calls kar sakta hai X-RateLimit-Remaining Current window mein kitni bachi hain X-RateLimit-Retry-After (ya standard Retry-After) Retry se pehle kitne second rukna hai

(Ek IETF draft inhe RateLimit-Limit, RateLimit-Remaining, RateLimit-Reset ke naam se standardise kar raha hai.)

Throttled requests drop ki ja sakti hain, ya baad mein process karne ke liye enqueue (jaise spike mein throttle hue orders gayab nahi hone chahiye).

docs.title: Detailed design
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph CFG[Rules]
      D[(Rules disk /<br/>config service pe)] --> WK[Workers] --> RC[(Rules cache)]
    end
    C[Client] --> RL{{Rate limiter middleware}}
    RC --> RL
    RL <--> RD[("Redis<br/>counters + timestamps")]
    RL -->|allowed| API[API servers]
    RL -->|"rejected: 429 + headers"| C
    RL -.->|"option: throttled ko enqueue"| MQ[[Message queue]]

docs.title: Problem 1 — race conditions
docs.text:
Do API servers ek hi user ki requests ek hi pal mein handle karte hain. Limit = 4, counter = 3.

Server A: GET counter → 3          Server B: GET counter → 3
Server A: 3 < 4 → allow, SET 4     Server B: 3 < 4 → allow, SET 4
Result: 5 requests allowed, counter bolta hai 4.  ❌

Read-check-write atomic nahi hai. Fixes:

  • Locks — sahi par slow; har request pe distributed lock latency maar deta hai.
  • Atomic operations — pehle INCR phir check (INCR naya value atomically return karta hai).
  • Redis mein Lua scripts — Redis script ko atomically chalata hai, toh poora read-modify-write ek step mein.
  • Sliding log ke liye MULTI/Lua block ke andar Redis sorted sets.

Token-bucket check ek atomic Lua script ki tarah:

-- KEYS[1] = bucket key ; ARGV = capacity, refill_per_sec, now_ms, cost
local cap    = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local rate   = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local now    = tonumber(ARGV[3])
local cost   = tonumber(ARGV[4])
local b      = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens = tonumber(b[1]) or cap
local ts     = tonumber(b[2]) or now
tokens = math.min(cap, tokens + (now - ts) / 1000 * rate)   -- lazy refill
local allowed = 0
if tokens >= cost then tokens = tokens - cost; allowed = 1 end
redis.call('HMSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', now)
redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], math.ceil(cap / rate * 1000) * 2)
return { allowed, math.floor(tokens) }

Java se Jedis/Lettuce ke through EVALSHA se call karo (script ek baar load hoti hai aur SHA se refer hoti hai).

docs.title: Problem 2 — kai limiters ke beech synchronisation
docs.text:
Tum kai rate-limiter instances chalaoge. Stateless web tiers ke saath, ek client ki lagatar requests alag-alag limiter instances pe ja sakti hain. Agar har instance counters local memory mein rakhe, toh client ko apni limit ka N× mil jaayega.

  • Sticky sessions (client ko hamesha same limiter pe bhejo) — chalta hai par na scalable, na flexible. Bacho.
  • Centralised data store (Redis) — saare instances same counters share karte hain. ✅ Standard answer.
