docs.title: Problem 3 — performance
docs.text:
• Multi-data-center / edge: door ke users ke liye door waale Redis ki latency zyada hai. Rate limiters ko users ke paas edge locations pe rakho (Cloudflare saikdon edge servers pe limiting chalata hai) aur traffic sabse paas waale pe bhejo.
  • DCs ke beech eventual consistency: regions ke across counters async sync karo; sync ke dauraan thoda over-allowance low latency ke liye acceptable trade hai.
  • Local pre-check: har instance pe ek chhota local token bucket rakho jo zyada tar decisions le aur samay-samay pe Redis se reconcile kare — kam network round-trips, thodi inaccuracy ki keemat pe.

docs.title: Problem 4 — monitoring
docs.text:
Metrics collect karo ye check karne ke liye ki limiter effective hai:

  • Algorithm sahi hai? Agar flash-sale ka bursty traffic bahut drop ho raha hai, toh strict window ki jagah token bucket (jo bursts sehta hai) better ho sakta hai.
  • Rules sahi hain? Agar bahut saari genuine requests ko 429 mil raha hai, rules zyada strict hain — dheele karo.
  • Track karo: har rule pe allowed vs throttled, p99 added latency, Redis errors, top throttled keys (abuse detection).

docs.title: Failure mode: fail open ya fail closed?
docs.text: Redis unreachable ho toh requests allow karein (fail open) ya block (fail closed)? Zyada tar APIs ke liye: fail open — perfect limiting se availability zyada important hai, aur requirement thi ki limiter ki failure system ko na giraye. Security-critical limits (login attempts, OTP sends) ke liye fail closed ya conservative local fallback limiter socho.

docs.title: Step 4 · Wrap up — extra topics
docs.text:
• Hard vs soft limits. Hard: threshold kabhi cross nahi. Soft: thodi der ke liye cross ho sakta hai (bursty par benign traffic ke liye kaam ka).
  • Doosri layers pe limiting. Humne Layer-7 (HTTP) limiter banaya. Layer 3 pe IP se iptables/firewalls se bhi limit kar sakte ho — sasta, par mota (users ya endpoints nahi dikhte). OSI layers: physical, data link, network (3), transport (4), session, presentation, application (7).
  • Client best practices limit se bachne ke liye:
    • Responses cache karo taaki baar-baar call na karni pade.
    • Limits samjho aur thode time mein bursts mat bhejo.
    • 429s/errors pakdo aur gracefully recover karo.
    • Exponential backoff + jitter ke saath retry karo, Retry-After ka respect karte hue.
  • Tiered limits — free vs paid plans ke alag buckets; SaaS mein per-tenant fairness.

docs.title: Interviewer follow-ups
docs.text:
Public REST API ke liye token bucket ya sliding window counter? Justify karo.

General public API ke liye main token bucket lunga agar chhote genuine bursts allow karne hain (page load pe kai calls jaati hain) O(1) memory ke saath, ya sliding window counter agar edge spikes ke bina smooth "N per minute" semantic chahiye. Dono per key O(1) hain aur Redis mein atomically banana aasaan hai. Fixed window (edge bursts) aur sliding log (memory) se bachunga jab tak limit chhoti aur exact na chahiye (login attempts).

Counters waala Redis cluster down ho gaya. Kya hoga?

Limiter ko fail open karna chahiye: error/timeout jaldi pakdo (tight client timeout ~5–10 ms), request allow karo, metric emit karo aur alert karo. Optionally conservative limits ke saath per-instance in-memory limiter pe fall back karo taaki abusive clients kuch had tak ruke rahein. Redis ko replicas + automatic failover (Sentinel/Cluster) ke saath chalao taaki aisa kam ho.

3 regions ke across har user ka 1 global quota kaise rate-limit karoge?

Options: (1) har user ko ek home region pe route karo jo uska counter own kare (simple, accurate); (2) har region local counter rakhe aur asynchronously sync kare — sync lag ke dauraan thoda over-limit chalne do; (3) quota ko regions mein baant do (jaise recent traffic share se) aur samay-samay pe rebalance karo. Strict global accuracy ke liye har request pe cross-region round trip chahiye — bahut slow — isliye approximate enforcement accept karte hain.

10M users aur har ek ke 3 rules ke counters ko kitni memory chahiye?

Sliding window counter: har (user, rule) ke 2 counters. Key ~40 bytes + value 8 bytes + Redis overhead ~50 bytes ≈ 100 B per counter → 10M × 3 × 2 × 100 B = 6 GB — chhote Redis cluster mein aaram se. Limit 100 waale sliding log ko per key 100 entries tak chahiye → ~100× zyada (saikdon GB).

Agar limiter auth se pehle chalta hai toh user ID kahan se aayega?

Ya toh limiting gateway mein authentication ke baad chalao (taaki verified user/API key padh sake), ya layered limits: auth se pehle mota per-IP limit (auth service ko credential stuffing se bachata hai), phir auth ke baad per-user / per-key limits.

Kya rejected requests client ke against count honi chahiye?

Policy choice hai. Unhe count karna (sliding-log variant jaisa) un clients ko saza deta hai jo 429 ignore karke thokte rehte hain. Na count karna sahi retry karne waale clients ke liye friendly hai. Abuse-sensitive endpoints pe count karo; normal APIs pe usually nahi — aur Retry-After publish karo taaki achhe clients wait karein.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
Inse bacho

  • Limiter sirf client pe lagana.
  • Counters ke liye relational database (har request pe disk latency).
  • Bina atomicity ke get-then-set → race conditions extra requests andar aane dete hain.
  • Load balancer ke peeche per-instance in-memory counters → har client ko N× limit.
  • Yeh batana bhool jaana ki limiter khud fail ho toh kya hoga.
  • 429 + retry info ki jagah 500/403 return karna.

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
Practice 1 — Token bucket trace karo

Capacity 3, refill 1 token/second, t=0 pe full. Requests t = 0, 0, 0, 0, 0.5, 1.2, 1.3, 3.0 pe aati hain. Kaunsi allow hongi?

Solution. t=0: tokens 3 → allow (2), allow (1), allow (0), reject (0). t=0.5: tokens 0.5 → reject. t=1.2: tokens 1.2 → allow (0.2). t=1.3: tokens 0.3 → reject. t=3.0: tokens 0.3 + 1.7 = 2.0 → allow (1.0). 8 mein se 5 allowed.

Practice 2 — Sliding window counter

Limit 100/min. Pichla minute: 84 requests. Current minute: ab tak 36. Ek request current minute ke 25% pe aati hai. Allow ya reject?

Solution. Previous ke saath overlap = 75%. Estimate = 36 + 84 × 0.75 = 36 + 63 = 99 < 100 → allow (count 37). Usi pal agli request ka estimate 100 → reject.

Practice 3 — OTP limiter design karo

Requirements: har phone pe 10 minute mein max 3 OTP requests, din mein max 10, aur har IP pe ghante mein max 100. Kaunse algorithm(s) aur data structures?

Solution. Chhoti limits jo exact honi chahiye → 10-minute rule ke liye Redis sorted sets mein sliding window log (ZREMRANGEBYSCORE, ZADD, ZCARD ek Lua script mein). Daily rule → phone:yyyy-mm-dd se keyed fixed window counter (calendar-day semantics theek hai). IP rule → sliding window counter. Teeno atomically check karo; koi bhi fail ho toh reject; Redis down ho toh fail closed (SMS mein paisa lagta hai aur abuse ka target hai).

Practice 4 — Leaky bucket sizing

Downstream payment gateway exactly 50 TPS allow karta hai. Flash sales mein tumhara checkout traffic ~20 seconds ke liye 200 TPS pe peak karta hai. Limiter design karo.

Solution. Gateway ke aage 50/s pe drain hone waala leaky bucket. 200/s ka 20 s spike 4,000 requests laata hai, jinme se spike ke dauraan 1,000 drain hoti hain → drops se bachne ke liye queue ko ~3,000 slots chahiye, aur aakhri request ~60 s wait karti hai. Synchronous checkout ke liye yeh bahut lamba hai → order accept karo, payment enqueue karo, "processing" return karo, aur complete hone pe notify karo; ya sale ke aage waiting-room lagao.

docs.title: Revision checklist
docs.text:
• Rate limiting kyun chahiye (DoS, cost, overload, fairness) samjha sakta hoon.
  • Client-side, in-server aur gateway placement compare kar sakta hoon.
  • Paancho algorithms trace, pros/cons aur kab use karna hai ke saath samjha sakta hoon.
  • Fixed-window edge problem numbers se dikha sakta hoon aur sliding-window-counter estimate nikaal sakta hoon.
  • Redis, rules cache aur headers waale 429 responses ke saath architecture bana sakta hoon.
  • Race condition samjha ke atomic ops / Lua se fix kar sakta hoon.
  • Instances aur data centers ke across limiters sync karna, aur fail-open vs fail-closed pata hai.

Aage: 05 · Consistent Hashing

docs.title: 05 · Consistent Hashing Design karo
docs.text:
⏱ 35 min read 🔥 Caches, KV stores, sharding, load balancers — sabke andar Book: Chapter 5

TL;DR

  • server = hash(key) % N keys ko barabar baant-ta hai — jab tak N na badle. Badla toh lagbhag har key alag server pe chali jaati hai → cache-miss ka toofan / bahut saara data move.
  • Consistent hashing servers aur keys dono ko ek ring pe rakhta hai (hash space ko gol mod diya). Key ka maalik hai clockwise chalte hue pehla server.
  • Server add/remove karne pe sirf ring ke ek arc ki keys move hoti hain — average k/n keys (k keys, n servers), lagbhag saari nahi.
  • Plain ring mein arcs uneven hote hain. Fix: virtual nodes — har server ring pe 100–200 jagah aata hai, toh load barabar ho jaata hai (std-dev ~5–10%).
  • Sorted map (TreeMap.ceilingEntry) se implement karo → O(log V) lookup. Dynamo, Cassandra, Riak, Discord, Akamai, Envoy/Maglev-style LBs use karte hain.

docs.title: Intuition: students ko exam halls mein bhejna
docs.text:
College students ko halls mein roll_number % halls_ki_ginti se bhejta hai. Mast chalta hai — jab tak exam ki subah ek hall ka AC kharab na ho jaaye. Ab % 4 ki jagah % 3, aur lagbhag har student alag hall mein bheja jaata hai, sirf kharab hall waale nahi. Har darwaze pe hungama.

Smart rule: halls ko ek gol corridor mein lagao; har student apne "seat number" waali jagah se clockwise chale aur pehle khule hall mein ghus jaaye. Ek hall band hua toh sirf uske students thoda aage agle hall tak chalte hain. Baaki sab pe koi asar nahi. Yahi consistent hashing hai.

docs.title: Rehashing problem
docs.text:
N cache servers hon toh server chunne ka seedha tareeka:

serverIndex = hash(key) % N

4 servers aur 8 keys lete hain. (Maan lo hash() yeh chhote numbers deta hai taaki hisaab aasaan rahe.)

Key hash hash % 4 Server (N = 4) user:alpha 10 2 S2 user:bravo 21 1 S1 user:charlie 32 0 S0 user:delta 43 3 S3 user:echo 54 2 S2 user:foxtrot 65 1 S1 user:golf 76 0 S0 user:hotel 87 3 S3

Har server pe exactly 2 keys — khoobsurat. Ab S1 crash ho gaya. Pool [S0, S2, S3] hai, toh % 3:

Key hash % 3 Naya server Move hui? user:alpha 1 S2 — wahin user:bravo 0 S0 ✔ (zaroori tha — S1 mar gaya) user:charlie 2 S3 ✔ bina wajah move user:delta 1 S2 ✔ bina wajah move user:echo 0 S0 ✔ bina wajah move user:foxtrot 2 S3 ✔ (zaroori tha — S1 mar gaya) user:golf 1 S2 ✔ bina wajah move user:hotel 0 S0 ✔ bina wajah move

8 mein se 7 keys move hui, jabki dead server pe sirf 2 thi. Cache ke liye iska matlab hai achanak cache misses ka toofan jo database ko pit deta hai. Sharded database ke liye matlab zyada tar data move karna. General rule: N se N±1 servers pe jaane se lagbhag N/(N+1) keys relocate hoti hain — almost sab kuch.

docs.title: Consistent hashing
docs.text: Consistent hashing aisi hashing scheme hai jisme slots ki ginti badalne pe average sirf k/n keys move karni padti hain (k = keys, n = slots), lagbhag saari nahi.

docs.title: Step 1 · Hash space ring ban jaata hai
docs.text: Badi output range waala hash function lo — jaise SHA-1 ka output 0 … 2¹⁶⁰ − 1 (practice mein systems MurmurHash ya xxHash jaise tez non-cryptographic hashes 32/64-bit range ke saath use karte hain). Is range ko gol mod do, taaki sabse bade value ke baad 0 aaye. Yahi hai hash ring.

docs.title: Step 2 · Servers ko ring pe rakho
docs.text: Har server ke naam ya IP ko same hash function se hash karo, aur us point pe ring pe rakh do.

docs.title: Step 3 · Keys ko ring pe rakho
docs.text: Har key ko same ring pe hash karo. Dhyaan do: ab % N nahi hai.

docs.title: Step 4 · Lookup — clockwise chalo
docs.text:
Key us server pe store hoti hai jo key ki position se clockwise chalte hue pehla milta hai.

S0 S1 S2 S3 k0 k1 k2 k3 clockwise chalo → pehla server key ka maalik

Har key (orange) ka maalik clockwise pehla server (teal) hai: k0→S0, k1→S1, k2→S2, k3→S3.

docs.title: Server add karna
docs.text:
S4 ko ring pe k0 aur S0 ke beech add karo. k0 se clockwise chalne pe ab pehla server S4 hai, toh sirf k0 move hoti hai (S0 se S4 pe). k1, k2 aur k3 bilkul nahi hilti.

Kaunsi keys move hoti hain? Exactly woh jo S4 aur anticlockwise pichle server (S3) ke beech ke arc mein hain. Pehle woh S0 ki thi; ab S4 le leta hai.

docs.title: Server hatana
docs.text:
S1 hatao. Sirf S0 (anticlockwise padosi) aur S1 ke beech ke arc ki keys — yahan k1 — move hoti hain, aur agle clockwise server (S2) pe jaati hain. Baaki sab wahin rehte hain.

flowchart TB
    subgraph B1["Pehle"]
      direction LR
      a1["S0 arc"] --- b1["S1 arc · k1 yahan"] --- c1["S2 arc"]
    end
    subgraph A1["S1 hatne ke baad"]
      direction LR
      a2["S0 arc"] --- c2["S2 arc · ab k1 bhi yahin"]
    end
    B1 -->|"sirf S1 ke arc ka maalik badla"| A1

Khud try karo — servers add/remove karo, aur dekho hash % N ke muqable kitni keys move hoti hain:

Widget mein kya notice karna hai

Har server ka 1 virtual node ho toh load bars bahut uneven hain aur "max/avg" aksar 2× ya usse bura. Virtual nodes ko 50+ tak le jao aur dekho spread 1.1× ki taraf simat jaata hai. Phir server add karo: consistent hashing lagbhag 1/(N+1) keys move karta hai; hash % N zyada tar keys hila deta hai.

docs.title: Basic ring ki do problems
docs.text:
1. Uneven partitions. Servers random points pe girte hain, toh unke beech ke arcs random size ke hote hain. Ek server ring ka 40% own kar sakta hai aur doosra 5%. Aur server hatne pe uska poora arc ek hi padosi ko milta hai, jis pe achanak double load aa jaata hai.
  2. Non-uniform key distribution. Arcs barabar hon tab bhi asli keys cluster ho sakti hain (hot ranges), aur ek server pe dher lag jaata hai.

docs.title: Virtual nodes (vnodes)
docs.text:
Har physical server ko ek baar rakhne ki jagah kai baar rakho — jaise S0#0, S0#1, … S0#199 — har ek ek virtual node jo wapas physical server S0 pe map hota hai.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Ring["Ring positions (clockwise)"]
      direction LR
      a["S0 · v3"] --> b["S2 · v7"] --> c["S1 · v0"] --> d["S0 · v9"] --> e["S2 · v1"] --> f["S1 · v5"] --> g["S0 · v4"] --> h["S1 · v2"] --> i["S2 · v4"]
    end

Yeh kaam kyun karta hai:

  • Har server ab ring pe bikhre kai chhote arcs own karta hai, toh uska total share average ho jaata hai. Har server ke ~100 vnodes ke saath load ka standard deviation mean ka lagbhag 10%; ~200 ke saath lagbhag 5%.
  • Server jaane pe uske kai chhote arcs kai alag padosi sokh lete hain — load ek server pe girne ki jagah phail jaata hai.
  • Alag-alag hardware: bade server ko 300 vnodes do aur chhote ko 100 → bade ko ~3× keys milengi.

Keemat: ring ki zyada entries store karni (metadata) aur membership badalne pe thoda zyada kaam. Sorted structure ke saath yeh kuch bhi nahi — 100 servers × 200 vnodes = 20,000 entries.

docs.title: Java mein implementation
docs.text:
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.security.MessageDigest;
import java.util.*;

public final class ConsistentHashRing<N> {
    private final NavigableMap<Long, N> ring = new TreeMap<>();
    private final int virtualNodes;

    public ConsistentHashRing(int virtualNodes) { this.virtualNodes = virtualNodes; }

    public synchronized void addNode(N node) {
        for (int i = 0; i < virtualNodes; i++) ring.put(hash(node + "#" + i), node);
    }

    public synchronized void removeNode(N node) {
        for (int i = 0; i < virtualNodes; i++) ring.remove(hash(node + "#" + i));
    }

    /** Key ki position se clockwise pehla node (end pe wrap around). */
    public synchronized N nodeFor(String key) {
        if (ring.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalStateException("no nodes");
        Map.Entry<Long, N> e = ring.ceilingEntry(hash(key));
        return (e != null ? e : ring.firstEntry()).getValue();
    }

    /** Clockwise N alag physical nodes — replica "preference list" (Chapter 6). */
    public synchronized List<N> nodesFor(String key, int replicas) {
        LinkedHashSet<N> out = new LinkedHashSet<>();
        for (N n : ring.tailMap(hash(key), true).values()) { out.add(n); if (out.size() == replicas) return new ArrayList<>(out); }
        for (N n : ring.values())                           { out.add(n); if (out.size() == replicas) break; }
        return new ArrayList<>(out);
    }

    private static long hash(String s) {
        try {
            byte[] d = MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5").digest(s.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
            long h = 0;
            for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) h = (h << 8) | (d[i] & 0xff);   // pehle 64 bits
            return h;
        } catch (Exception e) { throw new RuntimeException(e); }
    }
}
  • Lookup red-black tree pe ceilingEntry hai → O(log V), jahan V = total virtual nodes.
  • MD5 yahan sirf isliye kyunki JDK mein hai; production systems MurmurHash3 / xxHash use karte hain (bahut tez, non-cryptographic).
  • Har client (ya router) ko same ring dikhni chahiye. Membership aam taur pe gossip se phailti hai ya ZooKeeper/etcd jaisi coordination service mein rehti hai (Chapter 6).

docs.title: Thoda gehraai mein: alternatives jo bata sakte ho
docs.text: Technique Idea Kyun/kab Rendezvous (HRW) hashing Har key ke liye har server ka score = hash(key, server) nikalo; sabse bada wala chuno Na ring, na vnodes; perfectly even; har lookup O(N) — das-bees servers ke liye theek Jump consistent hash (Google) Ek chhota arithmetic function key → bucket 0..N−1 map karta hai, minimal movement ke saath O(ln N), memory nahi — par buckets sirf end pe add/remove ho sakte hain (numbered shards ke liye mast, random node failures ke liye bura) Maglev hashing (Google LB) Fixed-size lookup table banata hai, lagbhag perfect balance Load balancers ke liye bahut tez lookups; changes pe chhota disruption Bounded loads ke saath consistent hashing Har server ko average ke (1+ε) × pe cap karo; overflow agle server pe Hotspots rokta hai — kuch proxies/caches use karte hain (jaise HAProxy option, Vimeo)

docs.title: Asli duniya mein kahan use hota hai
docs.text:
• Dynamo-style databases mein partitioning — Amazon Dynamo, Apache Cassandra, Riak (Chapter 6 isi pe banta hai).
  • Discord — kisi guild/channel ka chat traffic sahi server pe route karna.
  • Akamai — 1997 ka original paper CDN servers pe web caches baantne ke baare mein tha.
  • Load balancers / proxies — Envoy ki ring-hash aur Maglev load-balancing policies, NGINX hash … consistent.
  • Distributed caches — Memcached client libraries (ketama), Redis client-side sharding.

docs.title: Interviewer follow-ups
docs.text:
Server add karne pe exactly kaunsi keys move hoti hain?

Sirf woh keys jinki position naye server aur anticlockwise pichle server ke beech ke arc mein hai. Woh naye server ke clockwise successor se naye server pe aati hain. Vnodes ke saath yeh kai chhote arcs hain — har naye vnode ka ek — aur har ek alag successor se keys leta hai, toh load existing servers se barabar khinchta hai.

Kitne virtual nodes use karein?

Itne ki load imbalance tumhari tolerance ke andar aa jaaye — aam taur pe har server ke 100–256. Zyada vnodes = better balance par zyada metadata aur membership change pe zyada ring entries update. Cassandra ka purana default har node pe 256 tokens tha, baad mein smarter token-allocation algorithm ke saath kam (jaise 16) recommend kiye.

Consistent hashing keys barabar baant-ta hai — kya isse load barabar ki guarantee hai?

Nahi. Yeh key count balance karta hai, traffic nahi. Ek hot key (celebrity profile, viral video) phir bhi ek server pe hi girti hai. Mitigations: hot keys ko aage cache karo, hot keys ko kai servers pe replicate karke reads baanto, key ko tod do (key#1..#n), ya bounded-load consistent hashing use karo.

Clients ko current ring kaise pata chalti hai?

Ya toh (1) ek router/proxy tier ring own karta hai aur clients usse baat karte hain; ya (2) har node ke paas ring hai aur membership changes gossip se phailte hain; ya (3) coordination service (ZooKeeper/etcd) membership store karti hai aur clients use watch karte hain. Changes ke dauraan thodi der ki asehmati tolerate hoti hai — jis node pe galat key aaye woh forward kar deta hai.

hash % N use karke offline re-shard kyun nahi kar lete?

Cache ke liye re-sharding matlab miss storm jo database gira sakta hai. Database ke liye matlab ~100% data move karna, jiske dauraan double-reads ya downtime chahiye. Consistent hashing membership changes ko sasta aur incremental banata hai, jo scale pe zaroori hai jahan nodes roz fail hote hain.

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
Practice 1 — Kitna hissa move hoga

Consistent hashing (bahut vnodes) ke saath 9 cache servers aur 9 crore keys hain. 10th server add karte ho. Roughly kitni keys move hongi? Agar hash % N use karte toh?

Solution. Consistent hashing: naya server ring ka ~1/10 leta hai → ~90 lakh keys move. hash % N: key tabhi wahin rehti hai jab h % 9 == h % 10, jo ~1/10 keys ke liye hota hai → ~8.1 crore keys move (90%).

Practice 2 — Weighted servers

Teen servers hain jinki RAM 64 GB, 64 GB aur 128 GB hai. 128 GB waale ko double keys kaise do?

Solution. Use double virtual nodes do (jaise 200, 200, 400). Uska ring share ≈ 400/800 = 50%, baaki dono 25% each.

Practice 3 — Lookup trace karo

Ring positions (0–99): S_A 15 pe, S_B 40 pe, S_C 72 pe. Keys ke hash 5, 16, 40, 41, 80, 99 hain. Har ek ka maalik kaun? Phir S_B hata diya — ab kaun?

Solution. Clockwise pehla server ≥ key (wrap ke saath): 5→S_A, 16→S_B, 40→S_B (barabar ho toh wahi maalik), 41→S_C, 80→S_A (wrap), 99→S_A. S_B hatne ke baad: 16→S_C, 40→S_C; baaki sab same. Sirf S_B ki 2 keys move hui.

docs.title: Revision checklist
docs.text:
• Numbers se dikha sakta hoon ki N badalne pe hash % N zyada tar keys kyun relocate karta hai.
  • Ring, clockwise lookup, aur add/remove pe exactly kaunsi keys move hoti hain — samjha sakta hoon.
  • Basic ring ki do problems aur virtual nodes unhe kaise fix karte hain (weighting ke saath) — samjha sakta hoon.
  • TreeMap se ring implement kar sakta hoon aur usse N replicas nikaal sakta hoon.
  • Pata hai ki keys ka barabar spread ≠ barabar traffic, aur hot keys kaise handle karein.
  • Ise use karne waale real systems aur kam se kam do alternatives (rendezvous, jump hash) bata sakta hoon.

Aage: 06 · Key-Value Store

docs.title: 06 · Key-Value Store Design karo
docs.text:
⏱ 60 min read 🔥 Sabse dense chapter — distributed systems ka core Book: Chapter 6

TL;DR

  • Key-value store ek bahut bada Map<key, value> hai jisme put(key, value) aur get(key) hain. Ek machine pe aasaan; asli challenge hai ise saikdon machines pe phailana jo fail hoti rehti hain.
  • CAP: network partition ke dauraan tumhe chunna padta hai consistency (CP — kuch requests mana karo) ya availability (AP — jawab do, shayad stale). Dynamo/Cassandra AP + eventual consistency chunte hain.
  • Consistent hashing (+ vnodes) se partition karo, har key ko ring pe agle N alag servers pe replicate karo, aur quorums se consistency tune karo: W + R > N ⇒ reads latest write dekhte hain.
  • Conflicts vector clocks se pakdo; failures gossip se; temporary failures sloppy quorum + hinted handoff se jhelo; permanent divergence Merkle trees se repair karo.
  • Storage engine: commit log → memtable → SSTables (LSM tree). Reads pehle memtable dekhte hain, phir har SSTable ka Bloom filter jo un files ko skip karwata hai jinme key ho hi nahi sakti.

docs.title: Intuition: kai branches waali library
docs.text:
Socho ek shehar ka library system 50 branches mein crore kitaabein rakhta hai.

  • Kaunsi kitaab kis branch mein? Kitaab ki ID pe based ek rule → partitioning.
  • Ek branch mein baadh aa gayi toh? Har kitaab ki copy 3 paas waali branches mein → replication.
  • Phone line band hai aur do branches same kitaab ka catalog card alag-alag update kar deti hain? Conflict pakadne aur merge karne ka tareeka chahiye → versioning / vector clocks.
  • Branches ko kaise pata chale ki doosri branch band hai? Har kuch minute kuch padosiyon se baat karti hain aur khabar aage badhati hain → gossip.
  • Ek branch ek din band hai — wapas aayi kitaabein kahan jaayein? Padosi temporarily rakh leta hai aur baad mein lauta deta hai → hinted handoff.
  • Lambe outage ke baad do branches kaise pata karein ki kaunse cards alag hain, bina saare 10 lakh compare kiye? Shelves ke summary compare karo, phir sirf alag waali shelves → Merkle trees.

docs.title: Step 1 · Scope
docs.text:
KV store (key-value database bhi kehte hain) unique keys ko values se map karta hai. Keys plain text ("user:42:profile") ya hashed ho sakti hain; values opaque blobs hain — strings, lists, JSON — store ko fark nahi padta. Famous examples: Amazon DynamoDB, Redis, Memcached, Apache Cassandra, etcd, RocksDB (embedded).

API:

void put(String key, byte[] value);
byte[] get(String key);

Hum kin requirements ke liye design kar rahe hain (har design trade-offs ka set hai — yeh hamare hain):

Requirement Target (hamare assumptions) Value size Aam taur pe ≤ 1 KB, hard cap 64 KB (bade blobs object storage mein) Total data Saikdon TB, badh raha hai — ek machine se kahin zyada Availability Individual nodes ya ek rack down ho tab bhi reads aur writes chalte rahein Durability Acknowledge hua write kabhi na khoye Elasticity Bina downtime nodes add/remove; data khud rebalance ho Consistency Har request pe tunable — default eventual, caller maange toh stronger Latency Region ke andar p99 ~10 ms se kam

docs.title: Single-server key-value store
docs.text:
Aasaan: in-memory hash table. Do tricks ise aage badhati hain:

  • Values ko compress karo.
  • Sirf hot data memory mein, baaki disk pe.

Par ek server ki memory aur disk aakhir khatam hogi, aur woh single point of failure hai. Hume distributed key-value store (distributed hash table) chahiye.

docs.title: CAP theorem
docs.text:
Distributed system teeno ek saath guarantee nahi kar sakta:

  • Consistency (C) — har client ko ek hi time pe same data dikhe, chahe kisi bhi node se baat kare.
  • Availability (A) — har request ko (non-error) response mile, kuch nodes down hon tab bhi.
  • Partition tolerance (P) — network partitions (nodes ke beech messages khona/late hona) ke bawajood system chalta rahe.
flowchart TB
    subgraph CAP
      C((Consistency)) --- A((Availability))
      A --- P((Partition<br/>tolerance))
      P --- C
    end
    CP["CP: jaise HBase, MongoDB (default), etcd/ZooKeeper"] -.-> C
    AP["AP: jaise Cassandra, DynamoDB-style, CouchDB"] -.-> A
    CA["CA: sirf bina partitions ke —<br/>distributed systems ke liye asli option nahi"] -.-> P

Key insight: distributed system mein network partitions honge hi (switches fail, cables kat-te hain, GC pauses partition jaise dikhte hain). Toh "P" optional nahi. Asli choice hai partition ke dauraan kya karna hai:

docs.title: Ek worked scenario
docs.text:
Teen replicas n1, n2, n3 ke paas key stock:item-77 = 10 hai. Network toot-ta hai: n3 ab n1/n2 se baat nahi kar sakta.

  • Ek client n1 pe stock:item-77 = 9 likhta hai. n1 n2 ko replicate karta hai — par n3 tak nahi pahunch pata.
  • Doosra client n3 se padhta hai.
Choice Kya hota hai Kiske liye achha CP n3 (aur shayad minority side) woh reads/writes mana karta hai jinke up-to-date hone ka confirm nahi kar sakta → partition theek hone tak error/timeout Bank balances, strict no-oversell inventory, leader election AP n3 10 ke saath jawab deta hai (stale). Dono taraf writes accept; conflicts partition theek hone ke baad reconcile Shopping carts, social feeds, likes, session data

PACELC — zyada complete version

CAP sirf partitions ki baat karta hai. PACELC jodta hai: Else (partition nahi), tab bhi tum Latency vs Consistency trade karte ho — jaise saare replicas ka wait karna consistent hai par slow. Dynamo/Cassandra: PA/EL. Spanner: PC/EC.

Hamara store: AP with tunable consistency.

docs.title: System components
docs.text:
Design inhi tukdon se banayenge, zyada tar Amazon ke Dynamo paper aur Cassandra/BigTable se liye hue:

  1. Data partitioning
  2. Data replication
  3. Consistency (quorums)
  4. Inconsistency resolution (versioning, vector clocks)
  5. Failures handle karna (gossip, sloppy quorum, hinted handoff, Merkle trees, DC outages)
  6. System architecture
  7. Write path
  8. Read path

docs.title: 1 · Data partitioning
docs.text:
Bada data ek server mein nahi aata, toh hum use todte hain. Do goals: data barabar baanto aur nodes join/leave hone pe kam se kam movement. Yeh exactly consistent hashing hai (Chapter 5):

  • Servers (virtual nodes ki tarah) hash ring pe; key ka maalik clockwise pehla server.
  • Automatic scaling: servers add/remove karne se sirf padosi arcs move hote hain.
  • Heterogeneity: bade servers ko zyada virtual nodes.

docs.title: 2 · Data replication
docs.text:
Durability aur availability ke liye har key N servers pe store hoti hai (N configurable, aam taur pe 3). Key ki position se clockwise chalo aur pehle N alag physical servers chuno — yeh key ki preference list hai.

flowchart LR
    K(("key0")) --> S1["s1 (coordinator)"] --> S2[s2] --> S3[s3]
    S1 -.- n1["replica 1"]
    S2 -.- n2["replica 2"]
    S3 -.- n3["replica 3"]
  • Virtual nodes ke saath agli N positions same physical server ki ho sakti hain → duplicates skip karo taaki N alag machines milein.
  • Ek data center ke servers saath mein fail ho sakte hain (power, network) → replicas ko racks / availability zones / data centers mein phailao.

docs.title: 3 · Quorums se consistency
docs.text:
Replicas ko sync rakhna hai. Define karo:

  • N = replicas ki ginti
  • W = write quorum: write tab successful jab W replicas acknowledge karein
  • R = read quorum: read tab successful jab R replicas jawab dein

Coordinator (jo bhi node request receive kare — client aur replicas ke beech proxy) request saare N replicas ko bhejta hai aur W (ya R) responses ka wait karta hai.

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant Co as Coordinator
    participant A as Replica A
    participant B as Replica B
    participant D as Replica C
    C->>Co: put(k, v)
    par N=3 ko fan out
      Co->>A: write
      Co->>B: write
      Co->>D: write
    end
    A-->>Co: ack
    B-->>Co: ack
    Note over Co: W=2 acks mil gaye → success
    Co-->>C: OK
    D-->>Co: ack (late, phir bhi apply hua)

W + R > N strong consistency kyun deta hai: jin W nodes ne write liya aur jin R nodes se tum padhte ho, unme kam se kam ek node common hona hi chahiye — toh kam se kam ek reply latest version laayega.

Config (N = 3) Behaviour Kab use karein W=1, R=3 Writes tez, reads ko sabse poochna padta hai Write-heavy, reads kam W=3, R=1 Reads tez, writes sabka wait karte hain Read-heavy, writes kam W=2, R=2 W+R=4 > 3 → strong consistency (overlap guaranteed), balanced latency Classic default W=1, R=1 W+R=2 ≤ 3 → sabse tez, sirf eventual consistency Caches, metrics, likes

Latency un W (ya R) replicas mein sabse slow se decide hoti hai jinka wait karte ho, isliye chhote quorums tez hain.

docs.title: Consistency models
docs.text:
Model Promise Strong Read hamesha sabse recent likha value deta hai. Kabhi stale nahi. Weak Read shayad latest write na dekhe — kab dikhega, koi guarantee nahi. Eventual Weak ka special case: writes ruk jaayein toh saare replicas aakhir same value pe aa jaate hain.

Strong consistency ke liye aam taur pe replica ko naye reads/writes tab tak mana karne padte hain jab tak saare replicas current write pe agree na karein — availability ke liye bura. Dynamo aur Cassandra eventual consistency chunte hain: concurrent writes alag replicas pe gir sakte hain, toh system ko conflicts pakadne aur reconcile karne padte hain. Yahi versioning karta hai.

docs.title: 4 · Inconsistency resolution: versioning aur vector clocks
docs.text:
Versioning har modification ko value ka naya immutable version maanta hai. Problem hai fark karna "B ne A ko replace kiya" (bas B rakho) aur "A aur B concurrently likhe gaye" (conflict jo merge karna hai) ke beech.

Vector clock [server, counter] pairs ki list hai jo har version ke saath judi hoti hai: D([S1, v1], [S2, v2], …). Jab server Si ek version likhta hai:

  • Agar clock mein [Si, vi] hai, toh vi badhao.
  • Warna [Si, 1] jodo.

Do versions X aur Y compare karna:

  • X, Y ka ancestor hai (conflict nahi — Y jeetta hai) agar X ka har counter ≤ Y ka matching counter.
  • X aur Y siblings hain (conflict) agar dono mein koi counter doosre se bada hai.

Worked example — partition ke dauraan shopping cart:

flowchart TB
    D1["D1 · cart = [milk]<br/>clock: (A,1)"] -->|"node A se likha"| D2["D2 · cart = [milk, bread]<br/>clock: (A,2)"]
    D2 -->|"phone B se likhta hai (partition!)"| D3["D3 · [milk, bread, eggs]<br/>clock: (A,2),(B,1)"]
    D2 -->|"laptop C se likhta hai"| D4["D4 · [milk, bread, tea]<br/>clock: (A,2),(C,1)"]
    D3 --> D5["D5 · client ne merge kiya · [milk, bread, eggs, tea]<br/>clock: (A,3),(B,1),(C,1)"]
    D4 --> D5
  1. Node A [milk] likhta hai → D1 (A,1); phir [milk, bread] → D2 (A,2). D1, D2 ka ancestor hai — D1 discard kar sakte hain.
  2. Partition hota hai. User ka phone node B se eggs jodta hai → D3 (A,2),(B,1). Laptop node C se tea jodta hai → D4 (A,2),(C,1).
  3. Baad ka read dono D3 aur D4 laata hai. Compare: D3 mein B:1 > 0, D4 mein C:1 > 0 → koi ancestor nahi → conflict.
  4. Client reconcile karta hai (cart ke liye: items ka union) aur A se wapas likhta hai → D5 (A,3),(B,1),(C,1), jo dono se descend karta hai.
enum Order { BEFORE, AFTER, EQUAL, CONCURRENT }

static Order compare(Map<String,Integer> x, Map<String,Integer> y) {
    boolean xBigger = false, yBigger = false;
    Set<String> nodes = new HashSet<>(x.keySet()); nodes.addAll(y.keySet());
    for (String n : nodes) {
        int a = x.getOrDefault(n, 0), b = y.getOrDefault(n, 0);
        if (a > b) xBigger = true;
        if (b > a) yBigger = true;
    }
    if (xBigger && yBigger) return Order.CONCURRENT;   // siblings → conflict
    if (xBigger) return Order.AFTER;                   // x, y se descend karta hai
    if (yBigger) return Order.BEFORE;                  // y, x se descend karta hai
    return Order.EQUAL;
}

Vector clocks ke nuksaan:

  • Complexity clients pe — unhe har data type ke liye merge logic likhna padta hai.
  • Clocks badhti jaati hain har us server ke saath jisne write coordinate kiya. Fix: length cap karo (jaise 10 entries) aur sabse purani hatao; isse kabhi-kabhi ancestry detect nahi hoti (rare, Dynamo ke experience mein accepted).

Alternatives jo bata sakte ho

Timestamps ke saath Last-write-wins (LWW) (Cassandra ka default): simple, par do concurrent writes mein se ek ko chupchaap kho deta hai aur clock sync pe depend karta hai. CRDTs (conflict-free replicated data types — counters, sets, maps jo apne aap merge hote hain) client-side merge code se bachate hain; Riak, Redis Enterprise, collaborative editors use karte hain.

docs.title: 5 · Failures handle karna
docs.text: Scale pe failures exception nahi — roz ki baat hain. Unhe detect aur resolve karna hai.

docs.title: Failure detection: gossip
docs.text:
Ek server ko sirf isliye dead declare nahi kar sakte kyunki ek doosra server aisa bolta hai. Har node se har node ko ping karwana (all-to-all multicasting) sahi hai par O(n²) messages — saikdon nodes ke saath bahut zyada.

Gossip protocol (decentralised failure detection):

  1. Har node ek membership list rakhta hai: member ID → heartbeat counter + local time jab woh aakhri baar badha.
  2. Har node apna heartbeat samay-samay pe badhata hai.
  3. Samay-samay pe har node apni list kuch random nodes ko bhejta hai, jo merge karte hain (bade counters rakhte hue) aur aage badhate hain.
  4. Agar kisi member ka heartbeat ek threshold time tak nahi badha, use offline maana jaata hai.
Node s0 ka view Heartbeat Aakhri baar badha (s0 ki ghadi) s0 1820 10:41:07 s1 1793 10:41:05 s2 1650 10:39:22 ← 100 s se stale → s2 down hone ka shak s3 1802 10:41:06

s0 phir doosron ko gossip karta hai "s2 down lag raha hai"; jab kai nodes alag-alag agree karte hain, s2 down mark hota hai.

docs.title: Temporary failures: sloppy quorum + hinted handoff
docs.text:
Strict quorum reads/writes ko block kar deta hai jab key ke designated N replicas mein se kam up hon — availability ke liye bura.

Sloppy quorum: designated replicas pe zid karne ki jagah ring pe pehle W (ya R) healthy servers chuno, dead waale skip karke.

Hinted handoff: agar server s2 down hai, uske writes agle healthy server, maan lo s4, pe hint ke saath jaate hain ("yeh s2 ka hai"). Jab s2 wapas aata hai (gossip batata hai), s4 data wapas de deta hai aur apni copy delete kar deta hai.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Co as Coordinator
    participant S1 as s1
    participant S2 as s2 (down)
    participant S4 as s4 (stand-in)
    Co->>S1: write k
    Co-xS2: write k (timeout)
    Co->>S4: write k + hint "owner = s2"
    Note over S2: ...wapas online
    S4->>S2: k hand off
    S4->>S4: hinted copy delete

docs.title: Permanent failures: Merkle trees ke saath anti-entropy
docs.text:
Agar replica lambe time ke liye gayab hai (ya hinted data kho gaya), replicas diverge ho jaate hain. Unhe sync karna hai, par terabytes mein har key compare karna bahut mehenga hai. Merkle tree (hash tree) do replicas ko bahut kam data transfer karke differences dhoondhne deta hai.

Banana (maan lo keys ek range mein hash hoti hain jo 8 buckets mein bati hai):

  1. Key space ko buckets mein baanto.
  2. Har key ki value hash karo; phir har bucket ki keys ke hashes se ek bucket hash nikalo.
  3. Upar ki taraf binary tree banao: har parent = hash(left child + right child). Root sab kuch summarise karta hai.
flowchart TB
    R["root: H(ab|cd)"] --> AB["H(a|b)"] & CD["H(c|d)"]
    AB --> A["a = H(b1|b2)"] & B["b = H(b3|b4)"]
    CD --> C["c = H(b5|b6)"] & D["d = H(b7|b8)"]
    A --> b1[bucket 1] & b2[bucket 2]
    B --> b3[bucket 3] & b4[bucket 4]
    C --> b5[bucket 5] & b6["bucket 6 ⚠"]
    D --> b7[bucket 7] & b8[bucket 8]

Do replicas compare karna: roots compare karo. Barabar → sync mein, khatam. Alag → dono children compare karo, sirf usi subtree mein recurse karo jiske hashes alag hain. Yahan sirf root → CD → c → bucket 6 ka path alag hai, toh sirf bucket 6 ki keys exchange hoti hain.

Kaam differences ke proportional hai, data size ke nahi. Example: 1 billion keys 10 lakh buckets mein → har bucket mein ~1,000 keys; agar ek key alag hai, toh ~20 levels chalte ho aur 1 billion ki jagah ~1,000 keys bhejte ho.

docs.title: Data center outage
docs.text: Power cut, network failure aur natural disasters poore DCs gira dete hain. Kai data centers mein replicate karo taaki users doosre se padh/likh sakein.

docs.title: 6 · System architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Cl[Client] -->|"get / put"| Co["Coordinator node<br/>(koi bhi node)"]
    Co --> n1[node] & n2[node] & n3[node]
    subgraph Ring["Hash ring — har node identical"]
      n1 --- n2 --- n3 --- n4[node] --- n5[node] --- n6[node] --- n1
    end

Koi master nahi hai. Koi bhi node client ka get/put le sakta hai; us request ke liye woh coordinator banta hai, ring se key ki preference list nikaalta hai, aur un replicas se baat karta hai. Kyunki har node same software chalata hai — request handling, gossip membership, replication, hinted-handoff storage, anti-entropy aur local LSM storage engine — tum identical boxes jod ke scale karte ho, aur koi ek box khone se kuch unique nahi khota. (Kuch clients "ring-aware" hoke request seedha replica ko bhej dete hain aur extra hop bacha lete hain.)

docs.title: 7 · Write path (LSM-tree, Cassandra jaisa)
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    W["put(k, v)"] --> L["1 · commit log mein<br/>append (disk)"]
    L --> M["2 · memtable mein<br/>likho (memory, sorted)"]
    M -->|"3 · memtable full → flush"| S["SSTable (immutable,<br/>sorted, disk pe)"]
    S -.->|background| CP["compaction:<br/>SSTables merge, overwritten/<br/>deleted keys hatao"]
  1. Write commit log mein append hota hai (sequential disk write — tez, aur crash ke baad memtable recover karne deta hai).
  2. Memtable mein insert hota hai, ek in-memory sorted structure.
  3. Memtable threshold pe pahunche toh disk pe SSTable (Sorted String Table) ki tarah flush hota hai: key-value pairs ki immutable, sorted file.
  4. Compaction background mein SSTables merge karta hai, overwritten values aur tombstones (deletion markers) hata deta hai.

Yeh design kyun? Writes sequential hain (random disk seeks nahi — Chapter 2 ki latency table yaad karo), toh write throughput bahut zyada hai.

docs.title: 8 · Read path
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    R["get(k)"] --> M{memtable mein?}
    M -->|haan| RET[value return]
    M -->|nahi| BF{"Bloom filters:<br/>kaunsi SSTables mein<br/>k ho sakti hai?"}
    BF --> SS["sirf wahi SSTables padho<br/>(nayi pehle)"] --> RET
  1. Memtable check karo — mili toh return.
  2. Warna har SSTable ka Bloom filter dekho ki kaunsi SSTables mein key ho sakti hai.
  3. Wahi SSTables padho (nayi pehle) aur value return karo.

Bloom filter ek paragraph mein: ek bit array plus k hash functions. Key add karne ke liye, jin k bits pe woh hash hoti hai unhe set karo. Query ke liye woh k bits dekho: koi bhi 0 hai toh key pakka nahi hai; saare 1 hain toh shayad hai. False negatives nahi, false positives tunable (~10 bits per key pe ~1%). Isse read path lagbhag har us SSTable ko skip kar deta hai jisme key ho hi nahi sakti.

final class BloomFilter {
    private final BitSet bits; private final int m, k;
    BloomFilter(int m, int k) { this.bits = new BitSet(m); this.m = m; this.k = k; }
    private int idx(String key, int i) {                 // double hashing: h1 + i*h2
        int h1 = key.hashCode(), h2 = (h1 >>> 16) | 1;
        return Math.floorMod(h1 + i * h2, m);
    }
    void add(String key)              { for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) bits.set(idx(key, i)); }
    boolean mightContain(String key)  { for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) if (!bits.get(idx(key, i))) return false; return true; }
}

docs.title: Sab jodke: ek request ka safar
docs.text:
Is chapter ko revise karne ka sabse tez tareeka hai ek write aur ek read ko har mechanism se guzarte hue dekhna:

Pal Kya hota hai Mechanism Keemat kya hai Client put(k, v) call karta hai Koi bhi node coordinator banta hai; k ko ring pe hash karta hai Consistent hashing + vnodes Har node pe ring metadata Coordinator replicas chunta hai Clockwise pehle N alag physical nodes, racks/DCs ke across Preference list Cross-DC bandwidth Ek replica down hai Agla healthy node write ko hint ke saath rakhta hai Sloppy quorum + hinted handoff Quorum overlap ki guarantee nahi rehti W acks aate hain Client ko OK; late waale bhi apply karte hain Quorum (N, W, R) Latency = W mein sabse slow Har replica pe Commit log mein append, memtable mein insert, baad mein SSTable flush LSM storage engine Background mein compaction I/O Baad mein get(k) Coordinator replicas se poochta hai, R ka wait; do versions dikhte hain Vector clocks Clients ko siblings merge karne padte hain Versions alag the Coordinator sabse naya stale replicas pe wapas likhta hai Read repair Reads pe extra writes Replica pe k dhoondhna Pehle memtable, phir sirf woh SSTables jinka Bloom filter "shayad" bole Bloom filters Har key ka ~10 bits RAM Poore time Nodes random peers se heartbeats exchange karte hain Gossip Detection mein seconds lagte hain, milliseconds nahi Samay-samay pe Replicas hash trees compare karke sirf alag ranges sync karte hain Merkle-tree anti-entropy Ranges badalne pe tree rebuild

docs.title: Interviewer follow-ups
docs.text:
N=3, W=2, R=2 ke saath kya read ab bhi stale data de sakta hai?

Steady state mein nahi — read set aur write set overlap karte hain. Par edge cases hain: sloppy quorum mein W acks designated replicas ke bahar ke stand-in nodes se aa sakte hain, toh overlap guarantee toot jaati hai; concurrent writes siblings bana sakte hain; aur fail hua write (W se kam acks) phir bhi kuch replicas pe gir chuka ho sakta hai. Isliye Dynamo-style systems ise "tunable" consistency kehte hain, linearizability nahi.

Read repair kya hai?

Jab coordinator quorum read karte hue dekhta hai ki replicas alag versions de rahe hain, woh client ko sabse naya (ya siblings) deta hai aur stale replicas pe latest version wapas likh deta hai. Hot keys pe divergence sasta fix hota hai; Merkle-tree anti-entropy un cold keys ko sambhalta hai jo kam padhi jaati hain.

Vector clocks ki jagah timestamps (last-write-wins) kyun nahi?

LWW simple hai aur bahut use hota hai (Cassandra). Par alag machines ki ghadiyan drift karti hain, aur LWW do concurrent writes mein se ek ko chupchaap gira deta hai — "last known location" ke liye theek, shopping cart ke liye galat jahan dono additions matter karte hain. Vector clocks concurrency detect karte hain taaki merge kar sako; suitable data types ke liye CRDTs apne aap merge karte hain.

Is system mein key delete kaise karoge?

Seedha hata nahi sakte — jis replica ne delete miss kiya woh anti-entropy ke dauraan key ko "zinda" kar dega. Iski jagah ek tombstone likho (version ke saath deletion marker). Tombstones normal writes ki tarah phailte hain aur compaction mein tabhi purge hote hain jab itna grace period beet jaaye ki saare replicas ne dekh liya ho (Cassandra: gc_grace_seconds).

CP store kab chunoge?

Jab partition mein correctness availability se zyada important ho: leader election aur locks (etcd/ZooKeeper), financial ledgers, inventory jahan oversell bilkul nahi chalega, unique-username registration. Yeh consensus (Raft/Paxos) use karte hain aur partition ki minority side pe requests reject karte hain.

Cluster join karne waale node ko data kaise milta hai?

Use ring pe vnodes (tokens) assign hote hain; har naye arc ke liye woh current owners (clockwise agle replicas) se relevant key ranges stream karta hai. Streaming khatam hone tak purane owners reads serve kar sakte hain; gossip nayi membership phailata hai taaki coordinators use route karna shuru karein.

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
Practice 1 — N, W, R chuno

(a) Session store: reads writes ke 10:1, ek second stale chalega, hamesha up rehna chahiye. (b) Configuration store jahan read ko aakhri write dikhna chahiye. Dono mein N=3. W aur R chuno.

Solution. (a) W=1, R=1 (ya W=2,R=1) — tez aur highly available; eventual consistency chalegi. (b) W=2, R=2 (W+R > N), ya agar writes kam hain aur reads sabse tez chahiye toh W=3, R=1. Agar partition mein bhi kabhi stale read nahi chahiye, toh CP system (etcd) use karo.

Practice 2 — Vector clocks compare karo

Har pair ke liye batao ancestor/descendant ya conflict: (i) (A,2),(B,1) vs (A,3),(B,1) · (ii) (A,1),(C,2) vs (A,2),(B,1) · (iii) (A,1) vs (A,1),(B,4)

Solution. (i) pehla doosre ka ancestor (2≤3, 1≤1). (ii) conflict — pehle mein C:2 > 0, doosre mein A:2 > 1 aur B:1 > 0. (iii) pehla ancestor (missing B ko 0 ≤ 4 maano).

Practice 3 — Bloom filter sizing

Ek node ki SSTables mein 20 crore keys hain. ~1% false positives chahiye. Bloom filters ko roughly kitni memory chahiye?

Solution. 1% ke liye ~9.6 bits/key (optimal k ≈ 7) → 200M × 9.6 bits ≈ 1.92 × 10⁹ bits ≈ 240 MB. Absent keys ke disk reads bachane ke muqable sasta.

Practice 4 — Merkle tree ki bachat

Do replicas mein 50 crore keys 2²⁰ (~10 lakh) buckets mein hain. 300 keys alag hain, sab alag buckets mein. Kitne buckets ki keys transfer hongi?

Solution. Sirf 300 alag buckets (~500 keys each) → ~1.5 lakh keys transfer, 50 crore ki jagah — data ka ~0.03%. Tree walk ~300 × 20 node hashes compare karta hai.

docs.title: Revision checklist
docs.text:
• CAP sahi bol sakta hoon ("partition ke dauraan C ya A chuno") aur CP/AP examples de sakta hoon, plus PACELC.
  • N alag servers ki preference list ke saath partitioning + replication samjha sakta hoon.
  • N/W/R, W + R > N overlap kyun deta hai, aur use case ke liye values chun sakta hoon.
  • Strong / weak / eventual consistency define kar sakta hoon.
  • Vector-clock example chala ke ancestor vs conflict decide kar sakta hoon; LWW aur CRDTs alternatives pata hain.
  • Gossip, sloppy quorum, hinted handoff, Merkle trees aur tombstones samjha sakta hoon.
  • LSM write path aur read path bana sakta hoon aur Bloom filter kaise kaam karta hai samjha sakta hoon.

Aage: 07 · Unique ID Generator

docs.title: 07 · Distributed Systems mein Unique ID Generator Design karo
docs.text:
⏱ 35 min read 🔥 URL shortener, chat, feeds, payments… sabko chahiye Book: Chapter 7

TL;DR

  • Ek database ka AUTO_INCREMENT kai machines ke saath nahi chal pata aur single point of failure hai.
  • Options: multi-master with step (simple, time-sortable nahi, scale karna mushkil), UUID (coordination nahi, par 128-bit aur random), ticket server / range allocation (central counter, numeric, par coordination point), Snowflake (64-bit = timestamp + datacenter + machine + sequence).
  • Snowflake classic requirements pe fit hai: 64-bit, numeric, roughly time-ordered, har machine pe ~40 lakh IDs/sec, har ID ke liye koi coordination nahi.
  • Kamzor point hai ghadi (clock): machine ki ghadi peeche chali gayi toh IDs repeat ho sakti hain — detect karo aur wait/fail karo. Doosri limit: custom epoch se sirf ~69 saal ke timestamps.
  • Modern alternatives: UUIDv7 / ULID — time-ordered 128-bit IDs jo UUID ki no-coordination khoobi rakhti hain aur achhe se index hoti hain.

docs.title: Intuition: hospital ke token numbers
docs.text:
Ek reception desk waala hospital token 1, 2, 3… deta hai — aasaan, par token ki line hi bottleneck ban jaati hai, aur woh desk band hua toh kisi ko token nahi milta.

5 desks khol do? Rule chahiye taaki do desks same number na dein. Desk 1 deta hai 1, 6, 11…; desk 2 deta hai 2, 7, 12… Chhatha desk khulne tak chalta hai. Ya har token ho "time + desk number + counter" — jaise 10:42:07 · desk 3 · #12. Bina kisi desk ke doosre se baat kiye unique, aur patients ko aane ke order se roughly sort bhi kar sakte ho. Yahi idea Snowflake hai.

docs.title: Step 1 · Scope
docs.text:
Clarifying baatcheet

Tum: Uniqueness ke alawa IDs ko kya satisfy karna hai? — Interviewer: Sirf numeric, aur 64-bit integer mein fit ho. Tum: Sortable honi chahiye? — I: Haan — agar A saaf taur pe B se pehle bana, toh A ki ID chhoti ho. Har millisecond ka strict order zaroori nahi. Tum: Throughput? — I: Total kam se kam 10,000 IDs per second, aur badhne ki gunjaish. Tum: IDs guess ho sakti hain toh chalega? — I: Is system ke liye chalega (yeh internal row IDs hain). Tum: Kai data centers? — I: Haan, kai.

Requirements: unique · numeric · 64-bit · creation time se ordered (approx) · ≥10K IDs/s · koi single point of failure nahi · low latency (local generate, ideally koi network hop nahi).

DB ka auto-increment kyun nahi? Distributed system mein kai databases (shards) hote hain, har ek ka apna counter → duplicates. Aur ek global counter DB bottleneck aur SPOF hai.

docs.title: Option 1 · Step ke saath multi-master replication
docs.text:
k database servers mein se har ek pe AUTO_INCREMENT use karo, par 1 ki jagah k se badhao:

k = 3 servers
DB1: 1, 4, 7, 10, …     (start 1, step 3)
DB2: 2, 5, 8, 11, …     (start 2, step 3)
DB3: 3, 6, 9, 12, …     (start 3, step 3)
✅ ❌ Plain DB features; numeric; zyada DBs ke saath thoda scale IDs servers ke across time-ordered nahi (DB3 ka #9, DB1 ke #10 ke baad ban sakta hai) Server add/remove karne se k badalta hai → renumbering ka jhanjhat Kai data centers ke across achhe se scale nahi hota

docs.title: Option 2 · UUID
docs.text:
UUID ek 128-bit number hai jo locally generate hota hai (jaise 09c93e62-50b4-468d-bf8a-c07e1040bfb2). Common version 4 random hai: 122 random bits. Collision ka chance bahut hi kam — ek duplicate ke 50% chance tak pahunchne ke liye ~86 saal tak har second 10⁹ UUIDs banane padenge.

String id = java.util.UUID.randomUUID().toString();   // koi coordination nahi
✅ ❌ Bahut aasaan; har server khud generate karta hai — na coordination, na SPOF 128 bits, 64 nahi Perfectly scale — servers freely jodo Time-ordered nahi (v4 random hai) Non-numeric ho sakti hai (dashes waali hex string) Random keys B-tree index mein writes bikher deti hain → page splits, kharab cache locality

docs.title: Option 3 · Ticket server
docs.text:
Ek akela, dedicated database jiska sirf kaam hai numbers dena (Flickr ne popular kiya):

-- ek row waali table; REPLACE auto-increment badhata hai aur nayi ID deta hai
REPLACE INTO tickets64 (stub) VALUES ('a');
SELECT LAST_INSERT_ID();

Har service ID ke liye ticket server ko call karti hai.

✅ ❌ Numeric, simple, small-to-medium scale pe achha Single point of failure — down hua toh koi kuch create nahi kar sakta Har ID ke liye ek network round trip Do ticket servers (odd/even) chalao toh sync problems wapas

Range allocation (hi/lo) — practical upgrade: har call pe ek ID ki jagah ticket server ek block deta hai (jaise 10,000 IDs). Har app server apna block locally khatam karta hai aur lagbhag khaali hone pe agla block maangta hai. Network calls 10,000× kam, aur ticket server ka outage tabhi chubhta hai jab blocks khatam ho jaayein. Nuksaan: IDs sirf roughly ordered, aur crash hua server apne block ka baaki hissa "barbaad" karta hai (gaps chalte hain).

docs.title: Option 4 · Twitter Snowflake
docs.text:
64-bit ID ko sections mein baanto, har ek ka matlab:

Section Bits Matlab Sign 1 Hamesha 0 (signed 64-bit types mein number positive rakhta hai) Timestamp 41 Custom epoch se milliseconds Datacenter ID 5 2⁵ = 32 data centers Machine ID 5 Har data center mein 2⁵ = 32 machines Sequence 12 Same machine pe same millisecond ke andar counter; 2¹² = 4,096 values; har ms 0 pe reset 
flowchart LR
    s["0<br/>sign · 1"] --- t["epoch se timestamp<br/>41 bits"] --- d["datacenter<br/>5 bits"] --- m["machine<br/>5 bits"] --- q["sequence<br/>12 bits"]

Datacenter aur machine IDs startup pe assign hoti hain (config ya ZooKeeper jaisi coordination service se) aur process chalte hue nahi badalti. Timestamp aur sequence program chalte hue bante hain.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text:
Approach Size Time se sortable Har ID pe coordination SPOF DCs ke across scale Multi-master step 64 ❌ Nahi Nahi Kharab UUIDv4 128 ❌ Nahi Nahi ✅ Ticket server 64 ✅ (globally) Haan (network call) Haan ❌ Range allocation 64 ~ (per block) Kabhi-kabhi Thoda Theek Snowflake 64 ✅ (≈ ms se) Nahi Nahi ✅ UUIDv7 / ULID 128 ✅ (ms se) Nahi Nahi ✅

Snowflake hamari saari requirements meet karta hai → gehraai mein chalte hain.

docs.title: Timestamp
docs.text:
41 bits milliseconds ke. Bits wapas shift karke time nikaalo:

id → binary → bits 63..22 lo (41 bits) → decimal → epoch jodo → Unix ms → date

Kitne din chalega? 2⁴¹ − 1 ms ≈ 2.2 × 10¹² ms ≈ 69.7 saal.

Isliye 1970 ki jagah launch date ke paas ka custom epoch use karte hain. Twitter ka epoch 1288834974657 hai (04 Nov 2010, 01:42:54 UTC) → unki IDs lagbhag 2080 ke aas-paas khatam hongi. 1970 se shuru karte toh 69 mein se 40+ saal pehle hi kharch ho chuke hote.

Timestamp high bits mein hai, isliye IDs time se sort hoti hain — aur kyunki IDs time ke saath badhti hain, nayi rows B-tree indexes ke end pe append hoti hain (achhi locality, random UUIDs ke ulat).

docs.title: Sequence number
docs.text: 12 bits → har machine pe har millisecond 4,096 IDs → har machine ~40 lakh IDs/sec. Agar kisi machine ko ek millisecond mein 4,096 se zyada chahiye, toh woh agle millisecond tak wait karti hai.

docs.title: Capacity check
docs.text: 32 DCs × 32 machines × 4,096 IDs/ms ≈ poore cluster mein har millisecond ~4.2 billion IDs. Hamari requirement 10K/s thi. Bahut headroom.

docs.title: Java implementation
docs.text:
public final class Snowflake {
    private static final long EPOCH = 1_288_834_974_657L;         // custom epoch (ms)
    private static final int  DC_BITS = 5, MACHINE_BITS = 5, SEQ_BITS = 12;
    private static final long MAX_SEQ = (1L << SEQ_BITS) - 1;      // 4095
    private static final int  MACHINE_SHIFT = SEQ_BITS;            // 12
    private static final int  DC_SHIFT = SEQ_BITS + MACHINE_BITS;  // 17
    private static final int  TS_SHIFT = DC_SHIFT + DC_BITS;       // 22

    private final long datacenterId, machineId;
    private long lastTs = -1L, sequence = 0L;

    public Snowflake(long datacenterId, long machineId) {
        if (datacenterId < 0 || datacenterId > 31 || machineId < 0 || machineId > 31)
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("ids must be 0..31");
        this.datacenterId = datacenterId; this.machineId = machineId;
    }

    public synchronized long nextId() {
        long ts = System.currentTimeMillis();
        if (ts < lastTs) {                                    // ghadi peeche chali gayi!
            long drift = lastTs - ts;
            if (drift > 5) throw new IllegalStateException("clock moved back " + drift + " ms");
            ts = waitUntil(lastTs);                           // chhota drift: bas wait kar lo
        }
        if (ts == lastTs) {
            sequence = (sequence + 1) & MAX_SEQ;
            if (sequence == 0) ts = waitUntil(lastTs + 1);    // is ms ke 4,096 khatam
        } else {
            sequence = 0;
        }
        lastTs = ts;
        return ((ts - EPOCH) << TS_SHIFT) | (datacenterId << DC_SHIFT)
             | (machineId << MACHINE_SHIFT) | sequence;
    }

    private static long waitUntil(long target) {
        long now = System.currentTimeMillis();
        while (now < target) { Thread.onSpinWait(); now = System.currentTimeMillis(); }
        return now;
    }
}

docs.title: Clock synchronisation
docs.text:
Snowflake maanta hai ki har machine ki ghadi theek hai. Asal mein:

  • Ghadiyan drift karti hain; NTP unhe theek karta hai, aur correction ghadi ko peeche le ja sakta hai. Agar ts < lastTs, toh bhole-bhaale code mein purane timestamps dobara use honge aur ID repeat ho sakti hai. Upar ka code chhote drift pe wait karta hai aur bade drift pe mana (alert) karta hai.
  • Leap seconds aur VM pauses bhi aise hi surprises dete hain. Kai companies jumps se bachne ke liye leap seconds ko poore din mein "smear" karti hain.
  • Machines ke across IDs sirf roughly ordered hain — do machines ki ghadiyon mein kuch ms ka fark, toh machine A ki ID machine B pe thoda pehle bani ID se chhoti ho sakti hai. Aam taur pe theek hai ("k-sorted").

docs.title: Bit sections tune karna
docs.text:
41/5/5/12 ka split pathar ki lakeer nahi:

  • Traffic kam par lifetime lambi → kam sequence bits, zyada timestamp bits.
  • Kai machines, ek DC → datacenter + machine ko 10-bit worker ID mein merge (1,024 workers).
  • Ek machine pe 4,096/ms se zyada chahiye → zyada sequence bits.

docs.title: Machine IDs safely assign karna
docs.text: Same (datacenter, machine) waale do processes duplicates banayenge. Worker IDs ZooKeeper/etcd ephemeral nodes, DB lease table, ya Kubernetes StatefulSet ordinals se assign karo — haath se config edit karke kabhi nahi.

docs.title: High availability
docs.text: Generator har service ke andar ek library hai (koi network hop nahi) — ya load balancer ke peeche ek chhoti stateless service. Dono tarah khone ko koi shared state nahi.

docs.title: Privacy / guessability
docs.text: Snowflake IDs creation time aur machine ne roughly kitni IDs banayi, yeh leak karti hain. Public-facing IDs ke liye jahan yeh matter kare (invoice numbers, URLs mein user IDs), ek opaque layer jodo: ID ko encrypt/permute karo ya alag random public ID dikhao.

docs.title: Thoda gehraai mein: UUIDv7, ULID, KSUID
docs.text:
Naye formats UUID ka "no coordination, 128 bits" model rakhte hain par timestamp pehle daalte hain, toh time se sort hote hain:

Format Layout Notes UUIDv7 (RFC 9562, 2024) 48-bit Unix ms timestamp + version bits + 74 random bits Standard UUID type, time-ordered → Postgres/MySQL mein index-friendly. Jab 128 bits chalenge, aaj ka great default. ULID 48-bit ms timestamp + 80 random bits, 26-char Crockford base-32 mein Lexicographically sortable strings; URL-safe KSUID (Segment) 32-bit seconds timestamp + 128 random bits → 160 bits, base-62 string Second tak sortable

Jab requirement 64-bit numeric bolti hai, tab Snowflake (ya Sonyflake, Instagram ki Postgres-based shard IDs, Discord ka Snowflake jaise variants) hi jawab hai.

docs.title: Interviewer follow-ups
docs.text:
Tumhara NTP daemon ek server ki ghadi 2 second peeche kar deta hai. Kya hoga?

2 second tak woh machine woh timestamps banayegi jo pehle use ho chuke hain. Sequence bhi restart hua toh duplicate IDs nikal sakti hain. Mitigations: now < lastTs detect karo; chhote drift pe ghadi ke aage aane tak spin karo; bade drift pe generate karna mana karo (request fail / node ko rotation se bahar) aur alert karo. NTP ko bhi ghadi step karne ki jagah slew (dheere-dheere adjust) karne ke liye configure karo.

Kaise guarantee karoge ki do machines kabhi same machine ID share na karein?

Static config pe bharosa mat karo. Startup pe coordination service se worker ID lo — jaise ZooKeeper mein ephemeral sequential node banao, ya DB mein lease ke saath row claim karo aur samay-samay pe renew karo. Lease kho gayi toh IDs banana band. Kubernetes mein StatefulSet pod ordinals bhi stable source hain.

Kya Snowflake IDs strictly increasing hain?

Har machine pe haan (process ke andar monotonic). Globally sirf approximately — millisecond se ordered, phir datacenter/machine bits se, aur alag machines ki ghadiyon mein thoda fark. Strict global order chahiye toh single sequencer (ya consensus log) chahiye, jo bottleneck wapas le aata hai.

UUIDv4 ko primary key kyun nahi banate?

Chalta hai, par 16 bytes hai (8 ki jagah) — use refer karne waali har table mein bade indexes — aur random inserts B-tree page splits aur kharab cache locality laate hain, jo scale pe write throughput girata hai. Agar 128 bits chalte hain toh UUIDv7 ordering problem fix kar deta hai.

Ek machine pe har millisecond 50,000 IDs chahiye. Kya badloge?

4,096/ms kaafi nahi. Bits churao: jaise machine space ke 8 bits (agar har DC mein machines kam hain) → 16-bit sequence = 65,536/ms. Ya same host pe alag worker IDs ke saath kai generator instances chalao.

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
Practice 1 — Haath se encode karo

Snowflake-style ID (Twitter layout) ke sections: timestamp = epoch ke baad 1,000,000,000 ms, datacenter = 3, machine = 17, sequence = 5. 64-bit ID ka formula likho.

Solution. id = (1_000_000_000 << 22) | (3 << 17) | (17 << 12) | 5 = 4,194,304,000,000,000 + 393,216 + 69,632 + 5 = 4,194,304,000,462,853. (Widget mein timestamp = epoch + 1,000,000,000 set karke verify karo.)

Practice 2 — Lifetime

Layout redesign karo: 1 sign + 39 timestamp bits (10 ms ki units) + 16 worker bits + 8 sequence bits (lagbhag Sonyflake). Kitne saal chalega, aur har worker ka max rate kya hai?

Solution. 2³⁹ × 10 ms ≈ 5.5 × 10¹² ms ≈ 174 saal. Rate: 2⁸ = 256 IDs per 10 ms = har worker 25,600 IDs/s, 65,536 workers tak.

Practice 3 — Approach chuno

Har ek ke liye ID scheme chuno: (a) Postgres waale single-region monolith mein order IDs; (b) global chat app ke chat message IDs; © public share links jo volume reveal na karein.

Solution. (a) Postgres BIGSERIAL/sequence theek hai — ek primary, distribution ki zaroorat nahi. (b) Snowflake — 64-bit, time-ordered, har chat server pe locally (Chapter 12 yahi use karta hai). © Random IDs (UUIDv4 ya random base-62 string) ya encrypted Snowflake — creation time aur counts expose mat karo.

docs.title: Revision checklist
docs.text:
• Samjha sakta hoon ki distributed system mein DB auto-increment kyun fail hota hai.
  • Multi-master step, UUID, ticket server, range allocation aur Snowflake ko size, ordering, coordination, SPOF pe compare kar sakta hoon.
  • Snowflake ka 1/41/5/5/12 layout bana ke har section samjha sakta hoon.
  • 69 saal ki lifetime aur 4,096 IDs/ms/machine limit nikaal sakta hoon, aur custom epoch kyun zaroori hai.
  • Clock-peeche-jaane waale case ke saath Java mein Snowflake implement kar sakta hoon.
  • UUIDv7/ULID aur unhe kab prefer karna hai, pata hai.

Aage: 08 · URL Shortener

docs.title: 08 · URL Shortener Design karo
docs.text:
⏱ 40 min read 🔥 Sabse common "pehla" design question Book: Chapter 8

TL;DR

  • Do APIs: shorten (POST long URL → short code) aur redirect (GET /{code} → Location ke saath 301/302).
  • Reads writes se kahin zyada (das hazaaron redirects/sec vs saikdon creates/sec) → redirect path cache-first hona chahiye.
  • 7 base-62 characters 3.5 trillion codes dete hain — saikdon billion links ke liye kaafi.
  • Code generation: hash + collision check (simple, DB/Bloom-filter check chahiye), unique ID → base-62 (collisions nahi, par sequential codes guess ho sakte hain), ya pre-generated key service (tez, collisions nahi, ek extra component).
  • 301 (permanent) browser ko cache karne deta hai → kam load, per-click analytics nahi. 302 (temporary) → har click tumhare paas → analytics. Product ke hisaab se chuno.

docs.title: Intuition: cloakroom ka token
docs.text:
Shaadi ke cloakroom mein tum bhaari coat dete ho aur ek chhota peetal ka token milta hai "K-47". Baad mein K-47 dikhate ho aur coat wapas. Token chhota hai, unique hai, aur khud mein bematlab — kaam sirf isliye karta hai kyunki cloakroom ek register rakhta hai: K-47 → Riya ka laal coat.

URL shortener exactly wahi register hai: aZ3kQ9x → https://example.in/very/long/path?with=params.

docs.title: Step 1 · Scope
docs.text:
Clarifying baatcheet

Tum: Links kaun banata hai — koi bhi anonymously, ya signed-in users? — Interviewer: Zyada tar signed-in marketers, par anonymous bhi allowed. Tum: Roughly kitne links bante hain, aur har ek kitni baar khulta hai? — I: Roz lagbhag 4 crore naye links; ek link apni zindagi mein ~50 clicks paata hai. Tum: Marketers ko click counts chahiye? — I: Haan, aage chalke — par redirect khud tez rehna chahiye. Tum: Short hissa kaisa dikhe, koi constraint? — I: Chhota aur URL-safe: sirf digits aur letters. Tum: Links hamesha zinda rehte hain? — I: Default lambi life (maan lo 15 saal); user pehle ki expiry set kar sakta hai. Tum: /diwali-sale jaise vanity names? — I: Nice-to-have.

Functional: URL short karo; short URL ko original pe redirect karo. (Stretch: custom alias, expiry, analytics.) Non-functional: redirects pe bahut high availability aur low latency; codes collide na karein; scalable; codes aasaani se enumerate na ho sakein (nice to have).

docs.title: Estimates (Chapter 2, worked example 4 se)
docs.text: Cheez Value Naye links 40 M/din → ~460 writes/sec Redirects (50:1) ~23K/sec avg, ~45K/sec peak 15 saal mein records ~219 B Storage ~250 B × 219 B ≈ 55 TB (plus replicas) Code length 62⁷ ≈ 3.5 T ≥ 219 B → 7 chars Hot-link cache (1 mahine ke links ka 20% ≈ 240 M × 250 B) ~60 GB → chhota Redis cluster

docs.title: API
docs.text:
POST /api/v1/links
     { "longUrl": "https://...", "alias": "diwali-sale" (optional), "expiresAt": "2027-01-01" (optional) }
  → 201 { "shortUrl": "https://sho.rt/aZ3kQ9x", "code": "aZ3kQ9x" }

GET /{code}
  → 301 ya 302,  Location: https://...        (unknown ho toh 404, expired ho toh 410)

docs.title: Redirect kaise kaam karta hai
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant S as sho.rt (redirect service)
    participant T as store.example.in
    B->>S: GET /aZ3kQ9x
    S-->>B: 301 Moved Permanently<br/>Location: https://store.example.in/catalog/kurta?...
    B->>T: GET /catalog/kurta?...
    T-->>B: 200 OK (page)

docs.title: 301 vs 302 — asli product decision
docs.text:
301 Moved Permanently 302 Found (temporary; 307 bhi) Browser behaviour Mapping cache karta hai; agle clicks seedha target pe Har baar shortener se poochta hai Hum pe load Kam Zyada Click analytics ❌ repeat clicks miss ✅ har click dikhta hai Baad mein target badal sakte hain? Mushkil (browsers ne cache kar liya) Haan Typical choice Pure redirect service, cost-sensitive Marketing links, analytics products (bit.ly-style)

(307/308, 302/301 ke method-preserving versions hain — tabhi relevant jab short URL pe POST aa sakta ho.)

docs.title: Sabse simple version: hash table
docs.text: Concept mein yeh ek map hai code → longUrl. Do functions: shorten(longUrl) → code aur resolve(code) → longUrl. Interesting hissa hai code generate kaise karein.

docs.title: Data model
docs.text:
Shuru mein relational table theek hai; 219 B rows pe shard karoge (ya DynamoDB/Cassandra jaisa KV store, kyunki har access primary key se hai).

CREATE TABLE links (
  code        VARCHAR(10) PRIMARY KEY,   -- 'aZ3kQ9x'
  long_url    TEXT        NOT NULL,
  owner_id    BIGINT,
  created_at  TIMESTAMP   NOT NULL,
  expires_at  TIMESTAMP   NULL
);
-- optional: har owner ke liye identical long URLs dedupe
CREATE INDEX idx_links_owner_url ON links (owner_id, long_url_hash);

docs.title: Approach A · Long URL hash karo, phir collisions resolve karo
docs.text:
Long URL ko standard function se hash karo aur pehle 7 characters lo. https://store.example.in/catalog/kurta?colour=indigo&size=m hash karne pe:

Hash Output size Output (hex) CRC32 32 bits → 8 hex chars 7e4f6003 MD5 128 bits → 32 hex chars ef6fccd4556105478a8f292ad9f21cf2 SHA-1 160 bits → 40 hex chars 6ab80c8af890410c521436aac154d5f54ace4960

Sabse chhota bhi 7 se lamba hai, toh hum truncate karte hain — jisse collisions badhte hain. Inhe resolve karne ke liye ek salt (predefined string ya counter) jodo aur tab tak re-hash karo jab tak code free na mile:

flowchart LR
    I[longUrl] --> H["hash(longUrl + salt)<br/>pehle 7 chars lo"] --> E{code DB mein<br/>hai?}
    E -->|nahi| S[code → longUrl save]
    E -->|haan, collision| A["salt = salt + 1"] --> H
  • Har attempt ek DB lookup hai → mehenga. Memory mein existing codes ka Bloom filter rakh ke tez karo: "pakka use nahi hua" waale jawab DB skip kar dete hain.
  • Achhi baat: same long URL aam taur pe same code deta hai (natural dedupe), jab tak salt na lage.

docs.title: Approach B · Unique ID → base-62
docs.text:
Ek unique numeric ID banao (Chapter 7 — Snowflake, ya range-allocated counter), phir use alphabet 0-9 a-z A-Z se base 62 mein badlo.

Worked example: ID = 3,141,592,653,589

3141592653589 % 62 = 27  → 'r'     (quotient 50670849251)
50670849251   % 62 = 7   → '7'     (quotient 817271762)
817271762     % 62 = 38  → 'C'     (quotient 13181802)
13181802      % 62 = 44  → 'I'     (quotient 212609)
212609        % 62 = 11  → 'b'     (quotient 3429)
3429          % 62 = 19  → 'j'     (quotient 55)
55            % 62 = 55  → 'T'     (quotient 0)
remainders neeche → upar padho:  "TjbIC7r"

Converter se check karo (ya koi bhi number try karo):

private static final char[] ALPHABET =
    "0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ".toCharArray();

static String toBase62(long n) {
    if (n == 0) return "0";
    StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
    while (n > 0) { sb.append(ALPHABET[(int) (n % 62)]); n /= 62; }
    return sb.reverse().toString();
}

static long fromBase62(String s) {
    long n = 0;
    for (char c : s.toCharArray()) n = n * 62 + new String(ALPHABET).indexOf(c);
    return n;
}
  • Banawat se hi collisions nahi — unique ID andar, unique code bahar. Koi DB existence check nahi.
  • Code length ID ke saath badhti hai: 64-bit Snowflake ID 11 base-62 characters tak jaati hai. 7 pe rehne ke liye chhote se shuru hone waala counter-based ID (range allocation) use karo, ya dedicated 42-bit ID space rakho.
  • ⚠️ Guess ho sakte hain: sequential IDs → sequential codes. Koi bhi …IC7r, …IC7s enumerate karke saare links scrape kar sakta hai. Fix: encode se pehle ID ko reversible permutation se guzaro (jaise chhota Feistel cipher, ya 62⁷ modulo ek bade odd constant se multiply) — ab bhi unique, par sequential nahi.

docs.title: Approach C · Pre-generated key service (KGS)
docs.text:
Random 7-character codes offline banao, keys_unused table mein rakho, aur ek chhoti Key Generation Service unhe baante. App servers batches (maan lo 1,000) memory mein le aate hain taaki har create pe koi remote call na ho. Used keys keys_used mein chali jaati hain (ya bas unused se delete).

  • ✅ Tez, collisions nahi, random dikhne waale codes.
  • ❌ Ek aur stateful service jo highly available chahiye; do servers ko kabhi same batch nahi milna chahiye (DB mein atomic "claim batch"); crash hue server ke keys kho jaate hain (theek hai — 3.5 T hain).

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text:
A · Hash + check B · ID → base-62 C · Key service Code length Fixed (7) ID ke saath badhti Fixed (7) Collisions Ho sakte → retry Nahi Nahi Extra lookups Har create pe DB/Bloom check Nahi Kabhi-kabhi batch fetch ID generator / KGS chahiye Nahi Haan (ID generator) Haan (KGS) Guessable Nahi Haan jab tak permute na karo Nahi Same URL → same code Naturally (bina salt) Nahi (lookup chahiye) Nahi (lookup chahiye)

Achha interview answer: permuted counter ke saath Approach B, A aur C ko alternatives ki tarah batate hue.

docs.title: Shortening flow (Approach B)
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    C[Client] -->|"POST /api/v1/links"| LB{{Load balancer}} --> API[API servers]
    API --> V{"valid URL?<br/>safe?<br/>rate limit OK?"}
    V -->|nahi| E[400 / 429]
    V -->|haan| D{"dedupe: is owner ne<br/>pehle short kiya?"}
    D -->|haan| R1[existing code return]
    D -->|nahi| ID[ID generator] --> ENC["permute + base-62"] --> W[(links DB)] --> R2[naya short URL return]
  1. URL validate karo (format, length limit jaise 2 KB), malware/phishing list se check karo, caller ko rate-limit karo (Chapter 4).
  2. Optionally check karo ki is owner ne yeh URL pehle short kiya hai ya nahi (long_url_hash se lookup) aur existing code return karo.
  3. Nayi unique ID lo, permute karo, base-62 mein encode karo.
  4. Row insert karo; short URL return karo.

docs.title: Redirect flow — ise tez banao
docs.text:
Redirects writes ke ~50× hain aur tez aur hamesha up hone chahiye.

flowchart LR
    U[User click] --> CDN{{"CDN / edge<br/>(optional, viral links ke liye)"}} --> LB{{LB}} --> RS[Redirect service]
    RS -->|"1. code GET"| CA[(Redis cache)]
    CA -->|hit| RS
    RS -->|"2. miss"| DB[(links DB<br/>sharded, replicas)]
    DB --> RS
    RS -->|"3. cache bharo"| CA
    RS -->|"301/302"| U
    RS -.->|"click event (async)"| K[[Kafka]] -.-> AN[(Analytics store)]
  • LRU ke saath cache-aside: hot links Redis mein rehte hain. Hamara hot set (~60 GB) chhote cluster mein fit.
  • Links immutable hain → caching aasaan (expiry/deletion ke alawa invalidation nahi).
  • Cache misses read replicas serve karte hain; table ko code se shard karo (hash-based) taaki data phaile.
  • Viral links ke liye edge/CDN bhi 301 response ko chhote TTL ke liye cache kar sakta hai.
  • Unknown code → 404. Expired → 410 Gone (aur lazily delete).

docs.title: Batane laayak extras
docs.text:
• Custom aliases: availability check karo (alias bhi bas ek code hai); namespace reserve karo taaki aliases generated codes se na takrayein (jaise generated codes exactly 7 chars, aliases ≥ 8 ya - waale).
  • Expiry: expires_at store karo; read pe check (lazy), plus expired rows purge karne ke liye periodic batch job; codes lambe quarantine ke baad optionally recycle.
  • Analytics: redirect path pe DB mein mat likho. Click event (code, time, IP se country, referrer, device) Kafka pe bhejo; dashboards ke liye columnar store (ClickHouse/BigQuery) mein aggregate karo.
  • Abuse: phishers ko shorteners bahut pasand hain. Target URLs scan karo (Google Safe Browsing-style), creation ko per user/IP rate-limit karo, users ko report karne do, aur flagged domains ke liye interstitial warning dikhao.
  • Availability: redirect service stateless; DB zones ke across replicated; cache replicated. DB down ho tab bhi cached hot links redirect hote rehte hain.

docs.title: Interviewer follow-ups
docs.text:
Do users same long URL short karte hain — same code ya alag?

Product decision. Same code space bachata hai aur shared analytics deta hai, par leak karta hai ki kisi aur ne bhi short kiya aur unke stats mix karta hai. Zyada tar products per-user codes dete hain aur sirf owner ke andar dedupe karte hain (owner_id + hash(long_url) se lookup). Anonymous links globally dedupe ho sakte hain.

Log saare short links enumerate na karein, iske liye kya karoge?

Sequential IDs expose mat karo: random codes (KGS / hash) use karo ya base-62 encoding se pehle counter permute karo. Scanners ko slow karne ke liye per IP GET rate-limit karo, aur dhyaan rakho ki private links (password-reset ya document links) sirf obscurity pe na tike hon.

10× traffic pe kya hoga?

Peak pe redirect QPS → ~450K. Stateless redirect tier horizontally scale karo, Redis cluster badhao (hot set ab bhi chhota), chhote TTLs ke saath zyada traffic CDN pe dhakelo, aur DB ko hot path se mostly bahar rakho. Writes (~4.6K/s) sharded store ke liye ab bhi aasaan.

55 TB kaise store karoge?

KV store (DynamoDB/Cassandra) ya sharded MySQL/Postgres mein code se shard karo, har shard ~1–2 TB → ~30–60 shards, har ek 3× replicated. Har access primary key se point lookup hai, toh yeh perfectly partition hota hai.

Random 7-char code banake seedha insert kyun nahi karte?

Yeh bina hash ke Approach A hai. Kaam karta hai: 3.5 T possible codes aur maan lo 200 B used ke saath random code ke taken hone ka chance ~6% hai — toh kabhi-kabhi retry, do baar shaayad hi. Insert pe unique constraint lagao aur conflict pe retry karo. Space bharne ke saath yeh bigadta hai, isliye aage chalke 8 chars pe jaane ka plan rakho.

docs.title: Practice
docs.text:
Practice 1 — Alag scale ke liye code length

Company-internal shortener roz 50K links banata hai aur hamesha rakhta hai (maan lo 30 saal). Base-62 mein kitne characters chahiye? Base-36 (lower-case + digits) mein?

Solution. 50K × 365 × 30 ≈ 548 M codes. Base-62: 62⁵ ≈ 916 M ✓ → 5 chars. Base-36: 36⁵ ≈ 60 M ✗, 36⁶ ≈ 2.2 B ✓ → 6 chars.

Practice 2 — Encode karo

ID 11157 ko alphabet 0-9a-zA-Z se base-62 mein badlo.

Solution. 11157 % 62 = 59 → 'X', q = 179; 179 % 62 = 55 → 'T', q = 2; 2 → '2'. Neeche→upar padho: "2TX". Check: 2 × 62² + 55 × 62 + 59 = 7688 + 3410 + 59 = 11157 ✓.

Practice 3 — Cache sizing

Pichle mahine ke 20% links ko 80% clicks milte hain. Har cache entry overhead ke saath ~300 bytes. Kitna cache?

Solution. 40 M × 30 = 1.2 B links/mahina × 20% = 240 M entries × 300 B ≈ 72 GB → jaise 3 × 32 GB Redis nodes (+ replicas).

docs.title: Revision checklist
docs.text:
• Do APIs likh sakta hoon aur 301 vs 302 ko product trade-off ki tarah samjha sakta hoon.
  • Assumptions se QPS, storage, code length aur cache size nikaal sakta hoon.
  • Hash + collision resolution, ID → base-62, aur key-generation service pros/cons ke saath samjha sakta hoon.
  • Haath se number ko base-62 encode kar sakta hoon aur pata hai sequential codes problem kyun hain.
  • Shortening aur redirect flows cache-first bana sakta hoon.
  • Custom aliases, expiry, analytics aur abuse prevention discuss kar sakta hoon.

Aage: 09 · Web Crawler

docs.title: 09 · Web Crawler Design karo
docs.text:
⏱ 45 min read 🔥 Queueing, dedup aur politeness ki soch test karta hai Book: Chapter 9

TL;DR

  • Crawler baar-baar: URL lo → download → parse → content dedupe → links nikaalo → filter → URLs dedupe → enqueue. Yeh web graph pe BFS hai.
  • Dil hai URL frontier: front queues priority decide karti hain (kaunse pages zyada important), back queues politeness enforce karti hain (har queue mein ek host, same host ki requests ke beech delay).
  • robots.txt ki izzat karo (cached), DNS cache karo (slow hai), crawlers ko geographically baanto, chhote timeouts rakho.
  • Content ko fingerprints/hashes se dedupe karo (near-duplicates ke liye SimHash) aur URLs ko Bloom filter / hash set se.
  • Spider traps (infinite URL spaces), redundant/bekaar content se bacho, aur pages ko fresh rakho — jitna badalte hain utna recrawl.

docs.title: Intuition: akhbaar ke stringers
docs.text:
Socho ek akhbaar desh ka har local notice board padhna chahta hai. Woh stringers ko shuruaati addresses ki list deke bhejta hai. Har board pe woh notices ki photo lete hain, likhe hue naye addresses note karte hain, aur office ki to-visit list mein jod dete hain. Rules:
